#6027. Chase Freedom Unlimited Review: No Annual Fee & 1.5x Points Everywhere

The no annual fee Chase Freedom Unlimited® is one of Chase’s most compelling cards for everyday spending, especially if you’re willing to put in the effort to maximize value. The card offers 3% cash back (or 3x points) on dining, 1.5% cash back (or 1.5x points) on everyday spending, and there are ways to get significantly more value than that.

I don’t want to bury the lede — if you collect Chase Ultimate Rewards points and use any personal Chase card other than the Chase Freedom Unlimited for your everyday spending, you’re not doing it right. The catch is that there’s a learning curve to using this card — for some people this will just be a good card, while for other people this will be an amazing card.

This post is my in-depth Chase Freedom Unlimited review, so let’s take a look at all the details of the card, starting with the very basics.

Link: Learn more about the Chase Freedom Unlimited®

Before I get into my detailed Chase Freedom Unlimited review, let me summarize some of the basics:

Here are my thoughts on the main Chase Freedom Unlimited pros and cons:

The Chase Freedom Unlimited is part of Chase’s “Freedom” card portfolio, and is an excellent complement to any of Chase’s cards earning Ultimate Rewards points. Before diving into all those details, let’s look at the Freedom Unlimited’s welcome bonus, eligibility, and fees, since those are obviously major factors people consider when applying for cards.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited currently has a welcome bonus whereby you can earn $200 cash back (20,000 points) after spending $500 within the first three months.

On the surface, points can be redeemed for one cent each, but you can potentially get a lot more value than that, as these points can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I value those at 1.7 cents each.

It’s worth mentioning that the Chase Freedom Unlimited comes with an introductory APR offer that breaks down into two parts: purchases and balance transfers. Enjoy 0% Intro APR for 15 months from account opening on purchases, then a variable APR of 18.49% - 27.99%.

For balance transfers: Enjoy 0% Intro APR for 15 months from account opening on balance transfers, then a variable APR of 18.49% - 27.99%.

These intro APR periods can be useful, but just make sure you pay off your entire balance before the offer ends. Otherwise, you’ll be stuck paying a high interest rate, which defeats the purpose.

Eligibility for the Chase Freedom Unlimited is unrelated to eligibility for any other Chase cards, so you could earn the bonus on this card and the Freedom Flex Card, etc. The Chase Freedom Unlimited is not available to those who currently have the card, or those who have received a new cardmember bonus on the card in the past 24 months.

Chase’s general credit card application rules, such as 5/24, generally apply, though that rule isn’t necessarily consistently enforced anymore.

There’s not a published credit score you need to get approved for the Freedom Unlimited, though I’d hope to have a score in the good to excellent range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited has no annual fee, which is unbeatable. You can also add authorized users to the card for no fee, so you can accrue rewards for their spending as well as your own. Obviously that’s a major upside of the card.

While the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a fantastic card for purchases within the United States, it does have 3% foreign transaction fees, so I don’t recommend using this card abroad.

If you’re looking for a great card with no foreign transaction fees, consider the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) or Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more).

The Chase Freedom Unlimited has an awesome rewards structure, which not only includes an excellent return on everyday spending, but also includes some valuable bonus categories.

Before we get into this, note that in each case the percentage cash back can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points, at a rate of one cent per point. I’ll talk more below about how that’s possible, but that’s really how you maximize value with the card.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 5% cash back on travel purchased through Chase Travel℠ (or potentially 5x Ultimate Rewards points). Purchases made outside the Chase travel portal will earn 1.5% cash back (or 1.5 Ultimate Rewards points per dollar).

The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 3% cash back on dining, including takeout and delivery (or potentially 3x Ultimate Rewards points). This is great for a no annual fee card, as this essentially makes this one of the best credit cards for dining spending.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 3% cash back at drugstores (or potentially 3x Ultimate Rewards points). This is an awesome bonus, since drugstores isn’t a category where you otherwise see many cards offering bonuses.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 1.5% cash back on everyday spending (or potentially 1.5x Ultimate Rewards points). The 1.5% cash back return isn’t that exciting, given that other cards offer 2% cash back. What is valuable, however, is the ability to earn 1.5x Ultimate Rewards points per dollar spent, as there’s no better Chase card for everyday spending.

Personally I value Chase points at 1.7 cents each, so to me the card offers the equivalent of a 2.55% return on everyday spending.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 1.5% cash back on everyday purchases, and 3-5% cash back in select bonus categories. On the surface, those rewards are really straightforward, as you can redeem the cash back for statement credits, a direct deposit in an eligible Chase account, for gift cards, or for travel booked through Chase Travel. You can even redeem your cash back toward Amazon purchases, though at the rate of 0.8 cents per point (so please don’t redeem that way!!).

However, if you’re looking to earn travel rewards, you can get a significantly better return on spending than that.

While the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a cash back card, in reality the card earns Ultimate Rewards points. You earn 1.5x points per dollar spent, and then ordinarily each point can be redeemed for one cent cash back. That’s how Chase arrives at the valuation of 1.5% cash back with the card.

However, if you have the Chase Freedom Unlimited in conjunction with another card that earns “premium” Ultimate Rewards points, then you can do significantly better. These cards include the following:

With one of those cards, suddenly your points are much more valuable. Transferring points between cards is easy and can be done online. You can learn more about that process in this post.

Personally, the way I like to redeem Ultimate Rewards points is to transfer them to airline and hotel partners, which include the following:

This can be the best way to redeem points toward premium travel experiences. If you want to redeem for first or business class travel or stay at luxury hotels, this option is for you.

One thing worth noting is that Chase recently devalued the transfer ratio to World of Hyatt to 4:3 for the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Ink Business Preferred. You’ll need the Chase Sapphire Reserve or Sapphire Reserve for Business to get the full 1:1 transfer rate with Hyatt. No matter which of these cards you have, points transfer to all other partners at a 1:1 ratio.

While my favorite way to redeem Ultimate Rewards points is through the transfer partners, there are also ways to redeem Chase points at an advantageous rate toward travel purchased through Chase Travel℠:

That increases the value of your points by up to 100% right there.

For a no annual fee card, the Chase Freedom Unlimited offers a solid selection of benefits and purchase protection, which cardmembers will certainly appreciate. Let’s cover those, though let me of course remind everyone to always check the guide to benefits for the latest terms & conditions associated with these perks.

With the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you can extend the time period of your United States manufacturer’s warranty by an additional year on eligible warranties of three years or less. If you’re making an expensive purchase, this could save you a huge amount.

With the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you’re covered for new purchases for 120 days against damage or theft of up to $500 per item, and up to $50,000 per account. Again, this makes the card an excellent option for everyday spending, given how much money purchase protection can save you.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited will reimburse cardmembers up to $1,500 per covered traveler and $6,000 per trip on prepaid fares that can’t be cancelled if your trip is canceled or cut short by sickness or another covered reason. More premium cards have more travel protections and higher limits, but this is pretty nice for a no annual fee cash back card.

With Chase Credit Journey, you get unlimited access to your credit score and more. This is free for Chase customers, including those who have the Chase Freedom Unlimited.

One of the great features of Chase cards is access to Chase Offers, which provides savings on purchases with all kinds of retailers. This program has saved me a significant amount of money, and having the Chase Freedom Unlimited gives you access to that.

With the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you get six months of complimentary DashPass membership. Note that when you take advantage of this, you’ll be auto-enrolled in a paid DoorDash plan after six months, at the rate of $9.99 per month. So you’ll want to be sure you cancel before the complimentary plan expires, assuming you don’t value it.

DoorDash DashPass gets you $0 delivery fees and lower service fees on eligible orders through both the DoorDash and Caviar delivery platforms. You get up to $10 off non-restaurant DoorDash orders each quarter, up to $40 a year. This perk is currently valid for enrollment through December 31, 2027.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited qualifies for 2% cash back on Lyft purchases made through the app — a 0.5% bonus on top of the card’s standard earning rate. This promotion runs through September 30, 2027.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited is one of the all around best cards for everyday spending. It’s a credit card that I have, and it’s one that I think is worth holding onto.

If you’re in the Chase Ultimate Rewards ecosystem and put everyday spending on cards in the portfolio, then picking up the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a must. However, the key is to have the card in conjunction with a card earning premium Ultimate Rewards points — the Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Ink Business Preferred, or Sapphire Reserve for Business — so that you’re really maximizing your rewards.

I’d also like to look a bit more closely at the best strategy to take with the Chase Freedom Unlimited.

I can’t emphasize enough that having the Chase Freedom Unlimited in conjunction with either the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve is probably the best card combo you can have. That’s because not only can you combine the benefits of the two cards, but this greatly increases the value you get from your Freedom Unlimited points.

For example, if you have the Sapphire Reserve and Freedom Unlimited:

There are currently two Chase Freedom products you can apply for — the Chase Freedom Unlimited and Chase Freedom Flex® Credit Card (learn more). Both cards have no annual fees, so what are the major differences between the cards?

The cards otherwise have overlapping bonus categories, like offering 3x points on dining and drugstores, etc. Personally I think both cards are worth having. If I could just have one, though, I’d probably choose the Freedom Unlimited, since it’s better for everyday spending.

Chase has two “Unlimited” cards — the Chase Freedom Unlimited and the Ink Business Unlimited® Credit Card (learn more). These cards are very similar — both have no annual fee, and both offer 1.5x points (the Ink Unlimited on business purchases). So, what’s the difference?

Other than those differences, the two cards are very similar. I have both of these cards (yes, I have a lot of Chase credit cards).

The Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more) is probably the closest competitor to the Chase Freedom Unlimited, regardless of whether you’re looking to earn points or cash back.

The Citi Double Cash also has no annual fee and offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back after you pay for that purchase in the form of ThankYou points. So you’ll earn 2.0 cents back on the dollar, rather than 1.5. Furthermore, in conjunction with a card like the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more) or Citi Strata Elite® Card (learn more), you can move points at the best possible ratio to travel partners.

Since I value Citi ThankYou and Chase Ultimate Rewards points roughly equally, this could also be an attractive card for everyday spending.

The reason some people may still prefer the Freedom Unlimited is because of the Chase Ultimate Rewards ecosystem. On top of that, the Freedom Unlimited has bonus categories, which the Citi Double Cash doesn’t have.

The Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card (learn more) is another competitor to the Chase Freedom Unlimited, and it has a few pros and cons. The Capital One VentureOne has no annual fee and no foreign transaction fees, and offers a minimum of 1.25x miles per dollar spent.

Those miles can either be redeemed for one cent each toward a travel purchase, or they can be moved to Capital One’s airline and hotel transfer partners.

The downside of the VentureOne is that the rewards structure isn’t as lucrative, on the surface. The upside, though, is the lack of foreign transaction fees, and the ability to directly transfer points to airline and hotel partners, even without having another card.

So which card is better depends on whether you’re looking for a “one size fits all” no annual fee card, or want to use it as part of a larger strategy.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited is a key card to maximizing your overall Chase Ultimate Rewards strategy, in conjunction with the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited has no annual fee, and offers a minimum of 1.5x points per dollar spent. Let me make my advice as concise as possible here: if you have the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve, then you absolutely should have the Freedom Unlimited, so you’re maximizing your return on everyday, non-bonused Chase spending.

#6026. Park Hyatt Dubai Reopening In 2027, After Full Renovation: First Look At New Rooms

In May 2026, the Park Hyatt Dubai closed, so that it could undergo a renovation. That was probably good timing, given the massively decreased demand we’ve seen for travel to the United Arab Emirates this year.

The hotel is expected to reopen in the spring of 2027, and the first pictures of the new room product have just been revealed, as flagged by rota. Let’s take a look at those details, but first, I’d like to briefly talk about why I have a soft spot for this property.

Dubai is a city that has endless hotels at all price points. I don’t have a single favorite hotel in the city, as it really depends on so many factors, from what you’re willing to pay, to the area you want to be in, to how big you want the property to be, to what you value most.

After all, the concept of hotels in Dubai is a bit different than in other cities, given that alcohol is primarily only served at restaurants in hotels. As a result, hotels are very much the social scenes, both for guests and non-guests.

Anyway, the 223-key Park Hyatt Dubai opened all the way back in 2005, and I can’t count how many times I’ve stayed there over the years, going back to just shortly after it initially opened. There’s a lot to like about the resort:

To me, it very much fits into the category of being an urban resort, in terms of being a destination, while having ideal proximity to things.

There are just some hotels where you have such fond memories for a variety of reasons, and for me, the Park Hyatt Dubai is definitely among them. In part, maybe it can’t help but remind me of the “good old days” of redeeming Alaska Mileage Plan miles for Emirates first class.

Remember being able to redeem 100,000 Alaska miles for Emirates first class from the US to basically anywhere in the world via Dubai, with a free stopover there, and no carrier imposed surcharges? And that says nothing of being able to fly from the US to London with a stopover in Mauritius, and layovers in Dubai twice on a one-way (IYKYK). 😉

In May 2026, the Park Hyatt Dubai closed for the main portion of its renovation. If you go to the hotel’s website, you’ll see the following restrictions:

Park Hyatt Dubai is currently closed as it embarks on a defining transformation – a moment of careful, considered renewal in pursuit of an experience that is more refined, more exceptional, and more authentically itself than ever before.

Behind the scenes, every space and every detail is being thoughtfully elevated – honouring the quality and commitment to luxury hospitality that have made this sanctuary on Dubai Creek so singular, while reimagining the perfect stay.

With an anticipated reopening date of Q1 2027, we look forward to sharing more updates as that moment approaches, and to welcoming you back to a truly reawakened Park Hyatt Dubai. Because true elegance never stands still. It evolves – and in evolving, it is perfected.

As it currently stands, the hotel is accepting reservations for stays as of April 1, 2027. Now, the hotel is accepting villa reservations as of January 1, 2027, but that’s separate from the main part of the hotel. We’ve known that everything about the hotel would change, but not many renderings had been shared up until now.

One thing is for sure — there’s no denying that the rooms were in desperate need of a renovation, given that they hadn’t undergone any meaningful updates since the hotel first opened.

The hotel has now updated its website to show pictures of the new room product, and you can find those renderings below. I’m conflicted here. On the one hand, this looks much more luxurious than the old setup. On the other hand, the design just looks incredibly generic, and like it could be anywhere. I wish we’d see a little more sense of place.

On the plus side, the hotel’s grounds and general bones otherwise have a decent sense of place, so I hope that’s at least maintained with the updates.

Leadership at the Park Hyatt Dubai had been vocal about how they hope to charge much higher rates after the renovation. I think it’s safe to say that’s all up in the air, based on how the situation in the Middle East evolves. As things currently stand, I see entry level rates in April that are $600+, while I see the lowest rates in summer at $350+.

I feel like that pricing is very much on the optimistic side, but again, there are lots of moving parts with the Middle East hotel situation.

The Park Hyatt Dubai closed in May 2026, and is currently undergoing a full renovation. In recent years we’ve seen a new beach club and new dining outlets added, but this should be by far the most meaningful update since the hotel opened over two decades ago.

The hotel is expected to fully reopen in April 2027, and the new rooms look like a huge improvement in terms of how luxurious they are. However, there’s definitely a sense of place missing, so I’m curious how the overall design evolves.

What do you make of the changes coming to the Park Hyatt Dubai?

Booking a table can be the least exciting part of a night out. However, the platform you use to do it can now earn you rewards worth anything from a few cents to a delicious discount on your bill.

OpenTable, DoorDash, Seated and now Resy all reward you for dining out, though each takes a different approach. OpenTable awards its own points, DoorDash issues credits for future orders, Seated offers rewards that can be redeemed for gift cards and Resy awards American Express Membership Rewards points.

As with your favorite coffee chain's loyalty program or a food delivery app subscription, the best option depends on where, how often and how much you eat out. Whichever you choose, you'll generally still earn rewards on eligible restaurant purchases when paying with a dining credit card, making your meal even sweeter.

In this guide, we compare what each program earns, what those rewards are worth and the fine print to watch so you can decide which one deserves a seat at your table.

*Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations.

Related: This overlooked dining program is one of the most generous and gets you $25 off your very first meal

OpenTable Regulars is free to join, and you'll earn 100 dining points for each reservation you book directly on OpenTable while signed in to your account and then complete. Reservations made through restaurant websites or third-party booking partners generally don't qualify. Points are posted only after you've dined, so canceled reservations and no-shows earn nothing.

Some restaurants in the program also offer bonus-point reservations worth 500, 750 or even 1,000 points at certain times. To find them, turn on the "bonus points filter" under special features in the OpenTable app.

Once you have at least 1,000 points, you can redeem them in the app's "Rewards" section at the following rates for U.S. members:

As for the redemption rate you'll get for each, they're:

That means a standard 100-point reservation is only worth 80 cents toward a future meal, and you'll need 20 of them to earn a $16 dining credit, which isn't very rewarding.

Dining credits work at participating OpenTable restaurants (look for the "Dining Credit Accepted" filter). After you redeem your points, you can add the credit to a reservation, which provides a digital Mastercard you can use toward eligible bills. Experience credits work similarly but only apply to certain prepaid experiences, such as prix-fixe menus and cocktail classes. Dining credits expire 12 months after you redeem them.

If you complete six reservations on OpenTable within 12 months, you'll then unlock Gold status for a year. Gold members get priority notifications when tables open up, a three-month complimentary Uber One trial for eligible new or returning members who do not have an active subscription and access to "Gold Tables," which promises harder-to-book tables at more than 500 participating restaurants in over 50 U.S. cities.

OpenTable also partners with Chase, Uber and Visa. Uber One members can book Uber One Exclusive Tables, eligible Visa cardholders can access tables and special events through the Visa Dining Collection and select Chase cardholders get exclusive tables and statement credits (more on that below).

Make sure you're actually turning up for your bookings, though. OpenTable will close your Regulars account and cancel all your points if you record four no-shows within 12 months. Your points also expire after 12 months of inactivity or after 3 years from the date you earn them, whichever comes first.

Related: Earn even more rewards when dining out with OpenTable

DoorDash is best known for delivery, but reservations are now available in select cities across the U.S., Australia and Canada. Its current market page lists 17 U.S. cities, plus Melbourne and Sydney in Australia and Toronto and Vancouver in Canada.

Rather than earn points, you earn promotional DoorDash credits when you book and complete an eligible reservation in the DoorDash app or on its website. The amount is shown before you book and now varies by restaurant, reservation time and membership status. Current U.S. listings commonly advertise $5 in credits, while some times display $10 or $12. Not every reservation earns a credit.

Credits are posted after you've paid for your meal and can be used toward eligible future DoorDash delivery or pickup orders. They typically can't be used to pay for taxes, fees or tips, expire six months after they're issued unless the offer says otherwise, have no cash value and can't be used to buy gift cards or alcohol.

Since the reward is a fixed amount, you don't earn more rewards for a higher food bill. A $5 credit is a 5% return on a $100 dinner but about 1.7% on a $300 tasting menu. A $10 credit would deliver returns of 10% and about 3.3%, respectively. That makes DoorDash Reservations especially appealing for smaller restaurant bills if you already use DoorDash.

DashPass members can earn more on eligible reservations, plus access exclusive prime-time tables and discounts on Lyft Black rides. However, the elevated reservation reward is no longer a simple fixed $2 boost across every listing, so check the offer shown before booking rather than assuming your membership guarantees a particular amount.

Check the restaurant's cancellation policy when you book. Late cancellations and no-shows may incur fees set by the restaurant, and DoorDash says excessive no-shows can result in suspension of your access to reservations.

Outside its reservation cities, DoorDash's "Going Out" tab also lists in-store offers at certain restaurants, with DashPass members earning extra rewards for repeat visits in some locations.

Related: Your complete guide to Chase and DoorDash

What is unique about this program is that you don't need to book through Seated: You link an eligible credit or debit card, then tap to activate the restaurants where you want to earn a higher reward rate before paying with your linked card. Eligible rewards then post automatically, with no receipts to upload.

Activations last until the end of the calendar month, and you can activate up to 25 restaurants per month (plus any monthly specials). Seated's app also advertises 5% back at participating restaurants, even without an activation, provided you open the app at least once every 30 days. Higher reward rates generally require activation, so it's worth activating your favorites at the start of each month and checking the offer terms in the app.

Rewards vary by restaurant but can be up to a generous 35% back, with the rate shown on each restaurant's page before you choose to activate it. Rewards are calculated on your eligible food-and-beverage total before tax and tip, so a restaurant offering 10% back would earn you $10 in Seated rewards on a $100 meal. Since each diner earns on the share they pay with their own linked card, splitting the bill doesn't cost anyone their individual rewards.

Seated partners with more than 2,500 restaurants in certain U.S. markets. Availability varies by city and neighborhood, so check the app for participating locations and current rewards before dining, rather than relying on a fixed city list.

You can then redeem Seated rewards for gift cards in the app's store tab, with available brands to choose from including Airbnb, Amazon, Dunkin', Nordstrom, Sephora, Starbucks, Target and Uber. Because rewards can then be converted to eligible gift cards at face value, TPG values them at $1 per $1 redeemed, provided you choose a brand you'd spend with anyway and meet any minimum redemption requirement.

The catch is that Seated rewards may expire after more than 30 days without qualifying account activity, so check the app's activity and expiration rules rather than assuming opening it alone preserves your balance. Seated also says its rewards can't be combined with other restaurant promotions, third-party deals (such as those available through Groupon) or discount offers.

If you're a new member, keep an eye out for a first-meal bonus offer of up to $10 through an eligible referral link or promotional offer, though this is not guaranteed for every member.

Related: Rove adds dining and in-store rewards in major platform expansion

Resy Rewards takes a different approach than the other three programs. It does not issue a stand-alone Resy currency. Instead, eligible U.S. American Express cardmembers earn 4 additional Membership Rewards points per dollar spent at participating restaurants, on top of the points their enrolled card already earns.

To participate, you must first enroll an eligible U.S. Amex card that earns Membership Rewards points in the Rewards tab of the Resy iOS app.

You must then book a participating restaurant through the Rewards tab, complete the meal and pay with the enrolled card. Merely dining at a participating restaurant or booking it through another part of Resy will not trigger the 4 bonus points per dollar. At launch, the program is only available through the Resy iOS app, meaning Android users cannot currently use it.

The initial New York City list includes restaurants like Carne Mare, Le Crocodile, Hearth, Kiko, Opto and Le Pavillon. American Express plans to expand Resy Rewards to additional U.S. cities and select Tock venues in 2027.

On a $100 eligible restaurant purchase, Resy Rewards would provide 400 bonus Membership Rewards points. Based on our valuation of 2 cents per Membership Rewards point, that is an estimated $8 in value (or an 8% return) before accounting for the card's standard earning rate.

Related: Don't overlook Resy: How to maximize dining experiences and save money with this Amex benefit

Because OpenTable and DoorDash reward reservations with a fixed amount while Seated pays a percentage of your bill and Resy pays a fixed number of points per dollar spent, the best option depends on how much you spend. Here's a comparison for $100 in food-and-drink purchases (before tax and tip), assuming the advertised offers apply and you can use the full value of the DoorDash credits on a later order:

If you spend $200 on a meal rather than $100, the OpenTable and DoorDash rewards stay the same, while the Seated rewards as a percentage of spending will quickly increase. Resy would also double to 800 bonus points, worth an estimated $16 with TPG's valuation of Amex points.

Seated can be the most rewarding option for larger restaurant bills, especially at restaurants that offer higher reward rates. However, its value depends on the percentage offered. DoorDash's fixed credits may still provide you with a better return on smaller bills or at restaurants that offer lower Seated rewards. Resy provides a consistent 8% estimated return from its bonus points — but only at its small number of participating restaurants at launch.

Related: The dining statement credits that save me over $1,000 every year

Certain restaurant purchases can also earn credit card rewards in addition to the benefits provided by these platforms. Combining these apps with a card that earns bonus points at restaurants can be an easy way to double-dip and earn more rewards. Some of the best options currently available include:

But it gets even better. Savvy diners keen on maximizing their rewards may be able to triple-dip by booking an eligible Sapphire Reserve Exclusive Tables restaurant through OpenTable and paying with their Sapphire Reserve card. Doing so will allow you to earn OpenTable Regulars points plus 3 Chase Ultimate Rewards points per dollar spent on the eligible dining purchase, even if you later receive a statement credit. Qualifying purchases at participating restaurants can also trigger the separate Sapphire Reserve dining credit, worth up to $150 per half-year.

Related: How to double-, triple- or even quadruple-dip on dining rewards

Resy Rewards offers a strong, straightforward points return at participating restaurants. However, the program is launching at only a handful of New York City restaurants and is available through the Resy iOS app, so most diners will not be able to use it regularly yet.

Seated has the highest potential return for larger dining bills. A restaurant offering 15% back would earn you $30 in rewards redeemable for gift cards on a $200 dinner, while a 35% offer would earn $70. Know, though, that higher rates generally require monthly activation, and you'll need to keep your rewards account active.

DoorDash Reservations can still be the best option for smaller meals when the booking carries a strong credit. A $10 or $12 reward can beat percentage-based programs on a modest check. The catch is that rewards now vary by reservation, availability is limited to select cities and the credits are less useful if you rarely order through DoorDash.

OpenTable Regulars is the least rewarding of the four for most standard reservations, with a 100-point booking worth just 80 cents at the best U.S. redemption rate. Still, it is the most broadly available of the four in the markets where its Dining Points program operates and offers useful extras, including bonus-point tables, Gold Tables and a three-month Uber One trial for eligible Gold members. Select Chase cardholders can also receive statement credits at eligible restaurants.

There's no single best dining rewards platform for everyone, as the right choice depends on where you live, how much you spend and how often you dine out.

Resy offers a compelling points return at participating venues, but its limited launch footprint and lack of an Android app make it more of a promising option than an everyday solution right now.

Seated can deliver the biggest reward on an expensive meal, while DoorDash can be particularly rewarding on a smaller bill when the booking offers a decent credit.

As for OpenTable, it remains the most broadly available of the four in the markets where its Dining Points program operates. Its nationwide coverage, Gold perks and Chase partnership make it worth considering, especially when you travel.

Since all four cost nothing to join, you may as well sign up for them all so you are ready the next time you want to book a meal. Just remember to show up for reservations or cancel within the restaurant's deadline, as no-shows can cost you points, credits or even access.

That's some food for thought before your next night out.

#6024. United Airlines’ Most Frequent Boeing 777-200 Flights In 2026

The Boeing 777-200 entered service in 1994 and was primarily aimed at US domestic airlines; the 777-200ER followed in 1997 with more of an international focus. The 777-200ER extends the range from around 5,240 nautical miles to 7,065 nautical miles (depending on mission profile). These are workhorses for United's transatlantic routes, as well as some inter-hub routes, routes to Hawaii, and select destinations in East Asia. The type is aging, with older examples struggling with fuel efficiency compared with modern aircraft, although as paid-off aircraft, they also offer much lower capital expenses for United.

Here is what to know about where United Airlines is flying its Boeing 777-200/ER fleet in 2026, according to data provided by Cirium, a data analytics company. The flight data below is for the full 2026 calendar year and includes both the 777-200 and the 777-200ER, as Cirium lacks distinct aircraft codes for the sub-variants. The data is also for the full year, even if the 777s were replaced with other aircraft partway through the year on the routes.

United Airlines operates a fleet of 74 Boeing 777-200/ER airliners, of which Planespotters.net lists 61 as active and 13 as parked. The overall age of the fleet is rapidly aging and is now 27.5 years old. These include 19 Boeing 777-200s, with the remainder being 777-200ERs. United is the launch customer and the largest operator of the 777-200, with the fleet being configured for domestic routes. The 777-200ER includes four examples with domestic configurations. The remainder of the 777-200ER is configured for international operations.

According to Planespotters.net, United has not divested any of its 777-200/ERs since 2005, after eight examples had been transferred to Indian and Brazilian operators. The oldest example in United's service is registered N777UA and was delivered in 1995, making it 31.5 years old. The youngest member of the family is registered as N27015 and was delivered in 2010. It is now around 26.7 years old.

Cirium's data shows United is operating the 777-200/ER from its six main hubs: San Francisco (12,591 route-pair flights), Newark (6,635), Houston (5,549), Washington Dulles (4,900), Denver (3,059), and Chicago O'Hare (1,165). Adding these directly would result in double counting of 1,759 flights due to flights between the hubs. For the full year, United is expected to operate a total of 32,140 flights with the aircraft carrying a total of 9.6 million seats.

Chicago O'Hare sees the fewest flights with United's Boeing 777-200/ERs. Its most frequent pairings (outbound and inbound) are to its other hubs, including 373 flights on the San Francisco pairing (1,604 nautical miles), 309 flights on the Los Angeles pairing (1,517 nautical miles), and 236 flights on the Denver pairing (772 nautical miles). The year is also seeing 174 flights from Chicago to Mexico's Cancun (1,255 nautical miles).

Denver is to see 3,059 United 777-200 family flights carrying 1.1 million seats. Its leading routes by distance and frequency are to Hawaii, including Honolulu (1,226 flights at 2,929 nautical miles), Maui (744 flights at 2,872 nautical miles), and Kona (238 flights at 2,894 nautical miles). That is a total of 2,248 flights on Denver's Hawaii pairings and 73% of the airports' total United 777-200/ER operations.

Other routes include Chicago O'Hare, already mentioned above (236 flights), Houston (225 flights), Cancun (174), as well as a limited number of flights to San Francisco, Orlando, and Washington Dulles. In other words, most of United's non-Hawaii paired 777-200/ER flights from Denver are to its other major hubs in the continental United States.

Examining the busy schedule of one of the most distinguished jets in the world's biggest fleet of airliners.

Washington Dulles has 4,900 United 777-200/ER operations, with the bulk of these being transatlantic flights to Western Europe. Dulles' most frequent pairing is with London Heathrow at 996 flights, followed by Germany's Frankfurt (744 flights). The next most common pairing is transpacific to Tokyo Haneda, with 728 flights. After that Japanese route, it's back to Europe with the pairings to Paris (656 flights), Lisbon (557 flights), and Rome Fiumicino (492 flights).

Other European pairings include Athens (168), Brussels (126), Barcelona (32), and Zurich (18). Domestic routes are to San Francisco (193 flights) and Los Angeles (136 flights). Most European routes from Dulles average between 3,000 and 4,000 nautical miles, although the route to Athens is considerably longer, reaching 4,492 nautical miles. United Airlines dominates Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD), accounting for roughly 66% to 70% of passenger traffic.

From Dulles, United connects the US capital with various intercontinental destinations in Europe, Asia, and even Africa. Somewhat surprisingly, given the US's strong demographic and cultural connections with South America, the only route to that continent operated by United is to São Paulo with Boeing 767-400ERs. Avianca also operates flights between Bogotá and Washington Dulles. The lack of flights is because airlines concentrate US–South America hubs in southern and coastal gateways (Miami, Houston) with stronger passenger demand.

In Houston, George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) is dominated by United Airlines, while William P. Hobby Airport (HOU) is dominated by Southwest Airlines. At IAH, United boasts around 74.1% of the passenger market share, perhaps more now that Spirit has collapsed. Spirit had around 5% of the market share. From Houston, the most frequent 777-200/ER route is to London Heathrow, whose pairing is seeing 1,397 flights in 2026.

Houston is also a significant gateway to South America, with the next busiest pairing being with Buenos Aires (942 flights). The only other South American destination is Chile's Santiago, with 209 flights. These are United's main routes to South America, meaning they aren't used very heavily in that direction. There are no frequent United 777-200/ER routes to Mexico, the Caribbean, or Central America. This is partly due to many of these destinations being within range of narrowbody aircraft. For example, United operates seven daily A320-family flights between Houston and Mexico City.

The third-busiest pairing is with United's West Coast hub of San Francisco (681 flights), with another 225 flights on the Houston-Denver route and 52 flights on the Houston-Newark route. The other regular routes are transatlantic routes to Germany, with the Frankfurt pairing getting 730 flights in 2026 and Munich getting 580. Munich is the longest route at an average distance of 4,708 nautical miles, followed by Frankfurt, Buenos Aires, London Heathrow, and Santiago — all of which are above 4,000 nautical miles.

Two major US airlines currently operate the Boeing 777.

The airport that hosts the second-most United 777-200/ER flights is Newark Liberty, with 6,635 operations. United Airlines holds roughly 60% to 68% of passenger market share at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), making it by far the airport's dominant carrier and largest hub. It is from Newark that United connects the New York region with much of the world, including many transatlantic destinations in Europe.

Even so, the single busiest city pairing is with San Francisco, with 1,314 flights, while the second-busiest transcontinental pairing is with Los Angeles, with 710 flights. Otherwise, transatlantic routes dominate the list and include Paris (863 flights), Dublin (728 flights), Milan (582 flights), London Heathrow (413 flights), Amsterdam (284 flights), Munich (205 flights), Barcelona (184 flights), and Rome (139 flights).

Other notable city pairings include Tokyo Haneda (593 flights) and São Paulo, Brazil (526 flights). The Tokyo route is notable for being one of the longest routes United is assigning its 777-200ERs, at an average distance of 5,877 nautical miles. Currently, United is operating a daily flight to Tokyo Haneda using its 787-9s, suggesting the 777-200ERs have been pulled off the route. United is also operating 787-9s on the twin Newark-Tokyo Narita route.

San Francisco is by far the busiest hub for United's fleet of 777-200/ERs in 2026, with a total of 12,591 operations. Being located on the West Coast, San Francisco also sees the largest range of destinations, with flights to Asia, Australia, New Zealand, Europe, and domestic destinations within the United States. The busiest pairing is the one mentioned above with Newark Liberty (1,314 flights).

European routes include Frankfurt (1,077 flights), London Heathrow (744 flights), Paris (656 flights), Munich (716 flights), Rome (410 flights), Barcelona (266 flights), Zurich (262 flights), and Amsterdam (238 flights). Routes to East Asia are Tokyo Haneda (730), Beijing (728), Osaka (714), Taipei (690), Seoul (273), and Tokyo Narita (239). Already mentioned above are other hub pairings with Houston, Chicago, and Washington.

San Francisco, along with Denver, is a major hub for flights to Hawaii's Honolulu (794). San Francisco is also the only hub where United's 777-200/ERs are flying to Australia (Brisbane with 524 flights and Sydney with 296 flights) and New Zealand (Auckland with 490 flights). The Sydney route is the longest one of all for United's 777-200ERs with an average distance of 6,447 nautical miles followed by Brisbane at 6,140 nautical miles. New Zealand is a bit closer at 5,665 nautical miles.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

"The overall age of the fleet is rapidly aging..." I'd argue that the rate of aging of the fleet has remained constant since day 1.

#6023. Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

Rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

Zinke’s wife, son, and sister currently serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

In a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he said when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke said.

None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

“While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” said Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Issue One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

“I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” said Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

“Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he said, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

Zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

It marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

The Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with plans to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

Zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services company Halliburton.

Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

Supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a company registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron said.

Since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s company, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which says it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

“We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he said, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

In 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

“If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail said about SEAL PAC's payments.

But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

#6022. Aeromexico 787s Get Makeover With New Business Class, Premium Economy

Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-new business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

I first covered this several days ago, when this was quietly announced at an industry conference, as flagged by Seth Miller at PaxEx.Aero. However, the airline has now released a video on social media with additional details, so I’d like to publish an update to reflect that.

To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet currently consists of 25 planes, including:

Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was announced by the company’s CEO at last week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

The plan is for the 787-9s to get all-new cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats currently on the planes).

The 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the cabins will be updated between 2029 and 2031, so that’s between three and five years from now (and that assumes no additional delays).

We’ll talk more about the new business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

The plane will also have 69% more premium seats than before. Currently, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the new premium economy cabin.

It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

Aeromexico’s new premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

Aeromexico has published the below video about its all-new cabins, which gives you a sense of what we can expect.

A post shared by Aeroméxico (@aeromexico)

For those who don’t want to watch the video, below are some screen grabs.

Side note — is this new, or has Aeromexico been doing a cute tequila service for a long time?!? If I knew Aeromexico was serving shots, I would’ve prioritized the airline much higher on my list of products to review. 😉

While details are otherwise limited, we know that Aeromexico’s new Boeing 787-9 business class suite is from Recaro, as the airline is reportedly the launch customer for this new seat. However, the exact product hasn’t actually been named.

I believe this might be an evolution of the Recaro R7 product (LATAM’s newest 787 business class), which in and of itself was already an evolution of the Recaro CL6720 product (Iberia’s newest A350 business class).

It seems that what was unveiled earlier this year was the new Recaro R7 Horizon concept, which is the same idea, but with upgraded technology and customization.

Aeromexico is planning some big upgrades to its Dreamliners. The Boeing 787-9s will be getting all-new cabins, including new business class suites, plus a premium economy cabin for the first time. There will even be a premium business product in the first row, with the products marketed as Premier One Suites Plus, Premier One Suites, and Premier.

As this happens, the 787-8s will be getting the old reverse herringbone seats from the 787-9s, so that will be a meaningful upgrade as well. You can expect these new cabins to roll out between 2029 and 2031, so unfortunately patience will be required.

What do you make of Aeromexico’s Dreamliner plans?

#6020. New York JFK Terminal 6 Is Almost Open: Airlines & Lounges Moving In

New York Kennedy Airport (JFK) is currently undergoing a $19 billion modernization. While this includes all kinds of updates, the two biggest developments are the opening of two new terminals — we’re talking about Terminal 6 and Terminal One (not to be confused with Terminal 1).

As you’d expect, the opening of both terminals has been delayed, since airport construction rarely runs on time. Per the latest updates, the expectation is that Terminal 6 will open before the end of 2026, while Terminal One will open in the first quarter of 2027.

Along those lines, it’s looking like we might just be days away from the opening of Terminal 6, so I’d like to cover all the details we know.

JFK Terminal 6 is expected to open with a phased approach as of December 2026. To cover the very basics:

The below video of the terminal should give you a good sense of what to expect in terms of the passenger experience, so I’d recommend checking that out.

All things considered, this new terminal moving is awesome, given the quality of terminals at JFK otherwise. For those originating or terminating in New York, this should be ideal. For those connecting to or from JetBlue in Terminal 5, this will also make connections much easier. Meanwhile for a limited number of other passengers, this might make connections a bit more complicated, for cases where airlines are moving away from their partners (like Cathay Pacific moving from American’s Terminal 8 to Terminal 6).

Roughly 17 airlines are expected to eventually operate out of JFK Terminal 6, though that will happen in two phases. Broadly speaking, we’ll see some JetBlue operations move there (since the airline is a core tenant), and on top of that, we’ll largely see airlines move from Terminal 1, Terminal 7, and Terminal 8.

So the expectation is that the following airlines will eventually operate from JFK Terminal 6:

There is still a bit of a mystery as to the order in which airlines will move to JFK Terminal 6. For one, there’s the two phases of the terminal opening, but even within each phase, it won’t fully be overnight.

We know that All Nippon Airways, Cathay Pacific, Condor, Frontier, Lufthansa Group carriers, and TAP Air Portugal, will move in the first phase. Meanwhile we know that Air India will move in the second phase. But for the remainder of the airlines, there’s a lack of certainty on that front.

Now, we’ll see if this sticks, and how accurate it is, but current schedule filings suggest that Condor will start operating out of Terminal 6 as of December 3, while Cathay Pacific will start operating out of Terminal 6 as of December 15 (thanks to Peter_ for flagging this). So it sounds like we could potentially be just over a week from the first airline moving, which would be awesome!

In terms of lounges, we have confirmation that Terminal 6 will have outposts from Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, Aer Lingus, and Air India. Hopefully the new lounges are ready to go as airlines make the move, but I wouldn’t consider that to be a sure thing, given the complexity of airport operations.

The Air India lounge definitely won’t open anytime soon, since the airline is only moving in the second phase. Meanwhile the Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, and Aer Lingus lounges, will hopefully open soon(ish). Of course I’m most excited to see what Cathay Pacific has in store, given its amazing lounge quality.

JFK Terminal 6 is expected to open before the end of 2026, and if current filings are to be believed, the move could happen as soon as early December. It appears that Condor and Cathay Pacific might be among the first airlines to move, so hopefully Cathay Pacific’s new lounge isn’t too far behind. So we’ll mark this as “developing,” but the completion of the first exciting phase of this $19 billion project is imminent.

Are you excited for the new JFK Terminal 6?

#6019. Capital One Venture Card Bonus: 75K Miles + $300 Credit Welcome Offer (Last Chance)

At the moment, the $95 annual fee Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card is offering a phenomenal limited time welcome bonus, making it the ideal time to apply. I’d like to provide an update that this is the last chance to pick up the card with this offer, as it’s expected to be pulled soon.

Not only is this among the best offers we’ve seen on the card, but this is also a reasonably priced travel rewards card that offers long term value, especially for everyday spending.

Link: Learn more about the Capital One Venture Card

The Capital One Venture Card is currently offering a limited time, lucrative, two-part welcome offer, whereby you can earn 75,000 Capital One bonus miles, plus a $300 Capital One Travel stays credit, after spending $4,000 within the first three months.

For context, Capital One miles can be redeemed for a minimum of one cent each, meaning the 75,000 miles will get you at least $750 in value. However, I value the miles at 1.7 cents each based on my latest analysis (see my methodology here), thanks to the value you can get by transferring the miles to travel partners. That means that to me, the 75,000 miles are worth $1,275.

There are lots of great ways to redeem Capital One miles, as they can be transferred to Capital One’s roughly 20 airline and hotel partners. That’s my preferred use of them, as you can get some amazing travel experiences this way.

Partners include programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue, Qatar Airways Privilege Club, Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, and more. These are all programs that allow you to really maximize your points and get outsized value. Just to give a couple of examples of Capital One mileage redemption opportunities:

That doesn’t include the value of the $300 Capital One Travel credit, which posts upon account approval (rather than upon completing minimum spending). The idea is that this can be used for a hotel or vacation rental booking through Capital One Travel in your first cardmember year (in the first 12 months), and it’s valid across one or multiple stays. In other words, you could use it to pay virtually nothing for a $300 hotel stay. All-in-all, I’d say the Capital One Venture bonus is worth up to $1,575.

By my valuation, the current Capital One Venture Card bonus is the best publicly available offer that we’ve seen in over five years, so that makes this the ideal time to apply, and I absolutely wouldn’t wait for a better offer. Quite to the contrary, when this limited time offer gets pulled, it’ll almost certainly be worse.

For context, below is a history of the publicly available bonuses that we’ve seen on the Capital One Venture in recent years.

As you can see, we’ve never seen a publicly available welcome offer of over 75,000 miles, in terms of the mileage component. We have in the past seen $250 travel credits offered along with the miles, and this time around the travel credit is bigger. So offers really don’t get better than this on the card.

When you look at the bonus terms on the Capital One Venture Card, you’ll find the following language:

You are not eligible for this product if you have received a new cardmember bonus for the Capital One Venture card or the Capital One Venture X card in the past 48 months.

As you can see, the card follows a 48-month rule, so you’re not eligible for the welcome bonus on this card if you’ve received a new cardmember bonus on this exact card or on the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (learn more) in the past 48 months.

Other than that, eligibility is unrelated to having any other credit card, and Capital One doesn’t have many consistent restrictions when it comes to getting approved for cards.

The Capital One Venture Card has a reasonable $95 annual fee, and offers a variety of perks beyond the excellent welcome bonus:

While the Capital One Venture Card is awesome, how does it compare to the Capital One Venture X Card, which is Capital One’s ultra premium credit card? The Venture X has a $395 annual fee, so the fee is significantly higher, but it also offers several great perks that should more than justify the annual fee. Among other things, the Venture X offers:

So when it comes to the Capital One Venture vs. Venture X, personally I think the Venture X is an even better value than the Venture. However, I know some people just want to avoid higher annual fee cards in general, so for those people, the Venture could be a better option.

The limited time Capital One Venture Card bonus currently offers 75,000 Capital One miles plus a $300 Capital One Travel credit upon completing minimum spending. This Capital One Venture bonus is significantly better than usual, so if you’re eligible for the card based on the 48-month bonus rule, I’d absolutely recommend applying. This is the last chance, as the offer is expected to be pulled soon.

Anyone plan to pick up the Capital One Venture Card with this great bonus?

As much as I love the holiday season, it's my least favorite time to travel. Flights and accommodations are expensive, airports are at their busiest and winter storms can upend even the best-laid plans.

A credit card can't help your family pack lighter or ensure your flight departs on time. But the right benefits can lessen the sting from some of travel's most predictable pain points.

Here are the cards that can make the biggest difference during a hectic holiday trip, organized by the problem they solve.

Few travel fees are more annoying than paying extra to bring your socks with you — especially now that roundtrip bag fees can feel higher than the cost of the clothes inside.

For a family checking multiple bags, this may be the most immediately valuable benefit on this list. A card with a relatively modest annual fee can pay for itself during holiday travel alone.

Many airline credit cards offer a free checked bag, so start with the airline you fly most.

Higher-fee airline cards often match or exceed the checked-bag benefits shown here.

Many of the same airline cards that waive bag fees also provide priority boarding benefits. On a packed holiday flight, I'll gladly get in line early if it keeps my carry-on out of the gate-check pile.

The $895 annual fee (see rates and fees) offers another way to lower the cost of bags or boarding. Its up to $200 annual airline incidental credit can reimburse eligible expenses such as checked bag and seat selection fees with one selected qualifying airline (enrollment required). This is a useful way for existing cardmembers to absorb a holiday expense.

The (see rates and fees) offers a broader alternative: Its $300 annual travel credit applies automatically to eligible travel purchases, including checked bag fees.

Related: Which airline credit cards offer the best priority boarding perks?

Ever spend more time in airport security than you do on the flight itself? TSA PreCheck, Global Entry and Clear+ earn their keep throughout November and December.

PreCheck provides expedited screening at eligible U.S. airports; Global Entry includes PreCheck and adds expedited processing when returning to the U.S. from abroad; and Clear+ uses biometric identity verification to speed up the document-check step of security (so some travelers use it alongside PreCheck).

And for travelers who frequently cross between the U.S. and Canada, Nexus can speed up passport control.

You don't necessarily need a premium card to get these application fees reimbursed. Options include:

I like this benefit because it works regardless of which airline you're flying and gives you something that's often in limited supply: time. Just apply well before your trip because Trusted Traveler applications take some time to process. You can't open a card on Monday and expect to breeze through security on Friday.

The information for the U.S. Bank Altitude Connect has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

A lounge won't make a delayed flight leave sooner, but a power outlet, snacks and a drink make the wait easier.

These lounge cards offer different benefits:

* Up to 10 visits per eligible Platinum Card, per year to the Delta Sky Club or to Grab and Go when traveling on a same-day Delta-operated flight

I've had all of these over the years, although lately my favorite card for lounge access is the Bank of America Premium Rewards Elite. The card's Priority Pass membership still provides credits at participating airport restaurants, which can be helpful when traditional lounges are full or there's nowhere left to sit.

There's a broader lesson there, too: don't choose a card based solely on how many lounges its network advertises. Check whether your airports have participating locations, whether there are restrictions on when you can visit and if it costs extra to bring your travel companions.

The information for the Bank of America Premium Rewards Elite has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Related: Is the Amex Platinum worth the annual fee?

Some premium-card credits seem easy to overlook until you arrive at midnight with no energy to navigate public transportation and ride-hailing fares are surging.

Food-delivery credits are also surprisingly useful at the hotel. I recently had Uber Eats delivered to my hotel because taking a cranky kid to dinner wasn't my idea of a good time.

For Uber users, both the and stand out. The Gold offers up to $120 in Uber Cash annually (distributed as up to $10 each month), while the Platinum offers up to $200 in Uber Cash annually (up to $15 each month, plus an additional $20 in December) for U.S. Uber rides and Uber Eats orders.

Uber Cash will only be deposited into one Uber account when you add the Amex Gold or Amex Platinum as a payment method and redeem with any Amex card.

Platinum cardmembers can also receive up to a $120 statement credit for an auto-renewing Uber One membership, Uber's paid membership program for ride and delivery savings (enrollment required).

The counters with up to $420 in DoorDash credits (a monthly $15 promo for any eligible order plus two $10 nonrestaurant promos, through Dec. 31, 2029).

Its complimentary DashPass membership (activate by Dec. 31, 2029) also unlocks Lyft Go at no additional cost, allowing you to earn Lyft credits on eligible rides. Separately, Sapphire Reserve cardholders receive up to $10 in monthly Lyft ride credits through Sep. 30, 2027. (You'll need to link your DoorDash and Lyft accounts and claim Lyft Go.)

These credits alone are not reasons to pay hundreds of dollars in annual fees. But they can be genuinely useful when you're otherwise staring down an expensive ride or going to bed hungry.

Hotel timing benefits are especially useful when checkout is at 11 a.m., your flight leaves after dinner and no one wants to tote an overstuffed diaper bag around for six hours while your toddler desperately needs a nap.

There are two ways a credit card can help: through a premium hotel-booking program or automatic hotel elite status.

Those looking for boutique hotel experiences can access The Edit by Chase Travel℠ with their . These bookings provide benefits like daily breakfast for two people and a $100 property credit. When available, early check-in, late checkout and room upgrades are also offered. Cardholders receive up to $500 annually in statement credits for eligible prepaid The Edit bookings (of at least two nights; split into two credits of up to $250 each).

Similarly, cardmembers can receive up to $300 in statement credits biannually (up to $600 per calendar year) on eligible prepaid bookings through Fine Hotels + Resorts, The Hotel Collection and Airbnb Luxe through American Express Travel®.

FHR bookings include guaranteed 4 p.m. checkout, daily breakfast for two and property or experience credits. Room upgrades and early check-in are also offered (subject to availability).

(THC and Airbnb Luxe bookings require a minimum stay of two consecutive nights. Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, FHR bookings will also require at least two nights to qualify for the lodging statement credit.)

These programs can be valuable when a nicer property is already part of the plan or you have annual hotel credits to use. Just don't let a possible upgrade or a few extra hours rationalize a room that costs twice as much as the hotel across the street.

Many hotel credit cards offer complimentary elite status. For example, the $95-per-year (see rates and fees) includes Discoverist status, which comes with 2 p.m. late checkout (when available).

Top-tier Globalist status extends that to a 4 p.m. checkout. The Hyatt card can help you work toward it with five qualifying-night credits each year plus two additional credits for every $5,000 spent.

Related: World of Hyatt Credit Card review: My favorite mid-tier hotel card

Hotel breakfast is one of those expenses that seems harmless until you're buying it for several people for several mornings.

These cards can help lower breakfast costs:

cardmembers can enroll in Hilton Gold status and receive breakfast or food-and-beverage benefits rather than having to apply for a Hilton card separately.

Rental car status is rarely about an upgrade from a sedan to an SUV, especially during a sold-out holiday week. The most valuable benefit is simply getting into a car and leaving the airport while everyone else is still waiting at the counter.

Capital One Venture X cardholders can enroll in Hertz President's Circle status**, which offers benefits including skip-the-line privileges, a wider vehicle selection, potential upgrades and a free additional driver. Meanwhile, the $95 Venture Rewards offers lower-tier Hertz Five Star** status.

cardholders receive Avis Preferred Plus and National Executive status, and cardmembers can enroll in complimentary elite status with Avis, Hertz and National.

In every case, the key is to enroll. Sign up and confirm your status appears in your account before you leave home.

**Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note, enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold Plus Rewards enrollment process (i.e., at hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program, and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply.

Related: How to stack Venture X earning and Hertz elite benefits

These perks are only useful if they are ready when you need them. Before your trip:

Related: 4 things you really need to do now in advance of holiday travel

For holiday travel, the best card isn't necessarily the one with the longest list of premium benefits; it's the one that solves the problem most likely to cost you money or patience. A family checking several bags may save more with a $95 airline card than an $895 premium card, while someone planning a dream trip may want every perk they can get.

Opening an expensive card solely to make one trip less miserable isn't the play here. But if you are already paying a premium annual fee, this is the time to use the benefits you've paid for all year.

Related: 10 real-world tips you need for flying this holiday season
