#6016. Delta Plans Seattle To Singapore A350 Flights, Carrier’s Third Longest Route

We know that Delta has huge growth aspirations across the Pacific, particularly to Asia. It’s an area where Delta has increasingly fallen behind United in recent years, but Delta now hopes to not only catch up, but even beat United. We’ll see what comes of that, and in particular, find out just how costly that growth is.

A few months ago, Delta executives publicly confirmed plans to return to Singapore, a destination that hasn’t been served by the airline since 2019, when that was an intra-Asia tag flight from Japan. Executives also confirmed out of which airport the service would operate. There’s now an additional update, as an announcement about the new route is imminent, which almost certainly points to a fall 2027 launch for the service.

As Delta executives view it, the airline is pretty maxed out in terms of its European potential, and in the long run, they see the most long haul growth potential in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa. So, what kind of expansion should we expect?

Back in August 2026, Delta Chief Commercial Officer Joe Esposito explicitly confirmed that the airline would return to Singapore. What was perhaps most interesting is that he also indirectly confirmed the hub out of which the service would operate — Esposito ruled out that the service could operate out of Los Angeles, so it’s pretty clear that the airline will operate this service out of Seattle (SEA).

That’s also what JonNYC reported in the past, and now we can take that a step further — Delta is holding an event in Seattle in early December 2026, and that’s when the airline is expected to announce the service.

My guess is that we’re looking at a fall 2027 service start, at best. At 8,070 miles, this will be Delta’s third longest flight, after its routes to South Africa, which are from Atlanta (ATL) to Cape Town (CPT) and Johannesburg (JNB).

One certainly wonders if this Singapore route could be operated by Delta’s new Airbus A350-1000s, which will feature an all-new passenger experience. While the plane has great range and per seat economics, the only thing I’d say is that it’s “a lot of plane” for a new market, in terms of the overall capacity (even with the very premium layout).

In both the Seattle and Los Angeles to Singapore market, Singapore Airlines is the only other carrier operating. So competitively there’s not a huge difference in that regard, though Los Angeles is a significantly larger market in terms of demand for Singapore, and for that matter, Singapore Airlines also has more service out of the airport. But perhaps Delta is also looking to beat Alaska to the punch in the Seattle market.

It’s fantastic to see Delta looking to grow its presence in Asia. Point-to-point flying to Asia is a market that United has basically had cornered in recent years, and competition is good for consumers.

It’s amazing to think for how many years Delta basically squandered its Asia advantage. Keep in mind that back in the day, Northwest had a robust Asia network, and after the merger with Delta, we saw that network decreased slowly but steadily, as Delta instead focused on routing everything through Seoul Incheon, and into the Korean Air network. So I’m happy to see a reversal of that strategy.

I also have to say that given Delta’s hubris, it’s kind of fun to see the airline having to increasingly play “catch up,” rather than coming in as the dominant carrier. And I think that very much sums up what’s going on in Asia.

The most basic structural disadvantage that Delta has is that United has a fortress hub in San Francisco (SFO), which is where a large part of its Asia network flies from. That’s fantastic for connectivity, not to mention San Francisco is a very strong market for Asia traffic.

Delta, meanwhile, is taking a split hub approach, flying out of both Los Angeles and Seattle. Obviously Delta is trying to make the best of its situation, but there’s no denying that this is an uphill battle:

It also has to be emphasized that in terms of actually transporting passengers profitably (or at less of a loss), United does a better job at that than Delta, despite its lower overall profitability. Comparing passenger revenue per air seat mile to cost per air seat mile, United is at 16.18 cents vs. 16.46 cents, while Delta is at 17.37 cents vs. 19.31 cents.

Delta is growing quite a bit in Asia at the moment. The airline has already launched flights to Hong Kong, with flights now on sale to Manila and Tokyo Narita. On top of that, Delta is expected to announce a new Seattle to Singapore route within the next two weeks, with a launch likely planned for the fall of 2027.

It’s great for passengers to see more competition across the Pacific, as Delta sure is making up for a lack of effort for years. However, the airline will also have quite the disadvantage compared to United for a long time…

What do you make of Delta’s plans to fly to Singapore?

Re comment about SIN completing a return to all major East Asian cities served by NWA: Let's not forget that Delta also served Bangkok, Busan, and Guangzhou (plus little but important Guam). If Delta is serious about being a major player in Asia and a truly global airline, it needs to return to these cities and add more Asian destinations like Kuala Lumpur and Jakarta. Convincing China Southern to repartner and perhaps join Skyteam (big ask) would be wonderful. China Southern is a 4-star airline but it's planes and service are better than Korean Air, in my experience.

I'm not so sure on the "most americans would book their flight" bit; I think it cuts both ways. My wife is like this. She prefers DL and all things equal she will choose DL out of familiarity, much as your Asians choose Asian carriers for the same reasons, even if she has to connect. I have only recently been able to get her on Asian carriers, and she sees the quality difference - yet it only matters about so much to her. When I am with her she will take the asian carrier because she lets me navigate any bumps - but when I am not, she'd rather fly DL because she knows what she'll get. Most US people have no idea the joys of J on CX or SG. I did a RTW jaunt last year to NZ on CX/SG/ANA. It blew her away. (first time on ANA/CX for me too, even got The Room and in The Pier, wow. SG Suites, well, I fly SG JFK-FRA a lot so at least I had an inkling.) But again, you have to read these boards to know any better; DL marketing makes their J look great too, you have to get stuck on their 767 and get their indifferent crew to know any better, and if you choose DL first, you'll never have a chance to know.Not to mention the hordes of uninformed people who still seem to think SkyMiles are worth something; they aren't on boards like these to know any better, and even then, the world of miles is just too complicated for them to want to spend attention on it. They go with the flow and that flow for them is on a US carrier.I would agree with your doubt the corporate aspects are drivers, for the reasons you say. It's all the premium leisure travelers. You see all the time in WSJ and others how Americans are traveling more and willing to spend on it and they want a piece of it. Will it be enough to make huge profits? Perhaps not, but it might be enough to pay for itself, and then they get the marketing aspects. And if you want to expand, you have to take these kinds of gambles, or you end up like AA. It's not like they can't afford the risk.

The real question that has not been discussed is how soon DL intends to start SIN, presumably from SEA as Ben surmises. Given that DL execs have said that DL will return to SIN, completing a return to all of the major E. Asia cities DL served prior to the NRT hub pulldown except for Beijing, it would seem that DL’s return to SIN will be within 18 months and likely sooner; even a winter 2027 SIN start would support a route announcement within the next couple months. A start in mid-summer 2026 would support an announcement within weeks. The A350-1000s are supposedly on track for delivery in the early spring of 2027 and likely will enter service in early summer. 35K deliveries for 2027 are still heavily loaded in the back half of 2027 but the first 20 of what will certainly be a fleet larger than 20 will be coming pretty quickly so DL’s route growth will accelerate in the latter half of 2027, into 2028 and into 2029 when the next wave of 359s and 339s start coming. Even w/ DL’s stated intent to return to SIN on top of MNL and HKG, DL has not given firm plans for starting LAX-ICN and JFK-ICN, both of which DL is certain to fly on its own metal. DL execs also just said that they want to fly AJS-ICN on their own metal which means that there will be non-hub or focus city routes from ICN to the US flown by both DL and/or KE. DL execs said their TPAC expansion would be aggressive and they are proving that they intend to add new routes quickly.

Am I the only one who thinks SQ is vastly overrated? Well trained flight attendants but mediocre food and outdated BC seats. Also, their contract lounge in SEA is forgettable. I think Delta’s newer planes are competitive.

Imagine being forced to fly Delta instead of SQ on this ultra long haul seated in economy with Dim Sum, TravelinPenis, and 0000 for company...pure Hell.

Last week, Rove introduced personalized shopping offers with earning rates of up to 25 miles per dollar spent. Now, Rove has launched Rove Status, a four-tier status program. Here's what you need to know about the new Rove Status program, including qualification requirements and perks available to members at each tier.

Here are the annual requirements for each Rove Status tier:

The qualification period each year runs from Jan. 1 to Dec. 31, and status earned based on qualifying activity in 2026 will be valid through Dec. 31, 2027. Qualifying miles and transactions are based on the purchase date for shopping, dining and gift cards and on the date the travel is completed (i.e., the date of the final flight on a ticket or the hotel checkout date).

You can earn qualifying miles and qualifying transactions through paid Rove travel bookings, shopping, dining and gift card purchases. Miles earned through paid miles boosts, tier-based shopping bonuses and elevated earning rates count toward status, while flat bonus promotions, referrals, partner transfers and miles not associated with a paid transaction do not.

Rove is retroactively counting transactions and qualifying miles throughout 2026. So, head to your Rove account to see your qualifying miles, qualifying transactions and elite status tier.

Related: The best ways to redeem Rove miles, including flights to Europe from just 88 miles

Each Rove Status offers some valuable perks:

I'm particularly excited about the free-night benefit for Rove Rate award stays. Rove Rate bookings aren't loyalty-eligible, but this is a great benefit for travelers who don't have elite status with a hotel loyalty program or are staying at properties outside their preferred program. Rove clarified that each free-night credit is based on the stay's average nightly rate, though charges due at the property (such as resort fees or local taxes) aren't included.

Rove also confirmed that this benefit can apply more than once during the same stay. For example, a Diamond member redeeming miles for a six-night stay would receive two nights free.

Parental pause lets eligible new parents extend their status expiration by up to 12 months. And the additional transfer bonus on top of eligible existing promotions for Platinum and Diamond members is additive, not multiplicative. So, a 40% transfer bonus would become a 50% bonus for Platinum members and a 55% bonus for Diamond members.

Related: Maximize your rewards by getting a fourth or fifth night free on award stays

Rove Status offers several potentially valuable benefits to members who already earn heavily on the platform. The free-night benefit on Rove Rate award stays is the standout, especially since it can apply multiple times on longer stays, while Platinum and Diamond members can also receive larger bonuses during eligible partner transfer promotions.

Since Rove is retroactively counting qualifying activity from throughout 2026, it's worth checking your account to see whether you've already earned status or are close to reaching the next tier.

#6014. Now hiring: Staff to power Democrats’ probes

Ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February. He will be a key player in leading oversight efforts next year — and so will Democratic staff. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.

That means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

Arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, said the pressure will be on from day one.

“Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan said.

Still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she says of staffers headed there for the first time.

The work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can quickly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

Some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

There’s every indication that pressure will continue in the new Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, said Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

“Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres said.

Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the new year, if they haven’t already, Melendres said.

“There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he said.

In addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the new Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

“For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a big part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres said.

Lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a big difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

For instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

Standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

Those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, said he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the new Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

“But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin said.

The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”

Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

“The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren said.

Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal said he won’t be deterred by the letter.

“There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” said Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”

“I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

“We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries said.

Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

Beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet announced — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

In prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

“I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin said.

#6013. American Airlines Will Displace Philadelphia Pilots—Blames Union For Rejecting A321XLR Staffing Deal

American Airlines says a “significant number” of Philadelphia pilots will be displaced from their current positions after their union’s board rejected a deal on staffing Airbus A321XLR flights to Europe. The airline is reopening a domestic Airbus pilot base and shrinking its international one for June 2027. That can change which trips pilots fly, the schedules they can hold, and potentially their commutes. American is blaming the union for rejecting what it calls an “objectively better path forward.” Aviation watchdog JonNYC shares the company’s message to pilots: When we publish our June 2027 vacancy announcement tomorrow, you will see that we are reopening a PHL A320 Domestic base (Section 17.S.1) and reducing the PHL A320 International base. This will, unfortunately, result in the displacement of a significant number of pilots from the PHL A320 International base (Section 17.D). The airline says it had agreed to a term sheet with the Allied Pilots Association, completed the contractual language, and expected a signed side agreement. The union’s board rejected it November 6. November 22, 2026 The dispute connects two things that don’t seem related at first blush: which pilots get lucrative extra trips, and how American makes sure its new Europe flights have qualified crews. I wrote in April about American’s new Aggressive Pick-up system. It gives pilots access to last-minute open trips on a first-come, first-served basis. Those trips can come with premium pay. Junior pilots gained access to flying that senior pilots had been accustomed to getting. That helps American cover flights and creates opportunities for junior pilots. It also takes income opportunities away from senior ones. The fight over “fixing” the system is largely about who gets the money. The union wanted seniority to count in those awards, along with priority for pilots based where the trip originates and fixes to message delays. American saw something it could trade for. The union’s September 18 negotiating update described the exchange: Pilots would get changes to the extra-trip pickup system. Seniority and in-base priority would play a role, and the parties would address problems with how trip opportunities reached pilots. American would get changes to monthly schedule bidding for its Europe operation. The airline wanted Atlantic Europe qualifications incorporated into its Preferential Bidding System, the software that builds pilots’ schedules. The memo calls this an “A320” issue because that’s the pilot fleet category, which includes the A321XLR. A pilot qualified to fly an Airbus domestically still needs the additional qualifications for this oceanic flying. “AE” means Atlantic Europe here. American needs the pilots qualified for those trips to be available to fly them. A large pool of Airbus pilots doesn’t solve the problem if the pilots who can fly to Europe are awarded domestic schedules, while pilots who haven’t completed the necessary training are entitled by seniority to the Europe trips. The union’s October 27 update explained limited changes to bidding rules for Airbus pilots in categories with current or future XLR Europe flying, paired with seniority protections in the qualification training plan. Pilots discussing the proposed agreement described the risk of qualified pilots being directed toward Europe trips or reserve assignments they wouldn’t otherwise choose, while unqualified pilots could lose access to trips their seniority would otherwise let them bid. Pilots across the airline could benefit from changes to extra-trip awards, while the scheduling concessions would fall on the Airbus pilots affected by Europe flying. And restoring seniority in those awards helps senior pilots at the expense of junior pilots who’ve been quick enough to claim the trips. There’s a distributional problem inside the union. Some pilots argued that the union was giving up too much: American needed flexibility for an important expansion, and the union should obtain more for it in broader contract negotiations. The union had also filed a grievance over American’s failure to implement the Line Check Pilot program from the 2023 agreement, so training capacity was already a point of contention. American’s response is to divide the Philadelphia Airbus pilot group. It will reopen a domestic category and reduce the international category. A smaller, separately staffed international group gives American a more manageable pool to qualify and schedule for Europe. That avoids needing the rejected changes to keep the existing group together. The airline is using the base and displacement provisions in its contract. Under the pilot contract, reductions in a bidding category generally displace the least senior pilots, with provisions for more senior pilots to volunteer. Displaced pilots exercise their seniority into other positions, which can set off further displacement. A pilot can remain in Philadelphia on the same aircraft family but have access to different trips and schedules. Others’ choices could mean changing bases, aircraft, or commuting arrangements. American’s 2027 Europe plans include Philadelphia–Porto beginning March 28 and Philadelphia–Vienna beginning May 6, both using the A321XLR. I toured the aircraft before it entered service. It has just 155 seats: 20 business class suites, 12 premium economy seats, and 123 in coach. American can offer a premium product across the Atlantic with fewer seats to fill than on a Boeing 787. That opens up routes and seasons where a larger aircraft is harder to justify. I liked the operational benefit of making last-minute trips available to pilots willing to fly them. Getting an airplane out on time has value, and senior pilots losing priority for some extra income standing in the way of operational reliability has been a key cause of Delta’s operational meltdowns. Management calls the rejected deal objectively better. That depends on whose schedule and income you’re counting. A senior pilot seeking premium trips and a Philadelphia Airbus pilot facing restrictions on monthly bidding are different pilots gaining benefits and incurring costs. Much of a union’s role is trading off the same or better total benefits between its members, rather than getting the best possible overall deal from the employer. And union politics play an important role, especially as the American Airlines pilots union remains in the midst of drama over whether it will stay independent or join the larger Air Line Pilots Association. That can change which trips pilots fly, the schedules they can hold, and potentially their commutes. American is blaming the union for rejecting what it calls an “objectively better path forward.”

Aviation watchdog JonNYC shares the company’s message to pilots:

When we publish our June 2027 vacancy announcement tomorrow, you will see that we are reopening a PHL A320 Domestic base (Section 17.S.1) and reducing the PHL A320 International base. This will, unfortunately, result in the displacement of a significant number of pilots from the PHL A320 International base (Section 17.D).

The union wanted seniority to count in those awards, along with priority for pilots based where the trip originates and fixes to message delays. American saw something it could trade for. The union’s September 18 negotiating update described the exchange: Pilots would get changes to the extra-trip pickup system. Seniority and in-base priority would play a role, and the parties would address problems with how trip opportunities reached pilots. American would get changes to monthly schedule bidding for its Europe operation. The airline wanted Atlantic Europe qualifications incorporated into its Preferential Bidding System, the software that builds pilots’ schedules. The memo calls this an “A320” issue because that’s the pilot fleet category, which includes the A321XLR. A pilot qualified to fly an Airbus domestically still needs the additional qualifications for this oceanic flying. “AE” means Atlantic Europe here. American needs the pilots qualified for those trips to be available to fly them. A large pool of Airbus pilots doesn’t solve the problem if the pilots who can fly to Europe are awarded domestic schedules, while pilots who haven’t completed the necessary training are entitled by seniority to the Europe trips. The union’s October 27 update explained limited changes to bidding rules for Airbus pilots in categories with current or future XLR Europe flying, paired with seniority protections in the qualification training plan. Pilots discussing the proposed agreement described the risk of qualified pilots being directed toward Europe trips or reserve assignments they wouldn’t otherwise choose, while unqualified pilots could lose access to trips their seniority would otherwise let them bid. Pilots across the airline could benefit from changes to extra-trip awards, while the scheduling concessions would fall on the Airbus pilots affected by Europe flying. And restoring seniority in those awards helps senior pilots at the expense of junior pilots who’ve been quick enough to claim the trips. There’s a distributional problem inside the union. Some pilots argued that the union was giving up too much: American needed flexibility for an important expansion, and the union should obtain more for it in broader contract negotiations. The union had also filed a grievance over American’s failure to implement the Line Check Pilot program from the 2023 agreement, so training capacity was already a point of contention. American’s response is to divide the Philadelphia Airbus pilot group. It will reopen a domestic category and reduce the international category. A smaller, separately staffed international group gives American a more manageable pool to qualify and schedule for Europe. That avoids needing the rejected changes to keep the existing group together. The airline is using the base and displacement provisions in its contract. Under the pilot contract, reductions in a bidding category generally displace the least senior pilots, with provisions for more senior pilots to volunteer. Displaced pilots exercise their seniority into other positions, which can set off further displacement. A pilot can remain in Philadelphia on the same aircraft family but have access to different trips and schedules. Others’ choices could mean changing bases, aircraft, or commuting arrangements. American’s 2027 Europe plans include Philadelphia–Porto beginning March 28 and Philadelphia–Vienna beginning May 6, both using the A321XLR. I toured the aircraft before it entered service. It has just 155 seats: 20 business class suites, 12 premium economy seats, and 123 in coach. American can offer a premium product across the Atlantic with fewer seats to fill than on a Boeing 787. That opens up routes and seasons where a larger aircraft is harder to justify. I liked the operational benefit of making last-minute trips available to pilots willing to fly them. Getting an airplane out on time has value, and senior pilots losing priority for some extra income standing in the way of operational reliability has been a key cause of Delta’s operational meltdowns. Management calls the rejected deal objectively better. That depends on whose schedule and income you’re counting. A senior pilot seeking premium trips and a Philadelphia Airbus pilot facing restrictions on monthly bidding are different pilots gaining benefits and incurring costs. Much of a union’s role is trading off the same or better total benefits between its members, rather than getting the best possible overall deal from the employer. And union politics play an important role, especially as the American Airlines pilots union remains in the midst of drama over whether it will stay independent or join the larger Air Line Pilots Association. #6012. Three Women Argued Over An American Airlines Delay—Then Got Kicked Off And Blamed For Missed Connections

Three women were escorted off an American Airlines flight from Knoxville to Charlotte on Saturday night after an argument with a flight attendant, costing passengers their connections. Retired Kansas City Royals vice president Mike Swanson called them “princesses” in his story of the November 21 incident. The plane was already late getting to Knoxville, before the women could have held it up. Mike Swanson’s video of passengers being escorted off his flight — November 22, 2026 In a follow-up on Twitter, Swanson explains that one woman complained to the flight attendant about how long it had taken to board. The flight attendant told the women they were ready to depart and to fasten their seat belts. The exchange escalated: The three got loud and the attendant wasn’t having it. They gone. Video shows two women walking toward the front with their belongings, followed by a uniformed officer. Swanson says three were removed. He says several passengers missed connections in Charlotte. Yelling at a flight attendant because your flight is late is a lousy strategy for getting home sooner. Last year I wrote about an American Airlines passenger who told a flight attendant to shut up during the safety demonstration and wound up getting the plane sent back to the gate. It appears this was American Eagle flight 5675 on November 21, operated by PSA Airlines using a Bombardier CRJ900, registration N557NN. That flight was scheduled to leave Knoxville at 8:04 p.m. and arrive in Charlotte at 9:28 p.m. It took off at 9:57 p.m. and landed at 10:34 p.m. Charlotte is a particularly bad place to lose your connection buffer. I’ve written about how arriving on a regional jet can mean waiting for a valet checked bag and then making a long walk from Concourse E. A late evening arrival also leaves fewer chances to recover with another flight that night. However, that aircraft’s inbound flight from Charlotte didn’t land in Knoxville until 8:35 p.m. It was supposed to have arrived at 7:34 p.m. The plane was still arriving 31 minutes after it should have departed on its next trip. The women weren’t responsible for the original delay. Removing them may have used up whatever chance remained to make his connection, but we don’t whether he’d have made it without the argument. Retired Kansas City Royals vice president Mike Swanson called them “princesses” in his story of the November 21 incident. The plane was already late getting to Knoxville, before the women could have held it up.

Mike Swanson’s video of passengers being escorted off his flight — November 22, 2026

In a follow-up on Twitter, Swanson explains that one woman complained to the flight attendant about how long it had taken to board. The flight attendant told the women they were ready to depart and to fasten their seat belts. The exchange escalated:

The three got loud and the attendant wasn’t having it. They gone.

Video shows two women walking toward the front with their belongings, followed by a uniformed officer. Swanson says three were removed. He says several passengers missed connections in Charlotte.

Yelling at a flight attendant because your flight is late is a lousy strategy for getting home sooner. Last year I wrote about an American Airlines passenger who told a flight attendant to shut up during the safety demonstration and wound up getting the plane sent back to the gate.

It appears this was American Eagle flight 5675 on November 21, operated by PSA Airlines using a Bombardier CRJ900, registration N557NN. That flight was scheduled to leave Knoxville at 8:04 p.m. and arrive in Charlotte at 9:28 p.m. It took off at 9:57 p.m. and landed at 10:34 p.m.

Charlotte is a particularly bad place to lose your connection buffer. I’ve written about how arriving on a regional jet can mean waiting for a valet checked bag and then making a long walk from Concourse E. A late evening arrival also leaves fewer chances to recover with another flight that night.

However, that aircraft’s inbound flight from Charlotte didn’t land in Knoxville until 8:35 p.m. It was supposed to have arrived at 7:34 p.m. The plane was still arriving 31 minutes after it should have departed on its next trip.

The women weren’t responsible for the original delay. Removing them may have used up whatever chance remained to make his connection, but we don’t whether he’d have made it without the argument.

I'm not one to tell you to rush into applying for a credit card just because there's a limited-time offer. After all, there's virtually always an increased bonus available somewhere.

But when a card I've personally used and recommended for years adds hundreds of dollars in extra value to its welcome offer, that's something I want to make sure you don't accidentally miss out on.

And that's exactly what's happening with the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card.

Right now, the card is offering 75,000 bonus miles after you spend $4,000 on purchases in the first three months, plus a limited-time $300 Capital One Travel stays credit to use on eligible hotel and vacation rental bookings during your first cardholder year.

That's at least $1,050 in potential travel value if you redeem the miles at 1 cent each toward eligible travel purchases and use the full $300 credit. And with just a low $95 annual fee, it's a compelling offer on a card that earns two miles per dollar on everyday purchases.

But here's the catch: Capital One has confirmed that this limited-time offer is ending soon.

Apply now for a limited-time offer on the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card: Earn more than $1,000 in travel bonuses with a limited-time $300 Capital One Travel stays credit, plus earn 75,000 bonus miles once you spend $4,000 on purchases within the first 3 months of account opening.

Here's why I think this is an offer worth considering before it disappears.

The Venture Rewards Card has maintained its $95 annual fee since its introduction, even as its benefits and welcome offers have evolved.

And right now, its welcome offer is among the highest-value publicly available offers we've seen on the card in recent years.

Redeeming the 75,000 bonus miles at 1 cent each toward eligible travel purchases would give you $750 in value. Add the limited-time $300 Capital One Travel stays credit, and you're looking at up to $1,050 in combined travel value. Talk about an excellent return for a $95 annual fee.

And if you're willing to transfer those miles to airline and hotel partners, TPG's November 2026 valuations put the miles at approximately $1,388 — bringing the total potential value, including the $300 credit, to up to $1,688.

But since Capital One has already told us this offer is ending soon, I'd expect that your days to get the $300 Capital One Travel stays credit as part of the bonus are very limited, so i'd suggest to act soon to take advantage of the bonus.

Related: Capital One miles: How to get maximum value when redeeming miles

One of my unwritten rules of earning points and miles is to never settle for earning just 1 point or mile per dollar spent. Sure, it's better than earning nothing, but why not get more out of your everyday purchases?

That's one of the reasons I've recommended the Capital One Venture Rewards Card for years. It earns at least 2 miles per dollar on every purchase, without having to keep track of rotating bonus categories or juggle multiple cards.

Not to mention, most other cards in its price range can't beat that earning rate.

TPG values Capital One miles at 1.85 cents each, meaning that earning rate represents a potential 3.7% return toward travel when you maximize the value of your miles through transfer partners.

That's an excellent return for a card with a $95 annual fee, especially if you don't want to have to juggle multiple cards to maximize every purchase.

Related: 7 types of purchases you should make with your Capital One Venture Rewards card

Another reason I've long liked the Venture Rewards card is that it offers both straightforward and more advanced ways to redeem miles.

You can keep things on easy mode and simply redeem them at 1 cent each to cover eligible travel purchases made with the card. That means you can book flights, hotels, rental cars, train tickets, or other qualifying travel purchases exactly how and where you want and then use your miles to offset those charges.

Since miles are worth 1 cent each when redeemed that way, a $600 travel charge put on the card would take 60,000 miles to offset. I've redeemed Capital One miles this way over the years, and I appreciate having that flexibility.

But when you want to stretch your miles further, transferring them to Capital One's airline and hotel partners (and periodic transfer bonuses) can unlock some excellent redemption opportunities.

Award availability varies, and taxes and fees may apply. But having both redemption options is what makes Capital One miles so appealing, whether you're new to points and miles or have been collecting them for years.

Related: Capital One airline and hotel transfer partners: How to maximize your miles

I'm a huge advocate for finding ways to spend less time waiting in airport security lines. That's why I think Global Entry and TSA PreCheck are two of the most useful travel programs to consider.

Global Entry applications are $120 and include TSA PreCheck benefits. And this $95-per-year card will cover that application fee once every four years, which is just another way it outperforms its annual-fee weight class.

Here's a tip: If you already have Global Entry or TSA PreCheck, you can use the card's application fee credit for a family member or frequent travel companion by charging their application fee to your card.

Related: These cards can get you free Global Entry or TSA PreCheck for less than $100 in annual fees

If you're looking for a travel rewards card with a low annual fee can comfortably meet the $4,000 minimum spending requirement in three months and are eligible for the welcome bonus, I'd strongly consider the Capital One Venture while this limited-time offer is still available.

I especially like it for travelers who want to earn transferable miles without having to manage multiple bonus categories.

On the other hand, if you are unlikely to use the $300 Capital One Travel stays credit or would need to spend more than normal to earn the bonus, this offer may not be the right fit.

TPG Tip: This card frequently offers new approved cardholders the option to use a virtual card before a physical card arrives, which could help if you have holiday shopping coming up soon.

Related: Are you eligible for the Capital One Venture Rewards' welcome bonus?

I've been recommending the Capital One Venture Rewards Card for years because it makes earning and redeeming valuable travel rewards simple, so even if you're not a points and miles expert, it's an easy winner.

The current welcome offer makes an already compelling card even more appealing, particularly if you're hoping to take 2027 trips with points and miles.

Between the 75,000 bonus miles and limited-time $300 Capital One Travel stays credit, there's more than $1,000 in potential travel value on the table, even before you start exploring how to stretch your miles further with transfer partners.

Capital One has confirmed that this offer is ending soon, and I  don't want you to wait too long if you're hoping to grab one of the highest public welcome offers we've seen on this card in years. If the card fits your spending habits and travel goals, now's the time to consider applying.

#6009. Latino Democrats celebrate midterm gains, with warning for party

California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, here at a 2020 news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center, is the chair of BOLD PAC. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.

But California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.

“Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said Sánchez, who leads the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

Failure to address rising costs and push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda could once again scramble the political calculus and spark another realignment in two years, said House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California.

“While Latinos shifted towards Democrats and … gave us this mandate as a party, Democrats must continue to earn their trust, not just every two years, but every single day,’’ he said.

Leaders of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus joined newly elected Latino members on Tuesday for a news conference to celebrate the recent wins and the role the group played in securing the House majority for Democrats. The caucus will boast 55 members in the next Congress, its largest roster ever, according to Sánchez.

BOLD PAC, the caucus’ campaign arm, invested heavily in Latino candidates this year, including in primaries.

California Rep. Salud Carbajal noted that BOLD PAC raised more than $18.5 million this cycle, which helped candidates leverage outside money.

Working-class majority-Latino districts in South Texas, Arizona and California were among the areas that provided Democrats with their biggest wins. Democrats capitalized on voter dissatisfaction over rising costs, the very issue that helped Trump and the GOP make significant gains among Hispanic voters just two years earlier.

But the wins weren’t limited to districts with sizable Latino populations.

Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who flipped a swing seat in Nebraska, credited BOLD PAC for playing a key role in her win.

“Yes, there are Latinos in Omaha, and those Latinos actually helped decide this race,’’ she said. “BOLD believed in me as a candidate, but they also believed in our community.”

Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who came to politics after a successful career as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, flipped a redrawn South Texas border district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

“A lot of people feel like they don't belong to either party. But there's one thing about Latinos is we belong to each other,’’ Pulido said. “It's very hard to be a Latino right now in this country. … I expect to see us united, more united than ever, because it's a tough time right now.”

Several of the winning candidates deployed novel strategies to reach voters. Pulido famously began performing at quinceañeras after his Republican opponent dismissed him as a performer.

Colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, who flipped a battleground district north of Denver, attended World Cup and Broncos watch parties. “If people don't hear our message, then it doesn't matter,’’ he said.

The candidates “met those voters where they were,’’ Sánchez said. “They went into those communities and interacted in a very real and meaningful way. That's something I think that strategists or consultants don't always get. It's not just about pumping out lots of television commercials.”

Amid those successes for Latino Democrats, Florida, home to one of the largest Latino electorates in the country, was a different story. Republicans held all three majority-Latino districts in the Sunshine State, though former news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, came within half a percentage point of unseating GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in a district that backed Trump by 15 points in 2024.

BOLD PAC did have a victory to celebrate in Florida, with Rep. Darren Soto, the deputy chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, narrowly prevailing in a district that Republicans redrew as one that no longer had a Latino majority.

“The redistricting wars ended up failing because of the investment by BOLD PAC,’’ Soto said.

#6008. American Airlines Loses O’Hare Gate Appeal—But United’s Plan To Drive It Out Of Chicago Is Failing

American Airlines just lost its appeal to undo Chicago O’Hare’s gate reshuffle. But it’s already bought two gates from Spirit, earned back gate space through its own growth, and survived United’s effort to push it out of Chicago. The airline’s position is stronger than when it sued, and judges haven’t finally decided whether the city broke its contract. The new ruling upholds the refusal to issue a preliminary injunction. The question of whether Chicago took American’s gates too early, after promising to give the airline a chance to grow into additional space first still hasn’t been resolved. I still think American has the better argument about the contract. I’ve also been skeptical from the beginning that they’d get an injunction, since money damages seemed possible. The November 19 appellate decision fits that distinction, although the trial judge’s preliminary reading of the contract was unfavorable to American. The judge accepted that Chicago made American an explicit promise The dispute goes back to the 2018 airport lease. United was getting gates freed up by Delta’s move to Terminal 5. American objected to widening United’s advantage, and Chicago agreed to three additional gates on the north side of the L concourse extension. The lease called for gate assignments following an attached map, with those assignments remaining in place for at least twelve months. American’s argument was that it needed to actually receive the promised capacity before that protected period could run. Otherwise United could grow using its additional gates while American waited for its own, and then the city would use the unequal flying to take gates away from American. The way gates work at Chicago O’Hare is that prior flying determines future gate space (or, technically, ‘linear frontage’). That’s the problem I identified when American first filed its lawsuit. The timing was part of the bargain that got American to support the redevelopment agreement in the first place. And the trial judget accepted that the city and American had agreed to tie the process to the three additional gates becoming operational: For purposes of this motion, that much—the Court has no doubt—was the deal. His position, though, is that the city’s fingers were crossed, suggesting that the explicit written commitment didn’t make it into the final lease, or at least that American couldn’t establish that it had: The language identifies completion of the Terminal 5 expansion and an airline’s relocation there as the triggers. It doesn’t separately name completion of American’s three gates. The additional gates appear on the map as common use space, which the city controls, rather than space reserved for American’s preferential use. The lease says it’s the complete agreement. The judge treated its language as unambiguous and excluded the earlier negotiations as a way to add a condition to it. American’s last additional gate became operational March 14, 2025. Under its reading, the protected year therefore ran through March 2026, and the next redetermination could begin April 1, 2027. Chicago instead treated the protected period as having begun in December 2023, allowing redistribution in 2025. The city’s reading is silly. The map is part of the signed agreement. Requiring the city to deliver the capacity shown there before starting a year of protected assignments doesn’t require inventing a promise outside the contract. And designating a gate common use doesn’t explain how a gate that isn’t operational can fulfill a promise intended to let an airline ramp up flying. Why American lost the injunction appeal The appellate court assumed American could satisfy the initial requirements for an injunction and still concluded that the harm from blocking the gate changes justified denying one. It was reviewing whether the trial judge abused his discretion, NOT deciding the contract dispute from scratch. American’s problem was that it didn’t establish losing the gates would destroy its Chicago hub. It planned to operate the same number of flights using fewer gates, with more flying at less attractive times and less room to recover from delays. That could cost money, make operations worse and harm passengers but it made the injury look measurable. That was my original point – that this would be a case for future damages rather than an injunction. Meanwhile, the other airlines had planned schedules around the redistribution. United projected more than 2,000 cancellations if it were blocked. That number was overblown but the court accepted that changing the arrangements would disrupt passengers, other airlines, and airport construction. And the expectation that American would win gates back in the next allocation (which it did) undercut the argument that it faced an irreversible decline. Timing hurt American, too. Chicago announced the redistribution in February 2025. American sued in May but didn’t request preliminary relief until July. By the September hearing, the October gate changes were imminent and preparations were well underway. American argued that the city shouldn’t get to invoke the hardships from correcting an agreement they deliberately broke. The appeals court rejected that approach because it saw a reasonable dispute over what the contract meant. In my view, Chicago (intentionally) muddied the contract issue enough to make it less clear. This decision doesn’t end American’s lawsuit. It upholds the denial of a preliminary injunction. The contract claims and potential damages are still unresolved. The court rejected the argument that implementation of the gate changes had made the appeal moot, since a court could still order an effective remedy. United’s strategy ran into the airport’s actual capacity Chicago seemed strongly inclined to help its hometown airline. United’s headquarters are valuable to the city, especially with rumors of a move to Denver hanging over the relationship. My coverage of the gate dispute even generated an angry phone call from Chicago “shadow mayor” Jason Lee. United saw a chance to turn American’s slow recovery from the pandemic into a permanent retreat. American had retired too many aircraft and couldn’t rebuild everywhere at once. Fewer Chicago departures meant fewer gates, which could make future growth harder. United CEO Scott Kirby tried to create pressure by talking up American’s Chicago losses and getting financial analysts to question why it should stay. United then announced additional flying on the morning of American’s earnings call, practically writing the questions for them. This was strategic flying. United clearly didn’t want all of that additional capacity. It wanted invesors to believe that any growth would be matched, so American couldn’t improve its gate position and would just lose more money trying. Kirby told analysts United would add “as many flights as are required” to protect its gate count. Then the Federal Aviation Administration intervened. The airport couldn’t handle the schedules airlines were filing, especially with construction constraining movement on the ground. Its summer order capped scheduled arrivals and departures at 2,708 per day from May 17 through October 24. The government used approved summer 2025 schedules as its baseline. It rejected rewarding airlines for filing unrealistic 2026 schedules to improve their negotiating position. United’s much larger proposed buildup didn’t entitle it to preserve that bigger share while forcing American to shrink. The government effectively called United’s bluff. The cap limited American, too, but it protected the existing competitive balance against United’s attempt to overwhelm it with additional flights. American had also grown enough during 2025 to earn back gate space in October’s redistribution. The returned space amounts to roughly three narrowbody gate equivalents. Separately, American acquired Spirit’s G8 and G10 gate leases for $30 million, which I was first to report. That reduces the practical stakes of this appeal, but it still seems that Chicago broke its agreement to benefit United. American needs Chicago to rebuild the business Kirby claims American loses so much money in Chicago that it should leave. Some version of those losses are real, created in part by the undersized schedule it had been flying. But the size and meaning of the losses get overstated. It requires assigning headquarters overhead to the hub that doesn’t disappear if the hub closes. And American would lose connecting traffic and credit card customers if that happened, too. American needs to be relevant in the largest markets where people spend heavily on cards. Retreating from Chicago would make AAdvantage less valuable to Chicago customers, and make its Citibank cards harder to sell and less attractive to spend on. Attributing credit card revenue to the customers and markets that generate it produces a different picture than spreading that revenue across flights throughout the network. That’s why Chicago belongs alongside American’s efforts to rebuild Los Angeles as gates return after construction, and its plans to bring Alaska Airlines into its Atlantic and Pacific joint ventures. They’re working to regain relevance in the largest spend markets in the country. The Chicago fight has also given employees something to rally around. In the post-earnings employee meeting I covered in January, Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper called United the “common enemy” and made it out to be a battle for loyalty and credit card performance. He reported roughly 20% growth in loyalty enrollments, card acquisitions, and local market share over the preceding nine months. Gary Leff is one of the foremost experts in the field of miles, points, and frequent business travel - a topic he has covered since 2002. you almost think DL decided to get out of the central terminal and into terminal 5 not just to avoid the costs of the rebuild but also to set up this catfight between AA and UA.

It is also certain that AA failed to look down the road to realize it needed to protect its ORD gates – many of which it did not use because the aircraft were repositioned to its failed AUS experiment. But the judge is correct that the City of Chicago made enough promises and put them in writing that AA does have the basis for the case to keep going.

UA has failed at not only pushing AA out of ORD – AA’s revenue rehab efforts are going well enough that they can afford to selectively invest in what strategically matters – but also in preventing UA from building a megahub that it dominates as DL does at ATL and AA does at DFW and to a lesser extent CLT. The competitive environment at ORD is obvious from average fares that are $100 lower than DL gets at MSP and DTW and over $50 less than AA gets at DFW and DL gets at ATL. ORD is just a financial drag for both AA and UA.

this could have turned out much worse for AA but they have what they need to fight at ORD.

During my time living in the Chicago area from the 1980s through the late 2010s, I first started flying mostly with American. They were the first airline where I got a free family trip, mostly thanks to matching a promotion Midway Airlines ran. I was never a frequent enough traveler to keep my miles active, and they would frequently expire. In my later years in Chicago, I flew more on United, as it had better international options than American. AA didn’t fly to Paris, it’s flights to Tel Aviv were not as convenient, and their Asian options were limited. This put nearly all of my flying on United. I was almost never more than Silver, as all my flying was in the cheap seats.

To capture more passengers, AA needs more international flights from Chicago to both Europe and Asia, and they need more airplanes, and likely the new international terminal to provide more international gates. The international flights could bring them more relevance for both local travelers and connecting travelers to those flights. And this will cause those travelers to take more AA domestic flights, where the bread and butter of revenue comes from, as well as drive more revenue.

I don’t understand why Kirby uses a competing airline’s profitability as a rationale for trying to force them out of a market. He made similar comments when DL initiated, or reinitiated their HKG route.

Remaining in an unprofitable market is the airline’s and their Board’s decision.

Kirby loves press coverage but his ongoing rants only further hinders his credibility.

Perhaps his time would be better invested in improving his customers’ experience at the service level. An extensive route network is only one component of an airline’s reputation.

This sentence shows a complete lack of understanding of Americans financials as they lose north of $1 billion in Chicago in 2026.

“The airline’s position is stronger than when it sued, and judges haven’t finally decided whether the city broke its contract.”

@”Gary No Math” actually it’s that I can do actual math, and the billion dollar claim is fuzzy math https://viewfromthewing.com/united-wants-american-airlines-out-of-chicago-ai-backs-its-1-1-billion-loss-claim-by-inventing-2-8-billion-in-costs/

#6007. American Airlines Passenger Admits Taking Business Class Pillows—The Airline Calls It A Favorite Confession

An American Airlines passenger confessed to taking home two pillows from international business class. Their husband sleeps with one every night and can’t sleep without it. The second pillow is a backup. American told them it was delighted the pillows had found a loving home. That’s a very different reaction from United Airlines, which told flight attendants to stop passengers from taking its Polaris bedding. And I think American has the right instinct here. A passenger is still talking about how much they love the airline’s business class product a year after the flight. This is also an unusually good advertisement for an airline pillow. We have to admit… this may be one of our favorite confessions. We’re glad those pillows found such a loving home, and even happier to hear they’re still helping you both get a great night’s sleep! Thank you for sharing the laugh and for choosing to fly with us. — americanair (@AmericanAir) November 20, 2026 I Have Airline Blankets On My Couch On my couch at home I have American Airlines blankets from before the US Airways merger, along with Etihad first class blankets. The Etihad ones are some of the softest, most comfortable blankets I’ve ever used. They remind me of those flights, and make me want to get back on board. About a year ago, at American’s event introducing its Airbus A321XLR, I took home a 100th anniversary pillow. (With permission.) When my daughter was in preschool, parents sent their kids with sleep sacks for nap time. I sent her with a United Polaris cooling gel pillow. United actually sent me a cooling gel pillow in a promotional package in 2018. They understood the value of getting the product into someone’s home when it was their public relations team doing the sending. So it was even more odd to see passengers spending thousands of dollars with them as scoflaws. An airline can buy advertising to tell me its business class bed is comfortable. A blanket I actually use at home lets me experience a little of that comfort again. An unusual souvenir also gives someone a reason to ask about a trip. Now I’m telling the story of the flight, remembering what I liked about it, and introducing somebody else to the product. United Wanted Its Pillows Back. Holiday Inn Gave Away More Towels. In 2017, United told flight attendants to watch for passengers taking its new Saks Fifth Avenue bedding. all pillows and blankets are to be left on the aircraft at the end of each flight, including the cooling gel memory foam pillow. United said even a few missing items per flight could add up to millions of dollars across its network. They laundered and reused the bedding over multiple flights. The same instructions allowed passengers to take amenity kits, slippers and pajamas where offered. I argued that United should see the marketing opportunity. They’d finally developed bedding that customers actively wanted to bring home! There ought to be a way to take advantage of that enthusiasm. Holiday Inn did. Back in 2003, I wrote about its towel amnesty. The IHG brand declared August 28 Towel Amnesty Day and forgave guests who’d taken towels over the years. They didn’t just promise not to chase anyone. Their original announcement included more than 60,000 souvenir towels to give away, plus a dollar for Give Kids The World for every towel story collected. They turned missing inventory into stories about people’s stays. In 2013, Hyatt actively encouraged guests to take its bath amenities. Those little bottles could remind you of the hotel the next time you used them. That meant the toiletries supplied in your room, not clearing out a housekeeping cart. And it doesn’t translate into permission to remove today’s large communal shampoo dispensers. What a shame those germ farms are. Some Of The Best Airline Souvenirs Are Meant To Leave Airlines already know that small objects can become a reason to remember them, talk about them, and even book them again. KLM’s Delft houses. The airline gives miniature Dutch buildings filled with Dutch gin to intercontinental business class passengers. They’ve been doing it since the 1950s, and release a new house each year on their October 7 anniversary. There’s even an app to track your collection. The airline has given you something to collect on a future trip. Lufthansa’s rubber ducks. These began in the bathrooms of the Frankfurt First Class Terminal in 2004. Lufthansa’s own anniversary history describes delighted guests taking them home. The airline embraced it and created special editions. A little bath toy became a recognizable part of an expensive first class experience. Delta’s trading cards. You can ask a pilot for one. Delta says it distributed more than 3 million in 2024 and produced over 5 million for its 2025 collection. This works in coach, too. The souvenir comes with a conversation with a pilot. Other airlines offer these now, too. Virgin Atlantic’s salt and pepper shakers. The little aircraft-shaped shakers famously carry the words “pinched from” and “Virgin Atlantic” underneath. The airline has joked publicly about passengers taking them. They’ve made the souvenir story part of the design, although I’d still ask before pocketing tableware. Virgin Australia had a particularly good version of this: its business class salt and pepper shakers fit together to make the Sydney Opera House. Passengers took them home. A generic salt shaker doesn’t give you much to talk about. A tiny Opera House does. Amenity Kits Are A Marketing Deal, Too An amenity kit is supposed to go home with you. The toothbrush and eye mask help during the flight. A useful bag can stay in your life for years. I’ve written about the economics of these partnerships, including United’s Brooks Brothers kits. The brand supplying the toiletries or putting its name on the bag can be subsidizing the airline’s cost. That may mean free or discounted products, shared costs, or payments for exposure to premium passengers. In other arrangements the airline pays for a luxury name. The skincare company gets its product into the hands of someone who might buy it again. The airline gets a more desirable amenity and an association with the brand. Taking the samples home and finishing them is part of the point. Where I’d Draw The Line For passengers, the starting point is what you’re being given. Amenity kits and their contents, pajamas and personal slippers where offered, children’s activity kits, and souvenirs handed out by the airline are generally yours to keep. Bedding, mattress pads, reusable noise cancelling headphones, glasses, dishes and metal cutlery are generally equipment for use during the flight. Ask before taking them. For the airline, I’d be generous with a small, distinctive item that a passenger loves, provided it’s inexpensive enough to give away and there’s enough stock to keep delivering the promised product. Give employees room to say yes. There are clear limits. Hotel guests taking televisions is absurd. I’ve covered hotels reporting stolen mattresses. I’d ask for the pillow, take the amenity kit, and happily accept a commemorative gift like American’s anniversary cushion. If the airline wants its bedding back, selling it is another way to let the passenger keep the memory. United’s own shop lists a Saks Fifth Avenue duvet for $34 (currently out of stock, with more due November 27). That may mean free or discounted products, shared costs, or payments for exposure to premium passengers. In other arrangements the airline pays for a luxury name. The skincare company gets its product into the hands of someone who might buy it again. The airline gets a more desirable amenity and an association with the brand. Taking the samples home and finishing them is part of the point.

For passengers, the starting point is what you’re being given. Amenity kits and their contents, pajamas and personal slippers where offered, children’s activity kits, and souvenirs handed out by the airline are generally yours to keep. Bedding, mattress pads, reusable noise cancelling headphones, glasses, dishes and metal cutlery are generally equipment for use during the flight. Ask before taking them. For the airline, I’d be generous with a small, distinctive item that a passenger loves, provided it’s inexpensive enough to give away and there’s enough stock to keep delivering the promised product. Give employees room to say yes. There are clear limits. Hotel guests taking televisions is absurd. I’ve covered hotels reporting stolen mattresses. I’d ask for the pillow, take the amenity kit, and happily accept a commemorative gift like American’s anniversary cushion. If the airline wants its bedding back, selling it is another way to let the passenger keep the memory. United’s own shop lists a Saks Fifth Avenue duvet for $34 (currently out of stock, with more due November 27). Pan Am would hand out small carry bags to celebrities with the corporate logo. Back then, Hollywood stars would have their picture taken as they walked down the mobile stairs to the tarmac while arriving in Paris, London, or Rome to shoot a movie. Also, the airlines would have its name or logo just inside the exit door of the prop or jet for additional photo publicity. If in doubt, just Google photos of when the Beetles arrive at JFK in 1964; John Lennon has a Pan Am bag in his hand.

I have the blue thin Delta blankets ( turned them into rags ), red AA thin blankets ( my dogs sleep on them ), and the newish thicker UA blankets ( from my recent trip to HKG ). Up next: Cathay blankets on my Feb trip.

I still have one of those PanAm bags given to me when I bought a ticket in F to Tokyo at their NYC office back in the 70’s. That flight was on their 747SP nonstop.

What kind of low life rips off bedding from their flight.

Bunch of thieves on these planes. Explains a lot when you think about it…

Gotta love people who rationalize stealing.

Weird to take a biz class pillow, but if you really think that will change your life, I say go for it. AA is wise to play along. Better to get the brand endorsement than look like a cheap scold.

I have some really soft warm blankets from American international first class that were brought home years ago along with wine glasses from BA Concorde, Easterna and Pan Am first class and I treasure these wonderful souvenirs and wonderful memories.

When you pay $10K+ for a roundtrip to Europe, cash, then does it really matter?

Sure, the points people and hoarders are gonna hoard, but surely, it doesn’t even register a rounding error against $10K for 7 hours of flight time.

When UA first rolled out its Polaris bedding, I commented to an FA what a great travel pillow they had. The FA told me to take it if I wanted. I still use it a lot, and there is the association with UA as the cover is emblazoned with “United” and “Polaris”–a constant reminder and, to me, great marketing. Same with the pajamas. But they’ve cut back on everything, which I think is a mistake, especially with other airlines stepping up.

Monetize it! Offer the bedding for sale if someone wants it bad enough. I’ve seen many a blanket wrapped around pax as they deplane. Not my monkey not my circus. Most of the pillows and blankets in the crash pad were DL or UA.

Qatar Airways has many different pillows with a city and a design destination tha they fly. I have +20 different ones in a guest room 😀

I took the soft gray blanket from AAs new business plus product. Am covered up on the couch with it now. I love it and yes it reminds that I want to fly J again!

Back in 1979 my family stayed at a Holiday inn in Los Angeles. My Mom took a towel. That towel lasted for a long time.

Delta Air Lines flight cancellations spilled into Monday after a tech outage snarled air traffic on Sunday. Combined with bad weather, it's made for a messy start to the Thanksgiving travel rush.

By 7:15 a.m. EST Monday, Delta had canceled at least 92 mainline flights for the day. That's about 2% of its planned schedule.

It came after the airline canceled or delayed thousands of flights on Sunday following a problem with a key system that automates weight and balance calculations.

The disruption led to mass delays at its Atlanta mega-hub — the world’s busiest airport — and cascaded to other airports around the country.

Delta said it had restored its automated system by late Sunday afternoon. But the disruptions continued to climb as the carrier worked to get operations fully back on track — and Mother Nature didn't help, either.

Delta's operations appeared to be improving on Monday, but travelers still had to deal with some residual disruptions from a messy Sunday at airports — especially on the East Coast.

Around 70% of the flight disruptions were due to the tech issues, the airline had said. The rest were tied to Sunday's weather problems, and air traffic control delays that resulted.

“We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism," Delta said in a statement to TPG.

Travelers had other problems to contend with as the Thanksgiving rush got underway, too.

Mother Nature also slowed air traffic at some major hubs.

Low cloud ceilings and poor visibility fueled flight delays and led to dozens of planes getting diverted.

New York’s LaGuardia Airport (LGA) was most heavily affected, with nearly 60% of all departing and arriving flights delayed Sunday, per FlightAware.

42 flights headed to LGA on Sunday were diverted to other airports, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium.

Many of those flights landed instead in Philadelphia; Albany, N.Y.; Harrisburg, PA; and Syracuse, N.Y.

These disruptions come a week after one of the most chaotic weekends at airports in recent memory.

More than 18,000 flights were canceled last weekend after an outage on Nov. 13 to critical Federal Aviation Administration technology.

Last week, a brief technical outage at United Airlines also fueled a host of flight delays.

What to do if you’re affected: This week, the TPG team put our heads together to offer some of our top tips for navigating a travel meltdown. Here’s what to know.

If your flight is canceled or significantly delayed, you’re entitled to a refund under U.S. Department of Transportation policy — but only if you choose not to fly.

If you get stranded in Sunday’s travel mess, it pays to know what the reason was for the disruption.

If you get stuck because of Delta’s tech outage, the carrier may be willing to pay for any hotel, meal and ground transportation costs you incur — if it’s a major delay. See details at FlightRights.gov.

The carrier on Sunday acknowledged it was providing those accommodations to passengers "when necessary."

If you get stuck because of bad weather, it's less likely your airline will offer any sort of compensation. But keep your receipts: If you paid for your trip with a credit card that has travel insurance, you might be able to file a claim and seek reimbursement.

These latest travel woes also coincide, of course, with the start of the Thanksgiving travel rush — with airports expected to be very busy with holiday travelers over the next few days.

All eyes are on next Sunday — Nov. 29 — which could be the busiest day of the year to fly.

Last year, the Sunday after Thanksgiving set the record as the most crowded day ever at U.S. airports.
