#6004. Etihad Launches U.S. Credit Cards With Elite Status—But Most Americans Should Skip Them

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Etihad has launched two U.S. credit cards, including a $499 card that offers Gold status after a single Etihad purchase. That’s the sort of benefit that usually gets my attention. But I wouldn’t recommend either card to most U.S. consumers.

Qatar Airways status that comes the first year with their premium card can get you into American Airlines and Alaska Airlines lounges on domestic trips (and American Airlines international business class lounge access). Emirates status lets you book first class awards that non-status members can’t. Etihad’s status doesn’t do either of those things, and you can earn their miles faster with other cards.

The two cards launched November 20 through First National Bank of Omaha. They’re Etihad’s first U.S. cobrands, with annual fees of $99 and $499.

Here are the main differences in the offers: Benefit   Etihad Guest Visa Signature   Etihad Guest Premier Visa Signature Annual fee   $99   $499 Initial bonus   40,000 miles: 10,000 after first purchase, plus 30,000 after $3,000 in spending within the first three billing cycles   60,000 miles: 20,000 after first purchase, plus 40,000 after $7,000 in spending within the first three billing cycles Etihad purchases   3 miles per dollar   5 miles per dollar Partner airline purchases   2 miles per dollar   3 miles per dollar Other purchases outside the U.S.   2 miles per dollar   2 miles per dollar Other U.S. purchases   1 mile per dollar   1 mile per dollar The initial offers require applying by February 3, 2027. Both cards waive foreign transaction fees. The Premier card also includes Priority Pass, a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fee credit every four years, and 3,000 miles after the first Etihad purchase and at each card anniversary. The status rules are: $99 card: Silver after your first Etihad purchase within 90 days. Keep Silver with $20,000 in annual card spending or $3,000 in Etihad purchases. $499 card: Silver at account opening, then Gold after your first Etihad purchase within 90 days. Keep Gold with $40,000 in annual card spending or $8,000 in Etihad purchases. Otherwise, you get Silver. Both earn one tier mile per dollar spent. The cheaper card caps this at 25,000 tier miles per calendar year, while Premier has no cap. These are status credits, separate from the miles you redeem for travel. So you can spend towards Etihad status. I like bonusing non-U.S. purchases, but if that’s meaningful to you then the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card is far better since it earns unlimited 3 points for every $1 spent on eligible foreign transactions. And I value Alaska’s miles far more than Etihad’s. But Etihad Gold Isn’t Qatar Gold When Qatar Airways launched its U.S. cards, the premium card’s first year of Gold status was immediately useful even to someone who never planned to fly Qatar. Qatar Gold is oneworld Sapphire. That means lounge access when flying American Airlines and Alaska Airlines, including domestic trips. It even gets you into American’s business class Flagship lounges on an eligible same-day itinerary. Etihad isn’t in an alliance. Their airline partnerships don’t turn Etihad Gold into an Admirals Club membership or give you those oneworld benefits on domestic American flights. The Premier card’s Priority Pass membership is a big nothingburger. Priority Pass is a drug on the market. Everyone offers Priority Pass. And Emirates gave its credit cards a purpose when it restricted first class awards to elite members. You need Silver status or higher to book a first class Classic Reward. You don’t need an Etihad card’s status just to redeem miles for the award you want. Etihad status can help when you actually fly Etihad, especially in coach. Lounge access and other benefits depend on your tier. But someone who mainly redeems miles for premium cabins already gets many of the things status would otherwise provide with their ticket. I’d Earn The Miles With A Different Card You don’t need an Etihad credit card to earn Etihad miles. Capital One, for instance, transfers to Etihad Guest at 1:1, and Venture and Venture X earn two miles per dollar on ordinary purchases. Citi and Bilt also offer transfers to Etihad. Put $40,000 of unbonused spend on the Etihad Premier card and earn 40,000 redeemable Etihad miles, while satisfying the spending requirement to keep Gold. Put that same spending on Venture X and earn 80,000 Capital One miles, which can become 80,000 Etihad miles. Or you can transfer them to a different airline. This is why I separate a card’s initial bonus and benefits from whether it’s worth using for spending. An Etihad bonus might help someone finish off an account for a specific award. That doesn’t make the card a good place to put their continuing spend. The narrow case I’d consider is someone who regularly buys Etihad coach tickets, will use the status benefits, and can retain Gold through $8,000 of Etihad purchases rather than diverting $40,000 of ordinary spending. For someone who wants Etihad miles for an occasional business or first class redemption, I’d earn transferable points with a better card. I wouldn’t pay $499 and give up half my everyday mileage earning just for Etihad Gold. #6003. Citi AAdvantage Executive Card Review: Better Lounges And More Status Credit

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

The Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] costs $695 a year, but I think it’s a better value today than it was at $595. American Airlines is investing seriously in its clubs again, and the card’s refresh added more credit towards elite status and benefits I can actually use.

I have the card. For a regular American Airlines flyer who wants Admirals Club access, it’s the place to start. The lounges are getting better, more are coming, and buying membership directly from American costs hundreds of dollars more.

When I covered the refresh, I thought the additional Loyalty Points alone justified the $100 annual fee increase for me. Citi has since added $200 in annual inKind dining credits, too.

The Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® includes full Admirals Club membership for the primary cardmember. American has priced standalone membership to make getting the card the obvious choice for someone eligible to apply. Here’s the current comparison: Option   Annual Cost   What You Get Citi AAdvantage Executive card   $695   Full membership, including guest privileges and eligible partner lounges Full membership bought from American   $1,200–$1,400, depending on status   Full membership, including guest privileges and eligible partner lounges Single membership bought from American   $750   Admirals Club access for the member, without guests or partner lounges Even an Executive Platinum member pays $1,200 for full membership. The card saves $505 before assigning any value to its miles, status bonuses or credits. Someone without status saves $705. And the card costs less than American’s restricted $750 membership option. There’s no annual visit allowance to ration and no spending requirement to unlock unlimited visits. Qualifying Citigold customers can receive a $145 annual relationship credit, reducing their cost further. What The Lounge Access Includes American has nearly 50 Admirals Clubs, with more than 60 partner lounges extending the membership’s reach. Under American’s access rules: You can visit Admirals Clubs on eligible same-day itineraries, including American Airlines and oneworld flights. You don’t have to buy the ticket with this card. You can bring two guests or your immediate family—a spouse or domestic partner and children under 18. Guests need eligible same-day boarding passes, too. The primary cardmember’s membership includes eligible partner locations, such as Alaska Lounges and Qantas Clubs. The flight requirements vary by partner. This doesn’t include Flagship Lounges or Flagship Dining. Executive Platinum status by itself doesn’t get you into Admirals Clubs on ordinary domestic trips. Neither does a typical domestic first class ticket. The card also has an unusually good deal for additional cardholders: $175 total for up to three authorized users, then $175 for each additional user. Use all three slots and that’s about $58 per person annually. Each authorized user can visit Admirals Clubs without you and bring their own eligible guests. They need their physical card, identification and an eligible same-day boarding pass. They get Admirals Club access, rather than full membership, so they don’t get the partner lounge benefit. For a family, $870 in total annual fees can cover a primary cardmember and three authorized users traveling separately, with guest privileges. That’s less than American charges one Executive Platinum member for standalone full membership. If you only want a few visits a year, the $350 annual fee Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® [See rates and fees] includes four annual Admirals Club passes. American Is Finally Building Clubs I Want To Spend Time In For years American underinvested in lounges. They closed clubs, and when they renovated others the result was often the institutional look I’ve called “modern hospital.” The newer design is a huge improvement. Washington National’s E concourse club, Denver, Newark and Philadelphia show where American is going: warmer wood, better lighting, comfortable seating and spaces that feel inviting. I like this aesthetic more than the newer United Clubs or Delta Sky Clubs. The food has improved, too. I still generally prefer Delta’s lounge food, but American has moved well beyond the old snacks-and-soup proposition. Their fall Admirals Club menus include beef barbacoa taco bars in Chicago, Denver and St. Louis; sesame orange chicken at several West Coast clubs and Phoenix; and Creole style chicken with white bean cassoulet at the New York and Newark clubs. I’ve covered American’s plan for a new, renovated or expanded lounge nearly every month, on average, over two to three years. That’s very different from what we saw for much of the past decade. Among the projects: Charlotte: A new Admirals Club exceeding 40,000 square feet, with showers and multiple bars and food stations. Dallas–Fort Worth: A 37,000 square foot Terminal C club, plus a Provisions location planned for Terminal F. Austin: A replacement club exceeding 12,000 square feet, with American’s first outdoor lounge terrace. Chicago, Nashville, Miami and Washington National: New or expanded clubs, including Chicago’s L concourse project and the refresh of National’s Concourse D club. There’s also the Provisions grab-and-go concept, already operating in Charlotte, with additional locations announced for New York JFK and Dallas–Fort Worth. Sometimes you want food to take to the gate more than you want a seat in a lounge. And the most valuable part of a club can still be its agents. I’ve written about the Austin agents who keep looking for better connections after I’ve left. Having someone help fix a disrupted trip can be worth more than everything you eat and drink in the lounge that year. The Initial Bonus And Who Can Get It The current public initial bonus is 80,000 AAdvantage miles after $8,000 in purchases within the first three months of account opening. The annual fee is $695. Those are redeemable miles. The initial bonus doesn’t count as Loyalty Points towards status, although eligible spending to earn it does. Under Citi’s terms, you aren’t eligible for the initial bonus if you’ve received an Executive card new account bonus within the past 48 months. The restriction also covers converting another Citi card into an Executive account when that other account earned a new account bonus within the last 48 months. Simply having a different AAdvantage cobrand card doesn’t disqualify you. Up To 40,000 Extra Loyalty Points Without Spending On The Card The card awards 10,000 additional Loyalty Points at each of four thresholds during the AAdvantage qualification year, which runs March through February: Account Reaches   Cumulative Executive Card Bonuses 50,000 Loyalty Points   10,000 Loyalty Points 90,000 Loyalty Points   20,000 Loyalty Points 165,000 Loyalty Points   30,000 Loyalty Points 240,000 Loyalty Points   40,000 Loyalty Points The last two bonuses were added in the refresh. You don’t have to earn the qualifying Loyalty Points by spending on this card. Flying, shopping portal earnings, hotel bookings and spending on other AAdvantage cards can get you there. The bonuses themselves count towards subsequent thresholds. Earn 80,000 Loyalty Points outside this benefit and the first two bonuses bring you to 100,000. For someone pursuing Executive Platinum, the card can supply 30,000 of the required 200,000 Loyalty Points. Earning 170,000 elsewhere gets you there. The fourth bonus comes after Executive Platinum, helping towards higher Loyalty Point Rewards: 210,000 earned elsewhere plus the four bonuses gets you to 250,000. This is why the Executive card can make sense alongside another AAdvantage card. I have the Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees], too, and its spending can help trigger these Executive card bonuses. Globe’s Flight Streak bonuses can also stack with them. The Credits That Help Pay For The Card The October inKind addition is especially useful to me. I already use inKind at restaurants I’d eat at anyway. Here’s how the recurring credits work: $200 inKind dining credit: $100 for January–June and $100 for July–December. Add the card and benefit in the inKind app, then apply the credit when paying a participating restaurant through the app. There’s no minimum spend, and you can use it across multiple checks. Unused credit doesn’t carry over. Tips aren’t covered, and authorized users share the account’s allocation. Up to $500 American Airlines Vacations credit: Up to $250 in each half of the calendar year. This covers eligible vacation packages and Experiences purchased through American Airlines Vacations. Packages require at least two travel components, such as a flight and hotel or flight and car. Up to $100 for inflight and eligible Admirals Club purchases: A calendar year statement credit for eligible purchases charged to the card. Club food and beverages qualify. The inflight benefit applies to eligible domestic American Airlines and American Eagle flights. I won’t value this at the full $100 because many of the drinks and snacks I’d otherwise buy are already included through my status or seat, but it can cover additional purchases for family or premium club drinks. Up to $120 for Avis and Budget: Each calendar year, for eligible prepaid rentals booked directly at avis.com or budget.com and charged to the card. Pay later reservations and bookings through other travel sites don’t qualify. Up to $180 in Lyft credits: Take three eligible rides paid with the card in a calendar month, then receive a $15 Lyft credit. The credit expires after 30 days. This improved from $10 to $15 per month, but three rides are still required. Starting February 1, 2027, Wait & Save rides won’t qualify. If inKind saves you $200 on dining you’d otherwise pay for, that leaves $495 of annual fee to justify with lounge access, status bonuses and the other benefits. One old benefit is being phased out: the $10 Grubhub credit per monthly billing statement. Accounts opened before August 23, 2026 retain it through August 31, 2027. New applicants don’t get it, and the old 25% inflight food and beverage rebate has ended (replaced by the annual $100 credit). Hotel, Rental Car And Airport Benefits The refresh also added Omni Champion status and the ability to earn an annual free night. Enroll in the status benefit before your stay, allowing up to 14 days for activation. Then complete a qualifying stay of at least two consecutive nights, booked directly with Omni in your name and paid with the Executive card. That earns 100 Omni Credits for a free night on a later stay, once per calendar year. Redeem within 12 months. Taxes and resort fees are included in the award. A two-night stay you were going to make anyway can produce a valuable additional night. You can also enroll in Avis President’s Club through August 31, 2028. This offers upgrades and other rental benefits, although it’s duplicative for members who already receive it by reaching 100,000 AAdvantage Loyalty Points. Other benefits include: First checked bag free on eligible domestic American Airlines itineraries for the primary cardmember and up to eight companions on the same reservation. You don’t have to pay for the tickets with the card. Priority check-in, priority security where available and Group 4 boarding for the primary cardmember and up to eight companions on the same reservation. Up to $120 towards Global Entry or TSA PreCheck every four years when you pay the application fee with the card. No foreign transaction fees and travel protections including trip cancellation and interruption, trip delay, lost baggage and rental car coverage for qualifying purchases. What I’d Actually Spend On The Card The earning rates are: 12 miles per dollar on eligible AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars bookings. 4 miles per dollar on eligible American Airlines purchases. 1 mile per dollar on other eligible purchases. Eligible spending earns one Loyalty Point per dollar. The category bonuses don’t multiply that: a dollar of American Airlines spending earns four redeemable miles and one Loyalty Point from the card. AAdvantage Hotels can separately award miles and Loyalty Points for the booking itself. The 12-mile rate is a strong reason to use this card when booking through American’s hotel and rental car platforms. I’d also use it where payment is required to earn a credit or benefit. For everyday spending, the decision is how much the additional Loyalty Points help you. American lets card spending make a real contribution to status, but earning one redeemable mile per dollar means giving up the rewards another card would have earned. You can keep the Executive card for its clubs and milestone bonuses while putting spending on a different card. After $150,000 in purchases during a calendar year, eligible American Airlines purchases earn five miles per dollar for the rest of that year. I wouldn’t do that just to earn one additional mile per dollar on subsequent airfare. For years American underinvested in lounges. They closed clubs, and when they renovated others the result was often the institutional look I’ve called “modern hospital.” The newer design is a huge improvement.

Washington National’s E concourse club, Denver, Newark and Philadelphia show where American is going: warmer wood, better lighting, comfortable seating and spaces that feel inviting. I like this aesthetic more than the newer United Clubs or Delta Sky Clubs.

The food has improved, too. I still generally prefer Delta’s lounge food, but American has moved well beyond the old snacks-and-soup proposition. Their fall Admirals Club menus include beef barbacoa taco bars in Chicago, Denver and St. Louis; sesame orange chicken at several West Coast clubs and Phoenix; and Creole style chicken with white bean cassoulet at the New York and Newark clubs.

I’ve covered American’s plan for a new, renovated or expanded lounge nearly every month, on average, over two to three years. That’s very different from what we saw for much of the past decade.

There’s also the Provisions grab-and-go concept, already operating in Charlotte, with additional locations announced for New York JFK and Dallas–Fort Worth. Sometimes you want food to take to the gate more than you want a seat in a lounge.

And the most valuable part of a club can still be its agents. I’ve written about the Austin agents who keep looking for better connections after I’ve left. Having someone help fix a disrupted trip can be worth more than everything you eat and drink in the lounge that year.

The current public initial bonus is 80,000 AAdvantage miles after $8,000 in purchases within the first three months of account opening. The annual fee is $695. Those are redeemable miles. The initial bonus doesn’t count as Loyalty Points towards status, although eligible spending to earn it does. Under Citi’s terms, you aren’t eligible for the initial bonus if you’ve received an Executive card new account bonus within the past 48 months. The restriction also covers converting another Citi card into an Executive account when that other account earned a new account bonus within the last 48 months. Simply having a different AAdvantage cobrand card doesn’t disqualify you. Up To 40,000 Extra Loyalty Points Without Spending On The Card The card awards 10,000 additional Loyalty Points at each of four thresholds during the AAdvantage qualification year, which runs March through February: Account Reaches   Cumulative Executive Card Bonuses 50,000 Loyalty Points   10,000 Loyalty Points 90,000 Loyalty Points   20,000 Loyalty Points 165,000 Loyalty Points   30,000 Loyalty Points 240,000 Loyalty Points   40,000 Loyalty Points The last two bonuses were added in the refresh. You don’t have to earn the qualifying Loyalty Points by spending on this card. Flying, shopping portal earnings, hotel bookings and spending on other AAdvantage cards can get you there. The bonuses themselves count towards subsequent thresholds. Earn 80,000 Loyalty Points outside this benefit and the first two bonuses bring you to 100,000. For someone pursuing Executive Platinum, the card can supply 30,000 of the required 200,000 Loyalty Points. Earning 170,000 elsewhere gets you there. The fourth bonus comes after Executive Platinum, helping towards higher Loyalty Point Rewards: 210,000 earned elsewhere plus the four bonuses gets you to 250,000. This is why the Executive card can make sense alongside another AAdvantage card. I have the Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees], too, and its spending can help trigger these Executive card bonuses. Globe’s Flight Streak bonuses can also stack with them. The Credits That Help Pay For The Card The October inKind addition is especially useful to me. I already use inKind at restaurants I’d eat at anyway. Here’s how the recurring credits work: $200 inKind dining credit: $100 for January–June and $100 for July–December. Add the card and benefit in the inKind app, then apply the credit when paying a participating restaurant through the app. There’s no minimum spend, and you can use it across multiple checks. Unused credit doesn’t carry over. Tips aren’t covered, and authorized users share the account’s allocation. Up to $500 American Airlines Vacations credit: Up to $250 in each half of the calendar year. This covers eligible vacation packages and Experiences purchased through American Airlines Vacations. Packages require at least two travel components, such as a flight and hotel or flight and car. Up to $100 for inflight and eligible Admirals Club purchases: A calendar year statement credit for eligible purchases charged to the card. Club food and beverages qualify. The inflight benefit applies to eligible domestic American Airlines and American Eagle flights. I won’t value this at the full $100 because many of the drinks and snacks I’d otherwise buy are already included through my status or seat, but it can cover additional purchases for family or premium club drinks. Up to $120 for Avis and Budget: Each calendar year, for eligible prepaid rentals booked directly at avis.com or budget.com and charged to the card. Pay later reservations and bookings through other travel sites don’t qualify. Up to $180 in Lyft credits: Take three eligible rides paid with the card in a calendar month, then receive a $15 Lyft credit. The credit expires after 30 days. This improved from $10 to $15 per month, but three rides are still required. Starting February 1, 2027, Wait & Save rides won’t qualify. If inKind saves you $200 on dining you’d otherwise pay for, that leaves $495 of annual fee to justify with lounge access, status bonuses and the other benefits. One old benefit is being phased out: the $10 Grubhub credit per monthly billing statement. Accounts opened before August 23, 2026 retain it through August 31, 2027. New applicants don’t get it, and the old 25% inflight food and beverage rebate has ended (replaced by the annual $100 credit). Hotel, Rental Car And Airport Benefits The refresh also added Omni Champion status and the ability to earn an annual free night. Enroll in the status benefit before your stay, allowing up to 14 days for activation. Then complete a qualifying stay of at least two consecutive nights, booked directly with Omni in your name and paid with the Executive card. That earns 100 Omni Credits for a free night on a later stay, once per calendar year. Redeem within 12 months. Taxes and resort fees are included in the award. A two-night stay you were going to make anyway can produce a valuable additional night. You can also enroll in Avis President’s Club through August 31, 2028. This offers upgrades and other rental benefits, although it’s duplicative for members who already receive it by reaching 100,000 AAdvantage Loyalty Points. Other benefits include: First checked bag free on eligible domestic American Airlines itineraries for the primary cardmember and up to eight companions on the same reservation. You don’t have to pay for the tickets with the card. Priority check-in, priority security where available and Group 4 boarding for the primary cardmember and up to eight companions on the same reservation. Up to $120 towards Global Entry or TSA PreCheck every four years when you pay the application fee with the card. No foreign transaction fees and travel protections including trip cancellation and interruption, trip delay, lost baggage and rental car coverage for qualifying purchases. What I’d Actually Spend On The Card The earning rates are: 12 miles per dollar on eligible AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars bookings. 4 miles per dollar on eligible American Airlines purchases. 1 mile per dollar on other eligible purchases. Eligible spending earns one Loyalty Point per dollar. The category bonuses don’t multiply that: a dollar of American Airlines spending earns four redeemable miles and one Loyalty Point from the card. AAdvantage Hotels can separately award miles and Loyalty Points for the booking itself. The 12-mile rate is a strong reason to use this card when booking through American’s hotel and rental car platforms. I’d also use it where payment is required to earn a credit or benefit. For everyday spending, the decision is how much the additional Loyalty Points help you. American lets card spending make a real contribution to status, but earning one redeemable mile per dollar means giving up the rewards another card would have earned. You can keep the Executive card for its clubs and milestone bonuses while putting spending on a different card. After $150,000 in purchases during a calendar year, eligible American Airlines purchases earn five miles per dollar for the rest of that year. I wouldn’t do that just to earn one additional mile per dollar on subsequent airfare. You cover all this, but I do think the updates to this card are excellent. Approaching Amex Platinum levels of refresh improvement.

– inKind is available in more places than you might expect. My local coffee shop is on inKind. My local pizza place is on inKind. Sure you can value the $200 at something less because of prepayment and because you can buy inKind giftcards for as low as $64.99 on Black Friday or whatever, but this is still as good as cash. This isn’t a Resy credit where you are likely sitting down for a meal, let alone a CSR OpenTable credit that’s available in tens of restaurants nationwide. The inKind credit covers lots of places that are on-the-go, picking up some pizza for dinner for the family on the way home types of charges. Even if you value the credit at only $130-150, it’s very cash-like in its use, and not illusory at all. And $100 every 6 months is 10x better than $10 a month at Grubhub.

– 20k more LPs is nothing to sneeze at, and also makes it much easier to get to the valuable 250k LP reward level. Would it surprise me if at some point soon AA raised the LPs required to reach status levels so that they align with when you get the 4x10k LP boosters? Nope.

– 12x versus 10x on AA Hotels / Cars is terrific! That’s an extra $3 in value per $100 spent (assuming you value a mile at 1.5cpm). And if you have any AA status, with any AA card, you are getting a good amount of additional base miles/LP on AA Hotels and Cars in addition to the 1x base/11x bonus miles you’re getting on spend. It’s not crazy to think that you might get an additional 15k base miles/LP for $1k of spend – the idea that you might get 27k miles (~$405 of value) and 16k LP on $1k of spend is a terrific return! And it’s 19.75k LP if you reached 60k LP and activated the 25% bonus on your LP through partners for a 6 month period. Basically half way to AA Gold on 1x$1k stay, and you’re getting an extra ~$30 in value per $1k (versus the previous 10x earning rate on AA Hotels).

-$100 inflight/club credit may not be that useful for solo flyers who are EP and get a free cheese plate already, but when traveling with the family – easy snacks to buy on board, the cost of which is now fully covered versus 25% off. Big improvement – unless you were already spending more than $400 a year on AA F&B on board (which seems unlikely for most people).

– Even if you value the AA Vacations credit at $0 (even with the current MaximizeMiles promotion I tend to think AA Vacations is more trouble than its worth given the restrictive cancellation policies plus the fact that you would likely earn more miles/LP booking your flight and hotel and car separately with AA / AA Hotels / AA Cars), AA/Citi are still delivering revised economics that more than offset the additional $100 AF.

Bottom line – this is a fantastic card refresh.

Are the loyalty points bonus thresholds retroactive? Meaning if I’ve already earned 100.000+ LPs for 2026 program year if I’m approved for the card will I “immediately” (or at least before Feb end) get the 20,000 point LP bonus?

“Up to $100 for inflight and eligible Admirals Club purchases:. … Club food and beverages qualify.”

Which clubs have did for purchase anymore? I’m the last 6 months I have tried BOS, LGA, CLT, ORD, DFW and none have food. Either the QR code only has drinks or I tried to order from the QR menu and was told they didn’t have any food anymore. I would often get a to go order from the lounge… Better than a sandwich from Hudson’s. The food at the lounge has improved, but it’s still less of a meal than what they had on the QR menu.

Was traveling on Japan Airlines from Chicago and the Sakura lounge in Narita did not accept card even though AA said we can use because it is part of One World Alliance. Not true….

The admirals Club at Dallas fort Worth was the worst Club I have ever been to and then they gave me food poisoning to boot

So yeah I’m done with being mistreated by American. Delta is much better and I have to say United has really been improving to the point I don’t try nearly so hard to fly Delta anymore

But American needs to stop torturing the passengers if they want people like me to come back it took a while to earn my loyalty and then in the last decade they resolutely lost it

Power plugs were hard to find in ORD and many UBS DO NOT WORK

#6002. Jeffries puts immigration bill high on Democratic priority list

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move quickly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

“One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries said, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”

The proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

“We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries said. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”

On healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for plans purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust new majority.

When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”

The New York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

“Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

Democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

Without an announced challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have said they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

Jeffries said Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”

This report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

#6001. Spirit Airlines Shut Down—Did It Forget To Cancel Its Internet? Comcast Wants $1.25 Million

Spirit Airlines stopped flying in May, but Comcast and its subsidiaries say it still owes $1.25 million in internet bills. Some charges are for locations Spirit says it left in 2024—but the providers say they haven’t produced records showing the service was canceled. Always keep proof when dealing with Comcast! Part of this sounds like Spirit forgot to turn off its internet when it moved out. According to the providers, on October 22 the airline authorized them to disconnect every location except Dania Pointe in Dania Beach, Florida. That was nearly six months after the airline stopped flying. Their November 19 court filing asks the bankruptcy judge to order payment and make Spirit decide whether to keep or reject the contracts. Comcast and its Masergy subsidiary say some services were still running when they filed. Spirit shut down on May 2 after it couldn’t obtain the money to keep operating. No one would continue to fund its massive losses. But the bankruptcy process to unwind its business remains ongoing. There are assets to sell, contracts to resolve, records to maintain and creditors arguing over who gets paid. I’ve covered the lawsuit from workers seeking 60 days of pay over the abrupt shutdown and the court-approved $668 million sale of a 27-aircraft portfolio. Much of that aircraft price represented lenders applying what Spirit owed them toward their purchase. The four internet providers list these unpaid balances: Provider Amount Claimed Comcast Cable Communications Management $219,743.41 Masergy Cloud Communications $164,626.99 Masergy Communications $849,646.45 Nitel $11,990.73 Total $1,246,007.58 Comcast acquired Masergy in 2021 and Nitel in 2025. This is for internet service at Spirit locations, not inflight wifi (which was provided by Thales). The providers say they’ve repeatedly sought payment. Spirit responded that some locations had been vacated in 2024, and that disconnection requests should have been submitted for others. You might expect the internet companies simply to get in line with Spirit’s other unpaid creditors. For bills dating to before the bankruptcy, that’s probably what happens. But these companies say they continued providing services after Spirit filed on August 29, 2025. Necessary expenses of running a company in bankruptcy can qualify as administrative expenses, which get priority over other unsecured debts, or else no one would keep supplying a bankrupt business trying to turn itself around. And services needed to sell its assets and administer the remaining business can continue to qualify. It’s unclear what treatment will apply to internet Spirit was no longer using, even if it hadn’t cancelled the contracts. Comcast needs to establish the benefit their services supplied to the bankruptcy estate. In fact, their motion cites In re Enron but that denied administrative priority for unused pipeline capacity that hadn’t benefited the estate. Internet connections supporting the Spirit Airlines liquidation are likely to get repayment priority But defunct services that hadn’t merely been cancelled might not. A hearing is scheduled for December 16, with responses due December 9. And even a successful priority claim doesn’t necessarily mean Comcast gets immediate payment. In Midway Airlines, a telephone equipment lessor won an administrative claim for unpaid lease obligations, but the appeals court upheld making it wait for payment alongside other administrative creditors. So Comcast may have to wait as long for payment as you wait on hold to schedule a service appointment. Topics on this pageBankruptcyComcastSpirit AirlinesFlorida+1 more More From View from the Wing

After shopping for everyone else over Black Friday and Cyber Monday, it's your turn on Travel Tuesday. As you plan something for yourself, Capital One wants to help you book it for less.

Beginning Dec. 1, Capital One will offer eligible cardholders limited-time savings on hotels, rental cars, flight-and-stay packages and premium vacation rentals through Capital One Travel.

Some of these deals are more useful than others. Here's who can use each one and how to tell whether the savings are worth booking now.

Capital One is highlighting five offers this year:

The Washington, D.C., hotel offer ends Dec. 7 or when supplies run out, whichever comes first. The Hertz offer runs through Dec. 15, while supplies last.

The other offers each carry their own booking window, travel dates and terms, which you'll find in your Travel Wallet once the deals go live.

Related reading: Capital One Travel: How to book flights, hotels and more

Travel Tuesday offers are available to eligible holders of the:

That's a wide group, but not every cardholder will see every promotion. Premium vacation rental discounts are targeted to select Venture and Venture X cardholders, and not all Capital One cardholders have access to Premier and Lifestyle Collection hotel stays.

To check your personal offers, log in to Capital One Travel starting Dec. 1.

Related reading: The best Capital One credit cards

This year's deals are a perfect example of "when it works, it really works."

Some offers can save hundreds, but only if they match a trip you already wanted to take.

The hotel discount could save you $150 off $500, for example. That's meaningful savings if Washington, D.C. or Florida are already in your travel plans. But if you're traveling anywhere else, that discount is irrelevant.

The complimentary fourth night sounds valuable, particularly if you were already considering one of Capital One's curated collections. But it's worth noting that Capital One Travel already offers the fourth night free at select Premier and Lifestyle Collection hotels — this isn't a new deal for Travel Tuesday.

Similarly, the vacation rental offer appears to be a version of a targeted offer already in my account. Without waiting for Travel Tuesday, I already have a $200 discount available toward premium rentals in my Venture X account. There's no indication that the upcoming deals will raise my offer, though Capital One advertises that some cardholders may be targeted for up to $500 off.

Additionally, Capital One's collection of vacation rentals skews toward higher-end properties. Even with a discount, budget travelers may do better searching a wider selection of properties on Airbnb or Vrbo.

Lastly, the 15% discount on qualifying Hertz rentals is great when Hertz is already competitively priced, but it might not be high enough to change your plans if another brand is offering a better deal. Keep in mind that the Venture card family includes Hertz elite status after enrollment: Eligible Venture X cardholders can enroll in President's Circle status*, while Venture and VentureOne cardholders can enroll in Five Star status*.

The flight-and-stay package discounts require more comparison shopping because Capital One hasn't shared a standard discount. You'll need to check the cost of booking the same flights and hotel separately.

*Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note, enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold Plus Rewards enrollment process (e.g. at Hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply.

The Venture X is the biggest winner. Cardholders may have access to the widest range of promotions. The card earns 10 Capital One miles per dollar spent on hotels and rental cars plus 5 miles per dollar spent on flights and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel.

Here are all of the Capital One cards that will get you the best deals on Travel Tuesday:

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture X, Venture Rewards and Venture X Business.

Related: Capital One Venture Rewards vs. Venture X: Are the premium perks worth $300 more?

Capital One’s Travel Tuesday deal lineup has some winning deals...and a few that likely won't be useful for most shoppers. The free fourth night is a standing perk, and the vacation rental discounts may already be in your Travel Wallet. Use this as your opportunity to re-familiarize yourself to card benefits you may have available year-round.

The genuinely new deals are the hotel discounts in D.C. and Florida, the Hertz savings and the flight-and-stay packages. If any of these fit your plans, even one well-matched offer can make a difference in your travel budget.

#5997. Hilton Diamond Guest Says He Gets Sent Next Door For Coffee—And Treated Like He Was Stealing Breakfast

I’ve written about people walking into hotels where they aren’t staying and helping themselves to a full breakfast. Somehow getting an actual guest a cup of coffee can be more complicated.

John Konrad’s account of the coffee dispute, November 21, 2026

In the second half of the thread, the manager talks up Homewood’s overnight oats. Konrad decides he’d like some after all. He’s refused because he’s registered next door. He raises his voice, objects to being told to calm down (no one in history has ever calmed down because they’ve been told to calm down), and eventually refuses an offered gym pass.

I AM A DIAMOND MEMBER BEING CROSS-EXAMINED OVER CHIA SEEDS.

The replies include plenty of people who think he’s being insufferable. One person who says they’ve stayed at both properties reports that guests routinely move between them. When a critic calls him a Karen, Konrad points back to his Curb Your Enthusiasm framing making himself part of the joke.

The two hotels have shared ownership by the Mian Companies. Signs direct Hilton Garden Inn guests to Homewood’s gym during construction. Homewood Suites Oxnard/Camarillo includes breakfast for its guests. Hilton Garden Inn has a different model. In the United States, eligible Gold and Diamond members who select the benefit receive a $10 daily food and beverage credit per person, for up to two registered guests. And asking for a room number when someone complains about a key is normal. A hotel employee can help with access. But a staff referral should make getting coffee easy. If the two hotels haven’t agreed on what guests can use, they need to sort that out between themselves. Meanwhile, People Really Do Walk Into Hotels For Free Breakfast I’ve covered people walking into a Drury Inn just to eat and people stopping at hotels for breakfast on their way to work. At many limited service properties, nobody checks. Looking comfortable in the lobby can be enough. At the aloft Dallas Love Field in 2022, I selected breakfast as my Marriott elite welcome amenity instead of 500 points. The Aloft and Element occupied the same building, with separate entrances. Breakfast meant walking over to the Element’s lobby buffet, which was included for guests staying there. Nobody asked my name, room number, or whether I’d selected breakfast. I could have taken the points and eaten anyway. Someone who wasn’t staying at either hotel could have walked in just as easily. This favors people who look like they belong. Konrad adds that he hadn’t shaved and his clothes were stained from boat work. He thinks that may explain some of the suspicion. There are real costs to feeding people who aren’t guests. There are also costs to policing breakfast: staff time, lines, and embarrassing the customers who are supposed to be there. A hotel can spend more trying to prevent a small loss than the food would have cost, especially if it chases away repeat business. Hotels Keep Getting Coffee Wrong I’ve been writing about the importance of hotel coffee for years. A business hotel ought to have drinkable coffee available around the clock, with real milk or cream. Guests arrive from other time zones, wake up early for flights, and get up before dawn to work. Their day have to start when the restaurant opens. At what was then the W San Diego, I was staying in the Extreme Wow suite. Still on East Coast time, I woke around 4:30 a.m. At about 5 I called the Whatever/Whenever line for coffee. They told me it wasn’t available until 6. They couldn’t provide whatever (coffee) whenever (in the morning). I wound up walking to Starbucks. I’ve also written about: The then-Andaz Wall Street removing its 24 hour lobby coffee, when rooms didn’t have coffee machines and room service wasn’t available around the clock. Hyatt Herald Square’s coffee stand opening 30 minutes late. Park Hyatt Washington offering 24 hour room service, but refusing overnight coffee. There was a Starbucks across the street there, too. And I don’t love Starbucks, they’re simply ubiquitous. And then there’s the time the Sheraton Macao investigated me for trying to steal coffee. I ordered six cups from room service. After pouring two, the pot was nearly empty. I called down, and they agreed to send four more. Instead, at 6:30 a.m. the delivery employee appeared at my door and announced: I am here to investigate. He insisted the machine was electronic, so it couldn’t have dispensed too little. Then he poured out what remained. Half a cup. There I was in my bathrobe, establishing that six cups and two and a half cups weren’t the same thing before he’d hand over the replacement coffee he’d already brought upstairs. Starwood apologized and offered 5,000 Starpoints. I declined. The hotel’s in-room dining manager apologized as well. They’d turned a short pot of coffee into a staff investigation, a corporate response, and an offer of points. Bringing the coffee would have been cheaper. I’ve also written about: The then-Andaz Wall Street removing its 24 hour lobby coffee, when rooms didn’t have coffee machines and room service wasn’t available around the clock. Hyatt Herald Square’s coffee stand opening 30 minutes late. Park Hyatt Washington offering 24 hour room service, but refusing overnight coffee. There was a Starbucks across the street there, too. And I don’t love Starbucks, they’re simply ubiquitous. And then there’s the time the Sheraton Macao investigated me for trying to steal coffee. I ordered six cups from room service. After pouring two, the pot was nearly empty. I called down, and they agreed to send four more. Instead, at 6:30 a.m. the delivery employee appeared at my door and announced: I am here to investigate. He insisted the machine was electronic, so it couldn’t have dispensed too little. Then he poured out what remained. Half a cup. There I was in my bathrobe, establishing that six cups and two and a half cups weren’t the same thing before he’d hand over the replacement coffee he’d already brought upstairs. Starwood apologized and offered 5,000 Starpoints. I declined. The hotel’s in-room dining manager apologized as well. They’d turned a short pot of coffee into a staff investigation, a corporate response, and an offer of points. Bringing the coffee would have been cheaper. I’ve covered people walking into a Drury Inn just to eat and people stopping at hotels for breakfast on their way to work. At many limited service properties, nobody checks. Looking comfortable in the lobby can be enough.

At the aloft Dallas Love Field in 2022, I selected breakfast as my Marriott elite welcome amenity instead of 500 points. The Aloft and Element occupied the same building, with separate entrances. Breakfast meant walking over to the Element’s lobby buffet, which was included for guests staying there.

Nobody asked my name, room number, or whether I’d selected breakfast. I could have taken the points and eaten anyway. Someone who wasn’t staying at either hotel could have walked in just as easily.

This favors people who look like they belong. Konrad adds that he hadn’t shaved and his clothes were stained from boat work. He thinks that may explain some of the suspicion. There are real costs to feeding people who aren’t guests. There are also costs to policing breakfast: staff time, lines, and embarrassing the customers who are supposed to be there. A hotel can spend more trying to prevent a small loss than the food would have cost, especially if it chases away repeat business.

Some hotels are designed solely as places to sleep at night while you are traveling. Others, however, are meant to be a part of your travel experience. Unless I am truly checking in for a quick overnight stay, I always seek out the latter. That mindset is exactly what led me to Palihotel Hollywood on a recent visit to Los Angeles.

Palihotel Hollywood is one of more than 20 boutique properties under the Palisociety umbrella; a collection of independently branded hotels that prioritize design, connection and individuality. These include Palihouse, Palihotel, Le Petit Pali, ARRIVE by Palisociety and a handful of independently branded properties. Earlier this year, several Palisociety properties joined the Marriott Bonvoy ecosystem as part of a larger partnership between Design Hotels and Marriott.

"Design Hotels and Marriott Bonvoy give us the best of both worlds," Palisociety founder Avi Brosh told me in an interview about the partnership. "We stay fully independent in how our hotels look, feel and operate, and we gain access to one of the largest and most loyal traveler communities in the world. For Bonvoy members, it means they can earn and use their points at a hotel that feels genuinely personal and local. For us, it means introducing Palisociety to travelers who might never have found us otherwise."

Palihotel Hollywood is located just two blocks from iconic Hollywood landmarks such as the Chinese Theatre and the Hollywood Walk of Fame. The hotel's walkability and quick access to the highway made it an easy choice for our California home base, but it was the way I felt while I was there that made it memorable.

The hotel is a fully renovated 1958 motor lodge that retains its original appeal, making it feel right at home on Sunset Boulevard.

"[At Palihotel Hollywood], we leaned into that history rather than erasing it. The dark green facade, striped awnings, the checkerboard pool deck and Benny’s on the Blvd all are meant to belong to this hotel and this stretch of Hollywood. You won’t find them anywhere else," Brosh said.

As soon as I stepped into the lobby, I felt transported to Hollywood's golden age. I'm about the furthest thing from a celebrity looking for a secluded hideaway, but if I were, I would have found it here.

Through the lobby's back doors, I found the hotel's secluded courtyard. Green and white striped loungers with peach-hued umbrellas for shade surrounded the pool. The pool deck was bursting with greenery, which made it feel even more homelike.

Back inside, there is a cozy bar behind the front desk for afternoon and evening drinks, a seating area for guests to commune and Benny's on the Blvd, the hotel's restaurant that serves breakfast, lunch, afternoon snacks, coffee, beer, wine and cocktails. You can dine at the counter or by the pool to soak up the California sunshine.

Each of the hotel's small, intimate spaces adds to the neighborhood feel, a quality consistent across the brand. All Palisociety hotels have fewer than 150 rooms, with Palihotel Hollywood clocking in at 74 rooms and suites.

"Each of our hotels is completely unique, inspired by the individual spaces we inhabit and the communities we call home," Brosh said. "What stays consistent across every Palisociety property is the sensibility: warm, layered interiors that feel collected over time, thoughtful in-room touches, a social heart where guests actually want to gather, and hospitality that feels relaxed and personal rather than scripted. Every hotel should feel like it could only exist where it is, while still feeling unmistakably ours," he added.

Each Palisociety property has its own personality, with custom details and design touches that reflect its locale. Palihotel Hollywood, for example, leans into that vintage Hollywood charm throughout the public spaces and guest rooms.

The hotel offers king, queen and two double-bed rooms, pool-view rooms with patios or balconies overlooking the courtyard and interior "night owl" rooms with no exterior windows.

My room had plush fabrics, light-colored walls and furnishings with jewel-toned accent pieces like the headboard and loveseat, marble bathrooms and retro touches like a Smeg minifridge. From a practical perspective, I appreciated the Nespresso coffee machine, nightstands on both sides of the bed, in-room steamer — and loved the touch of Diptyque bath products.

Marriott Bonvoy members get many of the same benefits at Palisociety properties as they would elsewhere. These include the ability to earn and redeem points and redeem free night awards. Where Palisociety and other Design Hotels differ is in the elite benefits.

Elite members still earn bonus points on stays and can receive a welcome gift of points. Room upgrades are subject to availability, as is late checkout. Benefits like lounge access, nightly upgrade awards, discounted member rates, mobile check-in and key and similar perks are excluded for Design Hotels.

A one-night stay at Palihotel Hollywood starts at around $185 or 43,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night.

When I asked Brosh how Palihotels keeps nightly rates reasonable while offering a bespoke experience, he told me, "We spend money where guests feel it and save it where they don’t. That means investing in the things you touch and use every day, like great linens, good lighting, Diptyque in the bathroom, a real coffee setup, and being disciplined about everything else. We also love working with existing buildings that already have soul, which lets us put our effort into character instead of square footage. Good design doesn’t have to be expensive. It has to be considered."

Palihotel Hollywood perfectly encapsulates the Palisociety ethos to "enhance the experiences of our guests and our communities by creating one-of-a-kind places filled with interesting people, friendly staff and trusty service."

If you are looking for an exceptional stay that feels comfortable and welcoming, where you can earn or redeem Marriott Bonvoy points and enjoy some of your elite status benefits, you'll feel right at home with Palisociety.

#5995. Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

The Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

Hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

That bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an important part of it.”

“I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” said Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”

The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

Hawley said that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

“They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley said. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very company that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”

A spokesperson for Roblox said in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

“We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson said. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”

Myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She said Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

She also said that Hawley’s new arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

“Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”

The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

#5994. American Airlines Drops Its Chicago Gate Lawsuit—But United Isn’t Getting The Retreat It Wanted

American Airlines is dropping its lawsuit over Chicago O’Hare’s gate redistribution. The airline tells me it has filed to dismiss the underlying contract case after losing its injunction appeal — even as it continues to insist Chicago broke its lease. The airline has recovered gate space, added flights, and is in a much stronger position in Chicago than when the case began. American says two subsequent gate redeterminations have increased its allocation, and it also bought two gates from Spirit Airlines. They’re putting their attention into growing the hub, including a new Admirals Club that doubles the current L concourse lounge’s footprint. In a statement shared with me, American says: We stand by our decision to advocate for a fair process, and today, we believe the best way to continue delivering on that commitment is to look ahead. As rebuild our Chicago hub from the pandemic, we have continued to invest in our operation, network and customer experience. Our focus now is on continuing that momentum and building an even stronger future at O’Hare. American’s filing goes further – it asks to dismiss the entire lawsuit with prejudice, including its claim for money damages. Chicago and United don’t object, and each side would bear its own costs and legal fees. Once approved, that closes the door on American returning to collect damages over the same 2025 gate redistribution. American Is Choosing To Drop The Case Earlier today I explained that losing the appeal didn’t end American’s lawsuit. The appeals court upheld the denial of a preliminary injunction because it accepted that undoing the gate changes would cause greater disruption than leaving them in place. It didn’t finally decide whether Chicago breached the 2018 lease, or whether doing so damaged American. The airline is now choosing to stop pursuing that underlying case. The airline maintains that the 2025 process violated its agreement and gave United an unfair head start, but says the changed circumstances at O’Hare make investing and competing there a better focus. I still think American has the better contract argument. The city promised additional gate capacity and a protected period to grow into it before another redistribution. The trial judge accepted that the promise had been made, but suggested that even if Chicago was breaking that promise it might not be enforceable. But the evidence in the case was pretty clear that Chicago was redistributing gates earlier than they’d promised to, and that the timing was part of American’s bargained-for consideration in signing the lease. I was skeptical from the beginning that American would get an injunction, because its losses seemed potentially compensable with money. But I also suggested that American had recovered its gate position so the value in litigation seemed almost beside the point at this point. More Flights, More Destinations, And Gates Coming Back Before American sued, it planned forup to 480 daily departures and a network of about 150 destinations. Summer 2025 represented 22% more departures and 25% more seats than the prior year. American now has more than 500 daily departures and service to more than 185 destinations in 20 countries and territories. Chicago is its third-largest hub, with nearly 10,000 employees. And their spring 2026 schedule called for more than 500 peak daily departures, with 30% more departures than spring 2025. American counts more than 30 new destinations added or announced from Chicago since the start of 2025. Naples launched in May 2025 and Honolulu that October. Maui starts December 17, while Tokyo Narita starts March 19, 2027. This growth earned back gate space in this October’s redistribution. Separately, it paid $30 million for Spirit’s G8 and G10 gate leases, which I was first to report. A Bigger Admirals Club And Better Facilities The new L concourse Admirals Club will replace American’s smallest and weakest O’Hare lounge next year. The current space is basically a sad room with a bar and a small conference room. It’s convenient to the L gates, but it isn’t much of a reason to choose American. The replacement will exceed 10,000 square feet and double the current footprint, with floor-to-ceiling windows, airfield views, and the newer design American has introduced in places like Washington National, Denver, Newark, and Philadelphia. The existing club remains open during construction. American’s rendering shows what they’re building: Refurbished gates K1 and L2A have reopened with larger waiting areas, and baggage claim carousels 30 through 33 are operating. American has also invested in the product passengers get once they board: Its O’Hare operation now offers a premium cabin on every flight, after replacing single class regional jets with aircraft offering first class and Wi-Fi. Chicago received the new Boeing 787-9s with 51 business class suites first. United Still Has To Compete With American In Chicago United wanted American to back away from O’Hare. Scott Kirby talked up American’s losses and tried to get financial analysts to pressure the airline to retreat. United filed more flying to keep American from improving its gate position, even though it didn’t independently want all of that additional capacity. The Federal Aviation Administration concluded that the airport couldn’t handle the schedules airlines had filed. Its summer flight caps used approved 2025 schedules as the baseline, rather than rewarding United for its much bigger proposed buildup. That protected American’s competitive position. The federal intervention and American’s recovered gate space have mattered more to its ability to stay and grow than the injunction appeal. American still has to make the flying work. But Kirby’s preferred answer—have American leave so United can dominate—would also cost American connecting traffic, local customers, and credit card spending. The airline tells me it’s seeing growth in local and business customers, AAdvantage enrollments, and credit card acquisitions. It’s also bringing in Margaret Mueller, former head of the Executives’ Club of Chicago, as vice president and managing partner for the market starting November 30. Her job includes local sales and business relationships. That’s where the larger schedule and lounge spending have to pay off. Chicago is one of the biggest credit card spending markets in the country. American needs a schedule customers can use and an experience they’ll choose if it wants them earning AAdvantage miles on their everyday spending. The new Admirals Club also gives them a more tangible reason to keep paying for the Citi AAdvantage Executive card. Earlier today I explained that losing the appeal didn’t end American’s lawsuit. The appeals court upheld the denial of a preliminary injunction because it accepted that undoing the gate changes would cause greater disruption than leaving them in place. It didn’t finally decide whether Chicago breached the 2018 lease, or whether doing so damaged American.

The airline is now choosing to stop pursuing that underlying case. The airline maintains that the 2025 process violated its agreement and gave United an unfair head start, but says the changed circumstances at O’Hare make investing and competing there a better focus. I still think American has the better contract argument.

The city promised additional gate capacity and a protected period to grow into it before another redistribution. The trial judge accepted that the promise had been made, but suggested that even if Chicago was breaking that promise it might not be enforceable. But the evidence in the case was pretty clear that Chicago was redistributing gates earlier than they’d promised to, and that the timing was part of American’s bargained-for consideration in signing the lease. I was skeptical from the beginning that American would get an injunction, because its losses seemed potentially compensable with money. But I also suggested that American had recovered its gate position so the value in litigation seemed almost beside the point at this point. More Flights, More Destinations, And Gates Coming Back Before American sued, it planned forup to 480 daily departures and a network of about 150 destinations. Summer 2025 represented 22% more departures and 25% more seats than the prior year. American now has more than 500 daily departures and service to more than 185 destinations in 20 countries and territories. Chicago is its third-largest hub, with nearly 10,000 employees. And their spring 2026 schedule called for more than 500 peak daily departures, with 30% more departures than spring 2025. American counts more than 30 new destinations added or announced from Chicago since the start of 2025. Naples launched in May 2025 and Honolulu that October. Maui starts December 17, while Tokyo Narita starts March 19, 2027. This growth earned back gate space in this October’s redistribution. Separately, it paid $30 million for Spirit’s G8 and G10 gate leases, which I was first to report. A Bigger Admirals Club And Better Facilities The new L concourse Admirals Club will replace American’s smallest and weakest O’Hare lounge next year. The current space is basically a sad room with a bar and a small conference room. It’s convenient to the L gates, but it isn’t much of a reason to choose American. The replacement will exceed 10,000 square feet and double the current footprint, with floor-to-ceiling windows, airfield views, and the newer design American has introduced in places like Washington National, Denver, Newark, and Philadelphia. The existing club remains open during construction. American’s rendering shows what they’re building: Refurbished gates K1 and L2A have reopened with larger waiting areas, and baggage claim carousels 30 through 33 are operating. American has also invested in the product passengers get once they board: Its O’Hare operation now offers a premium cabin on every flight, after replacing single class regional jets with aircraft offering first class and Wi-Fi. Chicago received the new Boeing 787-9s with 51 business class suites first. United Still Has To Compete With American In Chicago United wanted American to back away from O’Hare. Scott Kirby talked up American’s losses and tried to get financial analysts to pressure the airline to retreat. United filed more flying to keep American from improving its gate position, even though it didn’t independently want all of that additional capacity. The Federal Aviation Administration concluded that the airport couldn’t handle the schedules airlines had filed. Its summer flight caps used approved 2025 schedules as the baseline, rather than rewarding United for its much bigger proposed buildup. That protected American’s competitive position. The federal intervention and American’s recovered gate space have mattered more to its ability to stay and grow than the injunction appeal. American still has to make the flying work. But Kirby’s preferred answer—have American leave so United can dominate—would also cost American connecting traffic, local customers, and credit card spending. The airline tells me it’s seeing growth in local and business customers, AAdvantage enrollments, and credit card acquisitions. It’s also bringing in Margaret Mueller, former head of the Executives’ Club of Chicago, as vice president and managing partner for the market starting November 30. Her job includes local sales and business relationships. That’s where the larger schedule and lounge spending have to pay off. Chicago is one of the biggest credit card spending markets in the country. American needs a schedule customers can use and an experience they’ll choose if it wants them earning AAdvantage miles on their everyday spending. The new Admirals Club also gives them a more tangible reason to keep paying for the Citi AAdvantage Executive card. United wanted American to back away from O’Hare. Scott Kirby talked up American’s losses and tried to get financial analysts to pressure the airline to retreat. United filed more flying to keep American from improving its gate position, even though it didn’t independently want all of that additional capacity.

The Federal Aviation Administration concluded that the airport couldn’t handle the schedules airlines had filed. Its summer flight caps used approved 2025 schedules as the baseline, rather than rewarding United for its much bigger proposed buildup. That protected American’s competitive position. The federal intervention and American’s recovered gate space have mattered more to its ability to stay and grow than the injunction appeal.

American still has to make the flying work. But Kirby’s preferred answer—have American leave so United can dominate—would also cost American connecting traffic, local customers, and credit card spending.

The airline tells me it’s seeing growth in local and business customers, AAdvantage enrollments, and credit card acquisitions. It’s also bringing in Margaret Mueller, former head of the Executives’ Club of Chicago, as vice president and managing partner for the market starting November 30. Her job includes local sales and business relationships.

That’s where the larger schedule and lounge spending have to pay off. Chicago is one of the biggest credit card spending markets in the country. American needs a schedule customers can use and an experience they’ll choose if it wants them earning AAdvantage miles on their everyday spending. The new Admirals Club also gives them a more tangible reason to keep paying for the Citi AAdvantage Executive card.

Litigation is quite often a pressure point. In this matter, American may have lost the case (or is choosing not to pursue further), but gained significant benefits from having brought the litigation and keeping the pressure on. It doesn’t sound like from this article that any formal settlement was reached over this matter, but it did demonstrate to the powers that be in Chicago that AA is serious about competing at ORD and is not going anywhere.

American won by not giving up and refocusing its efforts on being relevant in Chicago.

Their new management has a “we have to fight to win” mindset that they will need in Chicago more than any other market.

The real question is where Chicago comes in priority compared to other opportunities; AA has lost share in NYC, BOS and LAX among large markets that are competitive w/ DL and UA. I don’t think AA has the bandwidth or the earnings to take on all of those markets and win given that UA and esp. DL have much higher earnings.

UA”s earnings will continue to be diluted because of having to fight against AA where average fares are much lower than competing hubs such as DTW and MSP as well as ATL and DFW.

in an industry where air travel is increasingly concentrating around the big 4, AA cannot afford to give up any more share and has to claw back what it can.

Man, I really want American to come back. They seem to have a change in attitude and perspective and intelligence. I hope it’s for real. I hope it sticks.

When a program with a transferable currency offers a transfer bonus, it’s important to run the numbers to determine whether it is worthwhile.

Generally, you won’t want to transfer your points or miles unless you have a specific redemption in mind.
