#5992. Delta Holding December 2 Seattle Event To Announce New Singapore Flight—And Pick A Fight With Its Former Partner

Delta Air Lines is throwing an Asian night market in Seattle on December 2, where they’ll finally reveal non-stop Singapore service. That would put Delta into a roughly 17 hour nonstop fight with Singapore Airlines, giving its customers a way to reach one of Asia’s most important business centers without changing planes in Seoul. Enilria reported the December 2 Seattle announcement several days ago and highlighted the invitation’s Asian theme. Aviation watchdog JonNYC has now corroborated that direction, reporting that the event has an “Asian destination inspired holiday night market theme,” then adding: “Singapore as in.” Heard the Delta Seattle event has an Asian destination inspired holiday night market theme — JonNYC (@xJonNYC) November 23, 2026 The invitation is for Delta Night Market at MOPOP, Seattle’s Museum of Pop Culture, on Wednesday, December 2 from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. It promises food, drinks, shopping and cultural experiences built around Asian destinations, along with city-inspired charms guests can collect. The line that caught Enilria’s attention: Seven destinations. One unforgettable night. Delta’s current and announced East and Southeast Asian destinations are Tokyo, Seoul, Shanghai, Taipei, Hong Kong and Manila. That’s seven airports when you count both Tokyo Haneda and Narita, but six cities. If they’re counting cities, Singapore makes seven. So I don’t take this to mean seven new routes, though of course there may be additional routes announced. . And there’s a more concrete clue than the party theme. In a July 29 presentation to a Pacific air traffic coordination group, Delta wrote: New markets announced for 2027 are Manila and Singapore. This Has Been Coming For More Than A Year I reported Delta’s plans to return to Singapore and Manila in October 2025. The following month, I wrote about their internal view that Europe was already pretty full, and that future long haul growth would lean heavily toward Asia, from both Los Angeles and Seattle. JonNYC has been all over this story. In August, Delta revealed at an event for its largest corporate customers that Singapore would follow closely behind Manila. Los Angeles–Manila is scheduled to begin March 28, 2027, initially three times weekly before going daily June 7. Delta last served Singapore in September 2019, as a flight from Tokyo Narita. They dismantled the connecting hub inherited from Northwest, moved their U.S.–Tokyo flying to Haneda and relied more heavily on Korean Air’s Seoul hub to get passengers elsewhere in Asia. Singapore Is A Market Delta Needs To Sell Singapore combines regional headquarters, finance, technology and a wealthy local market. For the multinational business traffic Delta wants, it has become more important than Hong Kong. There are now several times as many regional corporate headquarters in Singapore than Hong Kong. Hong Kong remains a major destination for the Greater Bay Area of China, while Singapore is where companies increasingly put the people managing businesses across the region. Plus, even for the China market Singapore increasingly matters. It’s the first stop for Nvidia chips before moving to Malaysia. Men just want to be seen 😂 https://t.co/a32B5SSQlV — Autism Capital 🧩 (@AutismCapital) November 10, 2026 Delta has been pushing Singapore traffic through Seoul on Korean Air. But a Seattle business traveler isn’t going to want that over a nonstop on Singapore Airlines, or for that matter the entire West Coast market is better served with a Singapore Airlines connection through Seattle, San Francisco or Los Angeles. Those choices can affect domestic flying and credit card spending as well. Meanwhile, Seattle is a shorter trip to Singapore than Los Angeles, which helps with fuel burn and payload on an already very long route. And Alaska is becoming a long haul competitor. It has announced Osaka and Tahiti for 2027, taking its announced Seattle intercontinental network to nine destinations, with a goal of at least 15 by 2030. Delta’s recent additions of Rome and Tokyo Narita have gone directly after Alaska. Singapore would give Delta a destination Alaska doesn’t fly itself. Delta has already invested in a Delta One Lounge and more gate access in Seattle. Adding a long business route gives them another way to sell that investment. The Seattle lounge photo below is courtesy of Delta. Delta’s Pacific Growth Hasn’t Produced Great Passenger Results I wrote last month that Delta’s Pacific passenger performance was trailing United and even American. Airline   Pacific passenger revenue per available seat mile, Q3 2026 vs. Q3 2025 Delta Air Lines   +5% United Airlines   +10.9% American Airlines   +11.3% Delta added 8% more Pacific capacity, while the share of seats filled fell two percentage points. Over two years, they added about 16% more flying while passenger revenue per seat mile barely moved. However, Delta reported $959 million in total Pacific operating revenue for the quarter against $756 million in passenger revenue. That’s another $203 million. Including it, total revenue per seat mile grew roughly 10%, rather than 5%. Delta doesn’t break out how much of that regional difference comes from cargo versus international joint venture settlements. Singapore has greater potential than adding a second Tokyo airport to go after Alaska. And it’s a stronger business market than Manila. There’s also an historical irony in taking on Singapore Airlines. The two airlines used to be partners. Singapore bought a 5% stake in Delta in 1989 and sold it a decade later, but their frequent flyer relationship lasted until May 2010. Back then, the best use of SkyMiles was redeeming for Singapore Airlines first class. Back then, the best use of SkyMiles was redeeming for Singapore Airlines first class.

#5991. What Washington Owes the Public in the Iran War

The administration will have to answer doubts....

A surprising bipartisan deal to trade other military funding for a quick wind-down of the war is actually in the works....

The United States need not wait for a nuclear attack before acting against a grave danger. But it cannot ask Americans to support an open-ended war on the strength of a danger alone. After more than eight months of conflict with Iran, the Trump administration owes the country a public account of what its campaign has achieved, what remains beyond its ability to verify, and what further fighting would accomplish. The case for preventing an Iranian bomb is strong. The case for continuing this war depends on whether continued force can achieve that end.

#5990. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five new air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”

Still, Cruz said the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization plan so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz said that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

For his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

“I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”

Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

“This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he said. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”

He called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy said, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

“I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy said. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”

Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he said that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

The telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

Bedford said Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”

The decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

Bedford said he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#5989. Grand Theft Auto VI and How We Spend Our Time

Your time on earth, no matter how long, is shorter than you think. Do you want to spend it doing chores in a simulated environment?

A gamer plays Grand Theft Auto VI during an unofficial launch party at OS Gaming Lounge in New York City on November 19, 2026.

Donald Trump just met with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China for a tripartite global summit — and nobody has any real news to report, except for Trump, so desperate for media attention that he’s giving interviews to anyone holding a hot mic and a video camera. The lack of news is not just because of a (predictable) blackout enforced by the Chinese Communist Party, but because the collective consciousness of America has shut down for the next few days. If you thought the traditional four-day Thanksgiving Day Weekend was typically slow, get ready for a one-and-a-half-week productivity dip in the economy as the video game Grand Theft Auto VI goes live across the nation. Even National Review, as sober-minded as it is, has more than a few fans of the series on its staff.

Every periodical you might care to read — even the political or news-based ones — has brought forward its big-think “review” of the game, now available on PlayStation and Xbox. For all I know we’ll be publishing one too. But I am not a gamer — not in the modern sense of the word, although I did whip out my copy of Battletoads for the NES the other day to prove that I’ve still “got it” — and this will not be a review of GTA VI. Instead, I want to talk about time spent — and time wasted.

A gamer plays Grand Theft Auto VI during an unofficial launch party at OS Gaming Lounge in New York City on November 19, 2026.

Jeffrey Blehar is a National Review staff writer living in Chicago. He is also the co-host of National Review’s Political Beats podcast, which explores the great music of the modern era with guests from the political world happy to find something non-political to talk about.

#5988. Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

But supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

“I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”

“And fortunately, I think that will fail.”

Several senators leaving the meeting said the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

That was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

“No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”

“Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”

Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

“They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she said.

Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday said at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”

“We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

But there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

“I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the new ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”

Several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve said many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

That included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who said he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”

Kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

“Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he said. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”

“The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he said. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but said, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

“I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he said. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for new leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

Senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

“They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan said.

Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

“We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”

“That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”

Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”

Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

“I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”

The real-world value of choosing the right credit cards for your everyday spending We frequently tout the incredible value you can get from top rewards credit cards — from bonus categories to welcome offers, lucrative benefits to monthly statement credits.

But exactly how much value can you get from matching the right credit cards to your spending habits?

Well, we recently set out to answer this very question.

We challenged three American households with a simple question: Can you make the money you’re already spending work harder for you?

Mollie and Kevin were up first. The pair recently moved in together ahead of their wedding, and they’re working through how to combine their finances while also saving for their dream honeymoon to Thailand and Vietnam. Both had travel rewards cards before the challenge, but they weren’t coordinating their purchases.

Plus, they were still using debit cards for some everyday expenses.

In short, they had room for improvement in how they made the most of the cards in their wallets.

They started by sitting down to map out their spending habits, which uncovered three primary categories being spread across multiple cards, without any rhyme or reason:

Plus, they had some major wedding expenses coming up, which gave them a great opportunity to snag a new card with a lucrative welcome bonus.

By coordinating their household spending, closing duplicate cards and opening a new one for the welcome offer, they’re now earning more from the same purchases they were already making.

The remaining balance of the catering bill for their wedding alone hit the minimum spending required to earn the welcome offer, and when all was said and done, the couple took home 120,000 points — worth nearly $2,500 based on TPG’s most recent valuations.

Next stop for Mollie and Kevin? Southeast Asia.

Next, we meet Amy, a single mom of two daughters in Maryland. She’s been earning rewards on her favorite hotel cobranded card for years, using it for basically every purchase she could — from utilities to groceries to clothing. She’s racked up nearly 400,000 points in the process, which have come in handy as her daughters have begun traveling for dance competitions.

However, she was concerned her hotel loyalty meant she was sacrificing some value. Could she shift some of her spending to a new card to diversify her rewards?

With back-to-school shopping and dance classes making up the bulk of her spending in the next month, she opted to add a new card to her wallet that offered solid rewards on all purchases — along with some easy-to-use statement credits.

And a large home repair bill accelerated her progress toward earning the welcome bonus — a great way to make the best of an unexpected expense.

She’s still keeping her old hotel card open, since it features a low annual fee, and she’ll still want to earn (and redeem) those points when it works. However, the rewards on her new card give her the newfound flexibility she didn’t have originally.

“I really had tunnel vision with the hotel points,” she admitted. “I was leaving money on the table."

Our final household focuses on Denver, a travel enthusiast who was thrown a pair of major life curveballs last year when her grandfather passed away, and her mom lost her job (and thus her source of income). She moved back home to help, and travel (understandably) shifted to the back burner.

While Denver charged many purchases to her favorite travel rewards card, she had other purchases pulled straight from her bank account. She was also worried that putting everything on her credit card would encourage her to spend more. However, there was a key opportunity in her new role as a caretaker: focusing on everyday spending rather than travel rewards.

Denver opted for a new cash-back credit card with bonuses at grocery stores, on streaming services and at gas stations. It even offered a one-time $300 cash-back bonus. These rewards can immediately help offset her household bills, like medication costs, be saved for an unexpected expense, or even go toward a future getaway with her family.

She’s continuing to pay her statement balance in full and on time, so it’s not about spending more; it’s about smarter spending based on her current situation.

After just a month, Denver is tracking toward nearly $1,500 in cash-back rewards in the first year — just by being more intentional with her everyday spending.

One of the most common questions we get here at TPG is, “What’s the best credit card for me?” And there’s a simple answer: “It depends.”

Everyone’s situation is unique, so there’s no one-size-fits-all approach to maximizing your everyday spending. And these three households demonstrate that exact phenomenon.

One went with a new travel card to maximize their wedding purchases. Another opted for a flexible rewards card to diversify her earnings. And the third focused on a cash-back card to support her family’s bottom line.

All of them are now getting even more value from the purchases they were already making.

This is the power of matching the cards in your wallet to your daily spending — while keeping a keen eye on earning the rewards that work best for you.

Don’t miss out on the chance to make your everyday purchases work harder for you. Analyze where you’re spending your money today, so you can unlock even more value tomorrow.

#5986. Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

Former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images)

Former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola said in a statement after the race was called.

The Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

Peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

She entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

But the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The New York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

Peltola has said she had no connection to the scheme.

Prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

Trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

The Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

"56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer said in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot."

In other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

The race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

There is no shortage of choices for a cruise to the Caribbean — the most popular cruise destination in the world. More than 200 cruise ships spend at least part of every year in the region, and cruise-selling websites list thousands of individual Caribbean sailings.

This can be great news for would-be Caribbean cruisers, but it can also be overwhelming. With so many options, where do you even begin? Which one of these ships and sailings is the best?

We get the latter question a lot, and we always answer the same noncommittal way: It depends. The best ship and sailing in the Caribbean for whom? The best for us? The best for you? The best for your kids?

When picking the best cruise in the Caribbean, as with choosing the best cruise anywhere, a lot comes down to personal tastes and preferences. Some people love the big-resort feel of the biggest-of-big ships. Others are horrified by the very idea of them. Some people demand (and are willing to pay for) the highest levels of luxury. Others are on tight budgets. The best cruise for a family with kids isn’t necessarily the same as the best cruise for a couple looking for romance.

What kind of cruiser are you? It’s important to think that through before narrowing down your choices.

The bottom line is that the best Caribbean cruise for you depends a lot on your travel style. Below, we'll help you narrow your choices by looking at Caribbean cruises by category. The good news is that in the Caribbean, there really is something for everyone.

If your idea of a great vacation is a week at a big, bustling resort filled with every sort of amusement known to humans, you'll probably want to start your Caribbean cruise search with a look at the biggest vessels from lines like Royal Caribbean.

If "more is better" is your mantra, skip the search and look up Legend of the Seas, the newest of the Icon class ships.

At nearly 250,000 gross tons, the 20-deck-high vessel is among the world’s biggest cruise ships, alongside its sister ships Icon of the Seas and Star of the Seas.

Some of the wow factors on these Icon Class ships include massive water parks, cantilevered infinity pools, huge glass domes encompassing an indoor AquaTheater for acrobatic and diving shows, and innovative new cabin and suite layouts for families.

Legend of the Seas will depart Fort Lauderdale, Florida, on six-, seven-, and eight-night Western and Southern Caribbean itineraries.

Southern Caribbean sailings head to the ABC islands and stop at Perfect Day at CocoCay. Prices at about $1,509 per person, based on double occupancy.

Western Caribbean itineraries call at Costa Maya and Cozumel in Mexico as well as at Perfect Day at CocoCay. Prices start at $1,264 per person, based on double occupancy.

With at least two sea days per sailing, passengers will have ample opportunity to explore all the attractions the ship has to offer.

Related: Yikes, does Royal Caribbean’s new Icon of the Seas really cost that much?

In the family cruise arena, it’s hard to top Disney Cruise Line. As you might expect, the line caters heavily to families in every way, from onboard attractions to family-friendly cabin configurations.

Disney's special brand of magic translates just as well at sea. Kids receive the royal treatment with high-quality kids’ clubs and onboard attractions such as the 765-foot-long AquaMouse water coaster. Plus, there are plenty of chances for photo ops with their favorite Disney characters.

Parents will find opportunities to unwind at adults-only sundecks and pool areas that are closed to kids; there are also bars and clubs that are off-limits to anyone younger than 18.

Additionally, many cabins on Disney ships feature extra pull-down bunks and sofa beds, allowing four or even five people to stay in a single cabin. Most cabins have two bathrooms — one with a sink and a toilet, and the other with a sink and a shower or tub. This is rare in the cruise world, and it's designed to make it easier for families sharing a room to get ready.

For family fun on the high seas, try a seven-night Eastern Caribbean cruise aboard Disney Treasure. Departing from Port Canaveral, the ship stops in Tortola, British Virgin Islands; San Juan, Puerto Rico; and Castaway Cay, Disney's private island.

Sail on a themed cruise for Halloween or Christmas, and you can enjoy special onboard activities and events.

Prices for seven-night Caribbean sailings start at $3,648 for two people sharing a cabin.

Related: The ultimate guide to Disney Cruise Line ships and itineraries

When it comes to affordability, the undisputed leader in the Caribbean cruise market is Carnival Cruise Line. Not only does Carnival offer lower fares than you'll find at most rival lines, but it also purposely deploys its Caribbean-focused vessels to a wider variety of U.S. home ports than any other line. The idea is that a large percentage of the U.S. population can reach a Caribbean-bound Carnival ship by car, saving the cost of flights.

Related: The ultimate guide to Carnival Cruise Line ships and itineraries

Carnival ships are packed with fun-focused attractions, including multiple pool areas, water parks with waterslides, basketball courts, miniature golf courses and even roller coasters on select ships.

The cruise line is known for its multitude of included-in-the-fare dining spots. Every vessel has two main dining rooms and a casual buffet eatery. Most ships feature two of the best quick-serve poolside dining venues you'll find on mass-market ships at sea: BlueIguana Cantina for burritos and tacos, and Guy's Burger Joint.

Carnival ships sail to the Caribbean from all the major Florida cruise hubs but also from ports as far-flung as Baltimore; Norfolk, Virginia; Mobile, Alabama; New Orleans; and Galveston, Texas.

The line's seven-day Western Caribbean sailings from New Orleans on Carnival Liberty are a solid choice for budget-minded travelers seeking an affordable Caribbean escape from the middle part of America. Stops include the Honduran island of Roatan; Belize City, Belize; and Cozumel.

Rates for seven-day sailings out of New Orleans start at $444 per person, based on double occupancy.

Related: 6 ways to get a deal on a cruise

Looking to dip your toes into cruising for the first time, but not sure you'll love it? A great option in the Bahamas and Caribbean region is Margaritaville at Sea.

Founded in 2022, the Florida-based brand is particularly known for short and affordable sailings that offer the perfect entry to cruising for someone who isn't yet ready to commit to something longer and more expensive.

The line's original vessel, Margaritaville at Sea Paradise, operates out of West Palm Beach, Florida, with sailings as short as two days — an unusually short length in a market where most sailings are at least three nights or longer. These short two-night sailings start at just $189 per person, based on double occupancy.

At that length and price, even if you discover cruising isn't for you, you haven't committed all that much in time and money to figuring that out.

But you may very well find that you love it — particularly the sort of cruising that Margaritaville at Sea offers.

With its ships themed around the signature laid-back, Jimmy Buffett–inspired aesthetic that Parrotheads have come to love, the brand leans into a fun, social atmosphere (as the song says, "It's five o'clock somewhere"). It's more laid-back than the traditional party-focused vibe you find on some lines.

And should you eventually want to try a longer cruise, Margaritaville at Sea now offers those, too. In addition to two-night sailings, Margaritaville at Sea Paradise also operates three-, four- and five-night voyages out of West Palm Beach. The addition of a second ship in 2024 — the Tampa-based Margaritaville at Sea Islander — brought sailings as long as 10 nights.

Rates for four-night sailings out of West Palm Beach start at $149 per person, based on double occupancy.

When it comes to solo cruisers, the king of the hill in the Caribbean is Norwegian Cruise Line — at least, among the big-ship lines. In 2010, the Miami-based cruise operator began adding entire zones for solo travelers to the center of every new ship it deployed to the region.

You’ll now find these zones on Caribbean-focused vessels like Norwegian Encore, Norwegian Breakaway, Norwegian Getaway, Norwegian Epic and Norwegian Prima. Each of these solo cruiser zones, which are unrepeated in the industry for now, includes dozens of cabins for solo travelers, all clustered together. There is also a private lounge with a bar and a TV where solos can mingle at daily happy-hour gatherings.

Known as Studio cabins, the tiny solo rooms in these complexes measure just 100 square feet, but they're superbly designed to maximize storage space. The cabins' futuristic design and the multicolored mood lighting are particularly noteworthy.

Related: These 8 solo cruise cabins are great for travelers sailing alone

One big caveat about Norwegian's solo cabins: Most are interior rooms without an ocean view. Instead, they have windows overlooking a corridor. Another downside is that these cabins are so popular that they often sell out far in advance, sometimes at fares not much lower than fares for a cabin booked for two.

Single cruisers seeking rest and relaxation should consider the seven-night Caribbean sailings aboard Norwegian Luna, which depart from Miami.

The 3,550-passenger ship offers no shortage of restaurants, bars, late-night entertainment, comedy and slick theater shows, including the tribute show, "Elton: A Celebration of Elton John." Norwegian's freestyle dining is another boon for solo travelers. Rather than being locked into set dining times with strangers, passengers are free to dine with newfound friends at a time that suits them.

Norwegian Luna sails the eastern and western Caribbean on seven-night sailings out of Miami. Western Caribbean cruises also include a day at Great Stirrup Cay, Norwegian's private island in the Bahamas, which is home to the Caribbean's largest water park.

Rates for a Studio cabin start at $398 per person.

Related: The best credit cards for booking cruises

For those who wouldn’t be caught dead on a vessel that doesn’t have butler service and free-flowing caviar, the Caribbean can be a tough spot. Many of the world’s most luxurious cruise ships spend a lot of time in Europe and Asia or on round-the-world cruises. For some luxury lines, the Caribbean is almost an afterthought.

Luxury sailings in the Caribbean are also concentrated in the winter months, from December through March. Between April and October, options are much more limited.

However, if an upscale cruise experience is what you seek, Seabourn Cruises can deliver. The line's seven-day "Caribbean Gems" itinerary aboard Seabourn Ovation should be on your radar.

Seabourn specializes in small ships carrying fewer than 600 passengers. The line markets its vessels as luxury ships with a yacht-like atmosphere, while still offering familiar cruise-ship amenities, including indoor lounges and multiple restaurants and bars.

The 600-passenger Seabourn Ovation offers all-suite accommodations, with every suite featuring a private verandah. These range in size from 251-square-foot entry-level suites to the 1,306-square-foot owner’s suites.

Along with a lavish spa and fitness center, multiple pools, restaurants and bars, and a dedicated sushi bar, Seabourn Ovation offers butler service and the line's signature caviar service, available anytime, anywhere.

Rates start at $3,279 per person, based on double occupancy.

Virgin Voyages appeals to vacationers averse to the traditional cruising experience who crave a hip, party atmosphere. Ships are blissfully free of children — cruisers must be over 18 — making it a prime choice for an adults-only cruise.

Virgin has unique onboard offerings such as the first tattoo parlor at sea, numerous included dining options, free exercise classes and an app that lets you simply shake your phone to order Champagne (which can then be delivered just about anywhere on board). Fares also include all meals, soda and basic Wi-Fi.

Virgin's first vessel, Scarlet Lady, launched in late 2021, and the line has since added three more ships: Valiant Lady, Resilient Lady and Brilliant Lady.

Ships are filled with stylish, adult-oriented bars promising a hopping scene late into the night, as well as hipster venues like a colorful karaoke lounge. Onboard entertainment is inventive and often edgier than what you might see on traditional cruises.

Cabins sport a minimalist look with futuristic touches, and suites exude a rock 'n' roll vibe with in-room turntables and peekaboo showers.

The line's five-night "Dominican Republic and Bimini Beach Club" itinerary — which visits Bimini, Bahamas, and Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic — is available on multiple ships out of Miami and is a top option. With two sea days, the sailing offers a good mix of onboard activities and port-of-call exploration. Party by the pool or swim with stingrays during your day at Virgin Voyages' Bimini Beach Club. Chill out on a powder-white beach or go waterfall hunting in the jungle in the Dominican Republic.

Rates start at $695 per person, based on double occupancy.

Related: Virgin Voyages cruise cabins and suites: Everything you want to know

For couples wanting to dial up the romance, Windstar Cruises offers a more intimate way to explore the Caribbean. Its small, yacht-like ships cruise at a leisurely pace, anchoring off small islands and calling at quiet harbors far from the big-ship crowds.

Windstar specializes in small ships carrying between 148 and 342 passengers each. The line calls them yachts, but the ships are more like small cruise ships, with indoor lounges and communal dining rooms.

The line's seven-night "Classic Caribbean" itinerary aboard Wind Surf is a good choice for couples, with stops at some of the region's most appealing islands.

The five-masted vessel carries just 342 passengers and offers four types of accommodations, ranging in size from 188-square-foot cabins to 376-square-foot suites.

None has a private balcony, but the ship's open decks offer plenty of room to take in the views.

One of Windstar's biggest draws is its watersports platform, which opens at the stern when the ship is anchored and conditions permit. Couples can go kayaking or stand-up paddleboarding, swim in the sea or simply float in the water while taking in the views of a harbor dotted with yachts.

Back on board, Wind Surf has multiple dining venues, a pool, hot tubs, a spa and a fitness center. The ship's smaller scale also makes for a less crowded experience than you'll find on the big resort-style ships.

The seven-night "Classic Caribbean" itinerary begins and ends in St. Maarten. Expect sun-kissed beaches, secret coves and gin-clear waters in idyllic ports like St. Barts, St. Kitts and Nevis, Guadeloupe, Dominica and St. Lucia.

All-inclusive rates start at $2,922 per person and cover Wi-Fi, gratuities and unlimited beer, wine and cocktails.

Google Flights Explore is one of the best-kept secrets when it comes to finding cheap flights. You may have a basic familiarity with Google Flights in general, but once you know how to use Explore to find deals, it’s a whole other game.

It can unlock hundreds of dollars in savings for your next dream vacation.

Let’s dig deeper into the tool and how you can use it to plan your trips.

Google Flights Explore is a feature nested within Google Flights. You can gain access to it either by clicking the “Explore” button on the toolbar in Google Flights or by going directly to the Explore page.

Google preselects the location closest to where you’ve logged in (in my case, New York City). Then, it shows you the cheapest flights worldwide.

An interactive map lets you indulge your wanderlust. Whether you want to visit a nearby national park or see the Australian outback, the world is available at the click of a mouse.

If you know you want to get away on specific dates but don’t have a specific destination in mind, use Google’s open-ended search functionality to find flight deals within your window of availability.

Using Google Flights Explore is not complicated. Once you play with it a bit, you'll figure it out easily.

You can set your home base pretty much wherever you want. I mentioned that my search defaults to New York City, but for the sake of the examples below, I chose to search from Houston.

Google displays a highlights bar with a few popular destinations on the left side and an interactive map on the right. Clicking any of the cities pulls up the dates and prices; in this example, Google tells me that I can fly round-trip to Orlando for as low as $60 or to New York City for just $109. You’ll also see the lowest price Google finds for hotels on the left-side bar, next to the bed icons.

As you zoom out, the whole world opens up. Google tells me that, in this case, I can fly to Honolulu for $388 or to Tokyo for $895.

You can also move the map around to zoom in or out on a particular region that may strike your fancy.

But let’s say I had my eye on a trip farther afield — perhaps Paris. I can zoom in on Europe, and when I click the Paris pin, Google will show me flight options I can click to book on the traditional Google Flights page.

In this case, Google Flights Explore says that Paris is pricey from Houston at a whopping $987. That might have me looking at a getaway in London instead, where flights are as low as $692.

You also see that prices are currently “typical,” so there aren’t any screaming deals right now. I might hold off on booking in this case, but you see what a powerful tool this can be.

Google Flights Explore defaults to one-week trips within a six-month window, but you can change the parameters to search for other dates, including with its “Weekend” and “2 weeks” search options.

You can also click the “Specific dates” tab to enter exact travel dates and choose the number of passengers, cabin class (economy, premium economy, business or first class) and round-trip or one-way flights.

In this example, I’ve selected business class for a trip during Christmas (when I know I’ll be off work). Prices are pretty high right now, but the search could help me set up some flight alerts to monitor prices.

What if you’re looking to depart from a different overseas airport? Just put in the airport you want to travel from. In this case, I set my “home” city as Tokyo for a weekend trip in May; here’s what Google Flights Explore pulled up for me.

This could be helpful if, say, you’ve found a one-way award ticket to Asia but haven’t been able to find a good deal using miles to return.

You can also select specific airline alliances in Explore, but not individual airlines.

But there’s a way around it if you’re intent on a specific airline: Just start your search in traditional Google Flights, where you can select airlines. In this case, I chose only American Airlines. When I change the search destination to “Anywhere,” it only shows American flights on the Explore page. That’s a fun little hack.

As one more aside, you can conduct broader regional searches — such as Mexico or the Caribbean — if you’re targeting a general area but don’t know exactly where you want to go. Here’s an array of options from New York to the Caribbean; I’ve also selected the “Oneworld” filter to focus on American Airlines or other Oneworld partner flights. Flying to Barbados for $317 round-trip sounds good to me.

Here’s a similar search for Mexico from a home base in Seattle. I’ve eliminated any specific filters in this example to widen my options.

I like the sound of nine days in Cancun for just $378 round-trip. It even includes a hotel option for as low as $59 a night.

You can also use Google Flights Explore on your mobile phone. It functions nearly the same as the webpage version. In a search on my phone, I found flights from New York City to San Francisco for as low as $150 round-trip.

Google Flights Explore can also prompt you to select “When to visit” to triangulate the best weather and thinnest crowds.

We’ve touched on many of the most useful filters on Google Flights Explore, but aside from home airport, destination, number of passengers, one-way or round-trip tickets, class of service and dates, you can also click on “All filters” to view a litany of other options. These include the number of stops, “travel mode” (places available by car and plane or just by plane), price, destinations and the number of bags you can take. You can also search in various currencies and languages.

Once you go to Google Flights itself, there are even more options. In my searches, I tend to keep the filters unchanged to get the biggest picture possible — but, of course, your plans may vary.

Google Flights Explore can also help you plan your vacation. It’ll start by helping you pinpoint a destination with bargain flights; once you’ve decided on flights, you can use Google Flights Explore to find hotels as well. When you click on the hotel bed icon in your initial search, it takes you to a whole “Hotels” tab in Google (which deserves its own guide at some point).

I’ve stayed at the Hilton Cancun Mar Caribe All-Inclusive Resort — but at $504 a night, it seems pretty pricey. A better option might be the JW Marriott Cancun Resort & Spa, bookable via Priceline for just $319 a night.

Google Flights Explore is one of the handiest trip-planning tools out there. I’ve found it’s an invaluable research tool when I’m trying to figure out when and where to go; you can find cheap trips anywhere in the world by simply plugging in your home airport. By using it as a jumping-off point and triangulating with Google Flights itself, you’re sure to find the perfect vacation.

It’s a powerful tool and well worth investing some time exploring. Just be careful — it will no doubt also inspire wanderlust.

#5979. Lame-Duck Senators Should Not Be Able to Block Good Judicial Nominees

The ‘blue slip’ privilege lets a single senator thwart a power that constitutionally belongs to the president and the entire Senate.

Senator John Cornyn (R., Texas) attends a hearing on nominations for director of national intelligence on Capitol Hill, November 18, 2026.

Senator John Cornyn recently blocked the nomination of the eminently qualified T. Elliot Gaiser to the federal district court in Texas, preferring a favorite-son candidate whom President Trump did not nominate. But the Constitution is clear: The nomination belongs to the president, not the distinguished senator. The constitutional power to “advise and consent” does not belong to a single senator, but to the Senate as a whole. Senator Cornyn’s use of a long-standing privilege conveyed by his colleagues usurps the power of both the president and the Senate.

The “blue slip” privilege does not exist in the Constitution or even in the Senate Rules. It is a practice of the Judiciary Committee not to advance a judicial nominee to a vote without the approval of both of the State’s senators. Invented in 1916, its scope and application are entirely within the discretion of the Senate Judiciary chairman, Chuck Grassley. He ought to use his discretion to put Gaiser’s nomination to a vote.

Dave Yost is senior counsel and vice president of policy innovation at Alliance Defending Freedom. He previously served as the attorney general of Ohio.

#5977. Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

The new office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

Britt, R-Ala., said the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

“This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” she said in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”

The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide said.

The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

Senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring

It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

“If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

The Capital One Venture Business and Capital One Venture X Business appeal to business owners who don't want to turn every purchase into a strategy session. Both offer straightforward earnings, useful travel benefits and access to transferable miles. But with annual fees of $95 and $395, they have to clear very different bars.

Here's what each card delivers year after year so you can decide if your spending and travel habits make paying their respective fees realistic.

The Capital One Venture Business has a $95 annual fee, making it a low-maintenance option for business owners who want to earn travel rewards without committing to an expensive card. But although the fee is low enough to shrug off at first, it's not low enough to ignore indefinitely. The good news is it doesn't take much to break even.

New applicants can earn 100,000 bonus miles after spending $10,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, that bonus is worth $1,850. That takes care of the first-year math rather convincingly, with the card's recurring features giving you a reason to renew.

The 2-mile-per-dollar rate is the card's quiet strength. It's useful as a catch-all for your business spending, whether you're buying printer ink, a new laptop or 500 branded tote bags for a trade show. There are no categories to track and no earning limits to keep in mind.

The trade-off is that you won’t earn extra in categories where your business spends heavily, such as advertising or shipping.

That earning rate can cover the fee even if you ignore the credits. Based on TPG's valuation, 2 miles per dollar spent represents a 3.7% return. That valuation assumes you transfer your miles to airline and hotel partners rather than redeeming them at a flat 1 cent each.

Compared with a no-annual-fee card earning 2% cash back, you'd need roughly $5,600 in annual spending to make up the $95 fee from ongoing earnings alone.

One of my favorite things about the Venture Business is that it comes with credits that can potentially offset the annual fee. Each year, cardholders receive up to $50 back (as a statement credit) on purchases from qualifying advertising or software merchants and a $50 credit for bookings through Capital One Business Travel. Use both and the card pays for itself.

You can also get up to a $120 credit for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck every four years, Hertz Five Star status*, access to the Capital One Lifestyle Collection and no foreign transaction fees. None of those would sell the card on its own, but they’re nice to have.

Cardholders also get free employee cards, customizable spending limits and expense management tools that can be meaningful to a growing business.

*Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note, enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold+ Rewards enrollment process (e.g. at Hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply.

The Venture Business is one of the easiest $95 decisions you'll make if you're a business owner who wants transferable miles and can naturally use at least one of its annual credits. Maybe you're running an online business, paying for monthly software subscriptions or spending money on advertising. You're already making those purchases, so you might as well earn miles along the way.

It's also a nice fit for someone who travels occasionally but doesn't necessarily need airport lounge access or a long list of premium travel perks.

If you want a simple earning structure, a manageable annual fee and flexible travel rewards, there's a lot to like about this card. But if you won't use those credits or transfer your miles, it's a tougher sell. In that case, a no-annual-fee card that earns cash back will probably do just as well.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture Business.

For business owners who travel regularly or put substantial spending on their cards, the Capital One Venture X Business offers a different kind of value. It has a much more noticeable $395 annual fee, but its value comes from a few large perks rather than a long list of small credits.

The card currently offers up to 300,000 bonus miles and a $1,000 Capital One Business Travel credit. New applicants earn 150,000 bonus miles after spending $40,000 on purchases within the first four months from account opening, plus another 150,000 bonus miles and the travel credit after spending $120,000 total during that period.

Based on TPG's valuations, the full 300,000-mile bonus is worth $5,550, before accounting for the $1,000 travel credit.

It's a spectacular first-year haul for a business that can comfortably meet the requirements. Still, the offer is enormous because the spending requirement is significant. If that isn't already in your business budget, don't stretch to hit it.

The Venture X Business is a pay-in-full card, meaning you should plan to pay the entire statement balance each month rather than paying over time with interest. Capital One may allow you to finance some purchases over time, but this isn't a good fit for a business that regularly needs more time to pay them off.

Like the Venture Business, this card shines at its base rate of 2 miles per dollar spent. It is particularly useful for large or irregular expenses that rarely fall into a traditional bonus category.

The portal rates add up if you book there regularly, though. If your business books $2,000 a year in hotels through Capital One Business Travel, that's 20,000 miles on the Venture X Business, compared with 10,000 on the Venture Business, or an extra $185 in value based on TPG’s valuations.

After the first year, the card's value rests largely on three recurring benefits:

Based on TPG's valuation, the bonus miles are worth $185, so the travel credit and anniversary miles alone cover the $395 fee. In that case, lounge access becomes additional value rather than something you need to count to justify the fee. It's all refreshingly clean math for a premium travel rewards card.

Other benefits include up to a $120 Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit, Hertz President's Circle status**, no foreign transaction fees and access to Capital One's Premier and Lifestyle hotel collections.

Another interesting feature is that Venture X Business has no preset spending limit. Your available purchasing power adjusts based on factors such as spending and payment history, which can be useful for businesses with larger or fluctuating expenses.

**Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note, enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold Plus Rewards enrollment process (e.g. at Hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply.

I can see the Venture X Business being especially appealing to business owners who travel frequently, whether for conferences, client meetings or personal trips funded by the miles they earn.

If you're regularly booking flights and hotels, the annual travel credit, elevated travel rewards and lounge access can be genuinely useful.

It’s a harder sell if you prefer to book travel directly, rarely travel or sometimes need to carry a balance.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture X Business.

Both cards earn Capital One miles, so redeeming them works the same way no matter which card you have. You can keep things simple or put in a little more effort for the chance at greater value.

The easy option is to redeem miles at 1 cent each, either to cover travel you’ve already charged to the card or to book through Capital One Business Travel. That gives purchases earning 2 miles per dollar spent a dependable 2% return toward travel.

For me, transfer partners are what separate these cards from ordinary cash-back options. Transfers can push the return well beyond 2%, especially when cash fares are expensive or premium-cabin award space is available.

And there's plenty of flexibility: Capital One has more than 15 travel transfer partners, including programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue, British Airways Club and Wyndham Rewards.

For example, 50,000 miles can cover $500 in eligible travel charges. But transferring the same balance to book an Iberia business-class award from Chicago to Madrid could save $2,500 or more, as just one example. That distinction matters when evaluating the annual fees since Capital One miles only beat cash-back credit cards if you intend to transfer miles to partners.

Capital One lets you move miles between your business and personal cards, making it easy to pool them before booking a big award.

Both cards have a lot going for them, especially if you're interested in earning straightforward transferable miles on everyday business spending.

The Venture Business card has a low annual fee with practical credits that can offset the annual fee, and its everyday earning and redemption rates match those of the pricier Venture X Business.

If you'll use the $300 travel credit, the Venture X Business is a better deal, even at more than four times the price. It tacks on anniversary miles and lounge access that add value to frequent flyers while maintaining the simplicity and flexibility of flat-rate travel earnings.

And if you don’t plan to transfer miles to airline or hotel partners, a no-annual-fee cash-back card may be all you need.

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Business

#5975. The Real Stakes of the Wilderness Years

Whether Republicans can come back from 2026 depends on whether there is an American political system to come back to.

As we get closer to final results from the 2026 midterms, the scale of the carnage comes more clearly into view. The question is not whether Republicans can recover from this, but whether the American system of government will be changed irreparably before they do. To what will Republicans return?

In the Senate, Democrats gained nine seats, the biggest swing since Republicans’ nine-seat pickup in 2014. With 56 senators, it’s the Democrats’ biggest majority since 2009–10, when they peaked at 60 seats. Republicans haven’t had that many Senate seats since 1922, when the caucus was 59 seats after the 1920 landslide that repudiated Woodrow Wilson’s progressivism and swept Warren Harding into office. If you’re wondering, the largest-ever Republican Senate caucus, in absolute numbers rather than as a share of the chamber, was 60 in 1907; the largest Democratic caucus was 75 seats at the peak of the New Deal in 1937. There’s a reason why Franklin D. Roosevelt thought he could get away with Court-packing with 75 senators.

Dan McLaughlin is a senior writer at National Review Online and a fellow at National Review Institute.

On “The Real Stakes of the Wilderness Years”

#5974. Democrats nominate Jeffries to be House speaker, a historic first

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

“It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries said at a press conference following the election.

While Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

“Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get big things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”

Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”

Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

“This is the beginning of a new bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

Jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the new majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

At his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

“We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

“I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”

Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

Pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

The entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

Jeffries said Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”

Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

“House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he said at his news conference.

#5973. Caring for Aging Loved Ones Is Not an Injustice

SNL’s ‘Sister’ skit has ignited a national discussion about caregiving, but are we taking the right lessons from it?

John Mulaney appears in Saturday Night Live’s “Sister” sketch

Saturday Night Live struck a nerve with its recent “Sister” skit, a spoof advertisement for a supposedly revolutionary elder-care service that is free, available around the clock, and conveniently happens to be your sister. The skit is funny because it captures something many families recognize: When an aging parent needs help, it’s often the women who step up, while male relatives carry on with their lives largely uninterrupted.

There’s certainly some truth to this, but there’s a difference between objecting to an unfair division of caregiving responsibilities and treating those responsibilities as inherently oppressive. The suggestion that our elder-care challenges are largely a product of sexism, or that women who take on these responsibilities have simply been conditioned to accept their own exploitation, misses the bigger issue. This interpretation not only diminishes the contributions of female caregivers but also feeds into a troubling cultural narrative: that caring for the people we love is an injustice rather than a responsibility inherent to family.

Heather Madden is the vice president for policy initiatives at Independent Women.

On “Caring for Aging Loved Ones Is Not an Injustice”
