Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

The highlights this week: The presidents of China, Russia, and the United States hold a historic trilateral summit in Shenzhen, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi receives a cold welcome in China, and fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s scandal continues.

The highlights this week: The presidents of China, Russia, and the United States hold a historic trilateral summit in Shenzhen, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi receives a cold welcome in China, and fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s scandal continues.

The first-ever trilateral meeting among the leaders of China, Russia, and the United States—held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathering this week in Shenzhen, China—was, as expected, little more than a photo opportunity.

Still, all three will be pleased with the pictures. U.S. President Donald Trump, smarting from his party’s overwhelming defeat in the midterm elections, gets to play statesman. Russian President Vladimir Putin gets to play peacemaker. And Chinese President Xi Jinping gets to play the man in charge—though nowadays that may be more accurate than not.

The official joint statement from the summit, issued by Chinese state news agency Xinhua, echoed themes that Xi has promoted throughout Trump’s second term: strategic stability, opposition to Cold War thinking and economic decoupling, and respect for the outcomes of World War II.

China and Russia routinely trot out that final point to justify their territorial claims today. The irony is rich for China, which was represented during the war by leaders of the Republic of China government, who later fled to Taiwan. (In Eastern Europe, meanwhile, the victorious power was the Soviet Union, not Russia.)

Before the meeting, there was talk that the Shenzhen trilateral might amount to a new Yalta Conference—the 1945 summit at which the three main victors of World War II divided up Europe.

This speculation drew on the long-simmering idea that the world might once again be carved into spheres of influence. But the idea that a new Yalta is possible at all is fundamentally misguided. Two of the three great powers today are bogged down in economically devastating wars of choice against smaller countries.

Crucially, it is clear that the world is not theirs to divide. Trump cannot force Ukraine to surrender or hand Taiwan to Beijing. Putin cannot restore Soviet grandeur by force. And China, for all its bluster, has yet to bring Taiwan to heel.

The Yalta fantasy also ignores how much weaker today’s great powers are than their 1945 counterparts. At the time, the Soviet military was the largest in the world, the U.S. economy was bigger than those of the rest of the developed world combined, and the diminished United Kingdom still ruled an empire that encompassed one-quarter of the global population.

Nor did the Yalta bargain of a world divided among superpowers hold. Rather than securing a lasting peace, it laid the groundwork for the Cold War and spawned bloodshed from Korea to Hungary within a few years. A grand bargain among China, Russia, and the United States today is even less likely to work.

For all the talk of a new world order, the summit produced little of substance. The three powers nominally agreed to engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, but with no advance diplomatic work and significant differences among their arsenals, not much will come of it.

The joint statement did have one effect, though. The leaders’ condemnation of the International Criminal Court handed China and Russia ideological ammunition, reinforcing the autocratic disdain for international institutions and human rights that all countries are meant to uphold.

But Beijing should not mistake the summit for a license to keep the terms of U.S.-China talks strictly about power. With Democrats set to take control of key China-related committees in the U.S. Congress in January, issues involving democracy and political dissidents will take on renewed importance, no matter what Trump or Xi would prefer.

Takaichi receives cold welcome. Hosting the APEC gathering gave China another opportunity to signal its displeasure with Japan. The bilateral relationship is still at a nadir, more than a year after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said a Chinese invasion of Taiwan could justify Japanese intervention.

As other leaders were greeted with fanfare, Takaichi was received at Shenzhen’s airport by a relatively low-ranking diplomat. I suspect there was also implicit misogyny at play: Chinese state media has denigrated Takaichi in sexist terms, as it did with former Taiwanese President Tsai Ing-wen.

Though Takaichi was largely sidelined at the APEC meeting, she did what she could to meet bilaterally with other leaders instead.

A magisterial China resource. Last month, scholar Endymion Wilkinson published the eighth edition of Chinese History: A New Manual, one of the most important books in the field of China studies. First published in 1973 as a relatively slim research guide of around 70,000 words, it now approaches 2 million and covers everything from Chinese cuisine to politics.

Wilkinson is now 85, but each new edition still contains substantial revisions and additions. The latest includes personal recollections from his stints in China: first as an English teacher at Peking University on the eve of the Cultural Revolution and later as the European Union’s ambassador from 1994 to 2001.

A remarkable work of erudition and dedication, the book remains a starting point for virtually any research into China.

Nvidia scandal updates. The fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s marital infidelities continues to widen, with the company facing legal scrutiny and a wider crackdown on U.S. chip exports. Huang had an affair with alleged Chinese asset Alice Huang; he resigned from his role last week and is set to testify before the U.S. Congress early next month.

Reporting suggests that Nvidia’s involvement in networks designed to evade U.S. export controls lies somewhere between active complicity and willful blindness. Alice Huang’s husband, who reportedly knew about the affair, also played a major part in building state-backed data centers designed to give China access to more computing power.

Alice Huang is now back in Beijing, beyond the reach of potential criminal charges in Singapore.

U.S. cybersecurity risks? As many tech services seemed to break in the last week, many people asked whether the outages were an ordinary screwup or a cyberattack. The consensus so far is that the problems were unrelated, caused by companies rushing to upgrade systems before the holidays.

But it’s worth remembering that China achieved deep penetration of U.S. infrastructure with Volt Typhoon, a state-sponsored hacking group, which was publicly exposed in 2024. The Trump administration dismantled the expert groups investigating Volt Typhoon early last year, and China could likely still shut down large parts of U.S. life if it chose to do so.

James Palmer is a deputy editor at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @beijingpalmer.bsky.social

#5885. House unveils 2027 calendar

The dawn sun lights the sky behind the U.S. Capitol dome in Washington in October. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Democrats unveiled a 2027 legislative calendar Friday that includes 33 voting weeks, as the incoming majority party looks to pass an ambitious agenda following massive midterm election wins.

According to the calendar released by soon-to-be House Majority Leader Katherine M. Clark, the chamber would convene for the first session of the 120th Congress with a rare Sunday gathering on Jan. 3. The first votes of the year would take place that week.

“House Democrats are hitting the ground running on January 3,” the Massachusetts Democrat said in a statement. “This calendar reflects the scale and urgency of our work ahead. Americans voted for a Majority that will move decisively to lower costs, protect healthcare, and hold the crooks accountable. Whether we’re working in DC or in our districts, that’s exactly what we’re going to do.”

In most months, the House will be in session for three weeks, with the exception of the annual August recess. That will be followed by four consecutive weeks of voting in September.

The calendar also includes a two-week break for Easter in March, while the Fourth of July falls on a Sunday.

The 33-week schedule suggests a jam-packed year for the House, following a year in which the chamber saw dozens of canceled session days because of floor impasses and a record-long partial government shutdown. The struggles of the outgoing Republican majority has even bled into the lame-duck session, with absences by dozens of lawmakers forcing outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., to send a letter to members Friday urging them to “remain fully engaged” in the closing weeks of the 119th Congress.

With the calendar released, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York has already outlined some of his top priorities for his presumptive speakership, including an ambitious health care agenda, immigration legislation and aggressive oversight of the Trump administration.

But even after flipping both chambers of Congress, Democrats face the uphill battle of working with President Donald Trump if they want their agenda signed into law.

Trump emphasized his “extreme” veto power during a news conference Friday, but he also said he thinks Jeffries and Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., are “smart.”

“They're going to send things my way, and I'm going to veto them, and then they're going to send more things, and I'm going to veto them,” he said. “I think after a month or so, they're going to send things, and I'm going to say, ‘I'm going to veto unless you want to do this and this and this.’"

The Senate calendar for next year has not yet been released.

#5884. Trump reversed the Pied Piper’s bargain, and voters stiffed him

When the pied piper loses his audience, we must ask whether the people have rediscovered their conscience or simply found a new tune to follow.

On Tuesday night, Donald Trump and his MAGA movement saw what happens when political influence collides with the everyday realities of the people it seeks to lead.

The 2026 midterm elections brought a dramatic shift in political power. Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, flipping Senate seats in states such as Texas and Kansas, which were long thought to be out of reach, and winning House districts Trump easily carried just two years ago.Â

Voter polls placed the presidentâs approval at approximately 38%, with roughly six in 10 voters saying he was a factor in their vote. But beneath those numbers lies a more consequential story. Americans are confronting the cost of living, the economic consequences of tariffs, the uncertainty of war with Iran and diminishing confidence in American leadership abroad.

Trump promised his voters he would drain the swamp, end foreign wars and bring prices down. Yet many Americans went to the polls questioning whether those promises had been kept. Unlike the Pied Piper of Hamelin, who rid the town of its rats, Trump now faces an electorate concerned that the problems he promised to eliminate have instead multiplied.Â

In the original story, the Piper fulfilled his bargain. He played his pipe, led the rats into the river and freed the town. But when the townspeople refused to pay him, he returned to exact revenge by leading away their children.Â

Over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.

Critics argue that Trump reversed that bargain. Rather than delivering the relief promised to ordinary Americans, the administration has left many struggling with economic uncertainty while continuing to demand political loyalty. Over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.Â Â

Trumpâs supporters see a different story. They point to immigration raids and mass deportations, deregulation and challenges to established political institutions as evidence that the president delivered on important commitments. From their perspective, voters who rejected those policies after experiencing the consequences resemble townspeople who accepted the Piperâs services, but refused to honor their bargain.Â

Both interpretations expose a fundamental ethical question: When does political loyalty cease to be an expression of shared principles and become an abdication of independent judgment?Â

In a democracy, voters are not obligated to follow the music indefinitely. They retain the right to question the destination, reconsider promises and withdraw their support. Political loyalty is not a debt citizens owe their leaders. It is a trust that leaders must continually earn.

Albert Hirschman, an American economist and author of âExit, Voice, and Loyalty: Responses to Decline in Firms, Organizations, and States,â distinguished between voice (working to change an organization from within) and exit (abandoning it). A vote against an incumbent is often itself an act of a voice. But where voters withdrew their allegiance from a party or movement altogether, Tuesday looked more like an exit. Hirschman saw loyalty as what keeps members inside, speaking up rather than leaving. His framework suggests that when loyalty silences voice instead, exit becomes the only remaining option.Â

But elected officials carry a different and greater responsibility.Â

Like the children of Hamelin, many Republican lawmakers followed the music toward an uncertain destination. Unlike those children, however, they had the authority â and the responsibility â to question where they were being led. Some embraced the presidentâs direction; others followed him despite reservations, knowing that dissent could invite a primary challenge. After all, they had seen others who challenged his leadership pay a considerable political cost. Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie and Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy lost their Republican primaries to Trump-backed challengers.Â

Political cooperation is essential to governing. But cooperation becomes ethically troubling when loyalty to an individual displaces the obligation to question, deliberate and act independently. The oath of office is not a pledge of allegiance to a president, a party or a political movement. It is a commitment to uphold the Constitution. A president can command attention, share public debate and place enormous pressure on members of his own party. But the ability to demand loyalty does not create a moral entitlement to receive it.Â

The children of Hamelinâs Pied Piper tale had no part in the broken bargain, yet they paid its price. In our democracy, ordinary Americans and future generations often inherit the consequences of political decisions, and today they are paying a price. Economic instability, weakened public trust and the costs of war do not disappear when an election ends. A leaderâs success cannot be measured solely by the number of people willing to follow along with them. It must also be measured by what happens to those who never chase the tune.Â

The election has shifted power in Washington. Democrats, after winning sizable, historic victories throughout the country, will soon have an opportunity to exercise congressional oversight and reinforce the institutional independence our constitutional system requires.Â

But changing who holds the instrument does not necessarily change the music.Â

Democrats now face their own ethical test. Will they exercise power with the transparency, accountability and respect for constitutional checks they demanded from their opponents? Will they welcome dissent within their own ranks? And will they resist the temptation to substitute partisan loyalty for independent judgment?Â Â

An election can change the balance of power overnight. It cannot, by itself, restore public trust or guarantee ethical leadership. That requires leaders willing to place constitutional responsibility above political convenience, institutions prepared to exercise meaningful oversight, and citizens who refuse to surrender their judgment to the most compelling voice in the room. The first six months of the 120th Congress must be defined not merely by a change in political power, but by a demonstrable commitment to ethical reform, transparency, and accountability. The American people did not vote simply for a change in leadership. They voted for a government worthy of their trust.

The Pied Piperâs greatest power was not simply his ability to play a captivating tune. It was his ability to persuade others to follow without questioning where their journey would end.Â

Political ethicist Dennis Thompson called this the problem of many hands: When many officials each contribute a small part to a collective outcome, responsibility seems to dissolve until no one bears it. So, when political loyalty becomes more important than independent judgment, who bears responsibility â the leader who plays the tune, or those who willingly follow? Thompsonâs framework does not allow individual lawmakers to hide behind presidential leadership, party discipline or collective decisions. Nor does it assign blame equally. Responsibility depends on each officialâs authority, knowledge, contribution and the alternatives available to them. By that measure, those who knew better and had the power to act cannot claim they were merely following the music from the leader in the red hat.

When the music finally stops, the question is not simply who will lead next.Â

It is whether we have learned to listen differently.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the headliners of this year’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, a ruling of state-sponsored genocide in Myanmar, and Anthropic’s record-setting public debut.

A week of high-level diplomacy capped off on Thursday with a trilateral summit featuring U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin. But although the meeting, which took place at a sprawling lakeside villa in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, was initially framed as an opportunity to pursue global peacemaking, analysts said it proved to be little more than a photo op.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the headliners of this year’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, a ruling of state-sponsored genocide in Myanmar, and Anthropic’s record-setting public debut.

A week of high-level diplomacy capped off on Thursday with a trilateral summit featuring U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin. But although the meeting, which took place at a sprawling lakeside villa in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, was initially framed as an opportunity to pursue global peacemaking, analysts said it proved to be little more than a photo op.

Heading into the dialogue, Trump was clear about what he hoped to accomplish. “The United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used,” the U.S. president said at the start of the summit. The three countries hold more than 90 percent of the world’s total nuclear weapons.

Yet the roughly 70-minute meeting concluded with no mention of future nuclear negotiations or a potential arms reduction treaty. Instead, the three leaders released a peace declaration that “reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.” It was one of just four items listed in the joint statement—and the last one mentioned.

No. 1 on the list was a commitment to reform the United Nations. The United States, China, and Russia are three of the five permanent members on the U.N. Security Council, granting them significant sway over the international body’s actions. Yet all three nations have repeatedly accused the U.N. of bias.

The second item said the three leaders “plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations” and “reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows.” It did not specify how much additional crude would be provided to help stabilize the market, though the United States has already made efforts to suspend sanctions on Russian oil—to the condemnation of Washington’s Western allies—to ease economic pressures.

Item three concerned the International Criminal Court (ICC) and similar bodies, with the three leaders arguing that these courts “must not abuse their jurisdiction,” particularly against state officials who they claim have immunity.

The Trump administration has sought to dismantle the ICC by questioning its status and imposing sanctions on its members; the court is a “rogue globalist organization,” Trump said on Thursday. Putin has similarly denounced the ICC’s authority, particularly after it issued an arrest warrant for him in 2023 citing alleged war crimes. Moscow denies the accusations.

The trio walked away from Thursday’s meeting with optimistic outlooks. Trump characterized the summit as a “Great and Highly Consequential Trip”; Xi described the talks as “positive, constructive, and fruitful”; and Putin said they were “open and candid.”

However, not everyone shared those sentiments. “It’s a historic embarrassment that people will remember long into the future,” U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said on Thursday. “It’s a betrayal of the United States by a president who loves nothing more than to bow down to our adversaries for a photo op.”

Guilty of genocide. The International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled on Thursday that Myanmar had committed genocide against the country’s minority Rohingya Muslim community beginning in August 2017. This is the first time that the highest U.N. court has found a nation directly responsible for genocide.

“The court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers,” ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said in the 9-6 ruling. The 15-judge panel, which included 2026 Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay, rejected the country’s defense that its so-called “clearance operations” were a legitimate campaign against insurgents.

Although the ICJ does not have an enforcement mechanism, the landmark decision could help determine future reparations for Rohingya survivors as well as prevent the current junta-led state from casting off its diplomatic pariah status; Myanmar’s military regime has recently tried to rebrand itself as a nominally civilian government.

The case, filed by Gambia in 2019, could also impact how the world’s top court handles similar genocide allegations linked to the wars in Gaza and Ukraine. Thursday’s judgment is “a demonstration of international justice & a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand,” U.N. chief António Guterres wrote on X.

Record IPO. Anthropic made its Wall Street debut on Thursday, and already, interest has exceeded expectations. In its initial public offering on Wednesday, the U.S.-based company behind the artificial intelligence chatbot Claude sold 980 million shares for $83 a pop, raising $83.1 billion. Such a blockbuster showing put Anthropic above SpaceX, the previous debut record-holder, to become the largest stock market opener in history.

On Thursday, the AI company began trading shares for the first time. It opened at $111.50 per share, pushing Anthropic’s market value to roughly $2 trillion.

Since Anthropic was founded in 2021, global interest in AI has skyrocketed, with the United States and China leading the charge. Trump has characterized its advancement as akin to the Industrial Revolution, and Xi has similarly invested tens of billions of dollars in its development. AI has become a growing component of modern warfare, driven global markets, and raised security and environmental concerns.

But as AI has become more powerful, some have begun to warn that the world should pull back. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei led calls in September to place guardrails on the tech’s advancement after former Anthropic employees warned of security risks. “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote at the time. “Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems.”

Trump’s Greenland win. Danish lawmakers unanimously approved a security deal on Thursday that will allow the United States to strengthen its presence in Greenland and the wider Arctic region. The deal, which expands on a 1951 defense agreement between the United States and Denmark, aims to defuse months of tensions over the Trump administration’s repeated threats to seize the semiautonomous, mineral-rich territory of Greenland.

“We have been through a difficult time, during which many people here at home have been concerned about our country and our future,” Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen wrote on Facebook on Thursday. “I hope that today’s decision will help bring greater calm and a sense of security.”

First announced in September, the new deal will allow the U.S. military to construct more bases on Greenland, “modernize and expand” its activities at Pituffik Space Base, and set up “defense areas” to bolster its Golden Dome ambitions. In exchange, the territory will remain under Danish control, and Greenland will respect its commitments to the United States if it chooses to seek independence.

One of the most anticipated video game releases is finally here. Grand Theft Auto VI rolled out at midnight on Thursday, starting in New Zealand and moving across time zones from Tokyo to London before finally reaching Miami—the inspiration for the game’s Vice City. More than 19 million copies of the open-world action-adventure game have already been sold, amounting to roughly $1.84 billion. Experts anticipate the game’s nearly 100 missions—in which players inhabit the world of a Bonnie and Clyde-like crime duo—to take around 50 hours to complete, so don’t be concerned if you don’t hear from your gamer friends over the next few days.

#5882. Elon Musk Owes South Africa Nothing

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa (left) and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk

Last week, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa arrived in Silicon Valley seeking investment. He also had a message for Elon Musk: Remember your South African roots and “give back.”

It is an extraordinary appeal from the leader of a country crippled by unemployment, corruption, and economic stagnation. His African National Congress bears most of the responsibility. Yet Ramaphosa came to America, begging bowl in hand, asking successful entrepreneurs to help repair the damage. His government, meanwhile, obstructs one of the most obvious ways Musk could help — allowing Starlink to operate in South Africa.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report. We sincerely thank all of you for reading this week’s edition when you could be playing Grand Theft Auto VI. As a quick note, SitRep will be off next week for the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday.

Alright, here’s what’s on tap for the day: Iran and the United States engage in a new tit-for-tat, Pete Hegseth makes an unexpected visit to Venezuela, and Donald Trump meets with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report. We sincerely thank all of you for reading this week’s edition when you could be playing Grand Theft Auto VI. As a quick note, SitRep will be off next week for the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday.

Alright, here’s what’s on tap for the day: Iran and the United States engage in a new tit-for-tat, Pete Hegseth makes an unexpected visit to Venezuela, and Donald Trump meets with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China.

The Iran war appears to be heating up (again), as diplomatic talks have hit a wall (again). The United States and Iran resumed strikes over the past week, ending a roughly two-month lull in the conflict.

The renewed fighting has come as Iran continues to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and amid an ongoing U.S. blockade on Iranian oil exports.

Tit-for-tat. Over the past six days, Iran launched a series of strikes on U.S. assets in Bahrain, which hosts the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet, and an air base in Kuwait that hosts U.S. forces.

Iran targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in Bahrain on Friday and took aim at a radar system at a helicopter base in the tiny island nation on Sunday. No damage was reported. Tehran said the attacks were in retaliation for U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers as well as ongoing drone surveillance operations.

On Tuesday, Iran targeted another radar facility in Bahrain with drones, which were reportedly intercepted; the United States retaliated with a strike on an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island. Iran responded on Wednesday with an attack on Ali Al Salem air base in Kuwait. There were no reports of damage. Bahrain also said it intercepted Iranian aerial attacks on Wednesday.

Under pressure. U.S. President Donald Trump has been vague about his plans in the war, and some reports suggest he is mulling over ordering expansive strikes. But Trump on Thursday indicated that he’s not in a hurry to escalate. “I am not rushing into any decision. We will see what happens after the beginning of the year,” Trump told Axios.

Trump’s comments came as Israel is reportedly pressing the White House to escalate with a fresh bombing campaign. Roman Gofman, the director of the Israeli intelligence agency Mossad, visited Washington this week, where he is said to have expressed concerns to U.S. officials over alleged Iranian chemical weapons development.

The United States also has intelligence that Iran has drawn up plans to potentially use a dirty bomb or chemical weapon in Washington, according to a CNN report. Trump on Tuesday said the United States was looking into the dirty bomb report and takes it “very seriously.” But he later downplayed the prospect of Iran actually using such a weapon in Washington, and he warned that “if it does happen, we’ll wipe them out.” Trump this week also told Fox News there’s “indication that Iran is looking at gasses, looking at bio, because we’ve shut them out with the nuclear.”

“And they’re looking at gas and biological weapons. Not nice. And we’ll see,” he said.

Expired. If Trump does decide to ramp up the war, experts have warned that it would be a huge gamble and would undoubtedly lead to further retaliatory attacks on U.S. forces and assets in the region. The U.S. intelligence community reportedly assesses that Iran has a stockpile of up to 2,500 missiles in its arsenal, despite prior claims from the Trump administration of such capabilities being destroyed. Iran also remains defiant in the face of continued U.S. economic pressure, and Tehran appears emboldened by major Republican losses in the midterm elections.

The United States still has significant military assets in the region, including two aircraft carriers (after yet another reshuffling that saw the USS George Washington leave the Middle East this week, following the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt). But the United States is also facing significant constraints, and the war has depleted stockpiles of key munitions. Due to such shortages, acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao this week told senators that U.S. forces resorted to firing expired munitions in the war.

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made a surprise trip to Venezuela, where he signed a defense cooperation agreement with the country that the United States invaded in January. The Defense Department did not share details of the trip with the U.S. press, with the main images and details coming from Venezuelan state media.

Meanwhile, Politico reported that Hegseth’s personal lawyer, Tim Parlatore, also works for the son of a Libyan warlord who has been accused of war crimes.

The Pentagon nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve to be permanent chief of staff of the U.S. Army, a role that he has been carrying out in an acting capacity since the ouster of Gen. Randy George in April.

Democrats on Wednesday officially nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be speaker of the House, making him the first black person to serve in that role should he be confirmed.

What should be high on your radar, if it isn’t already.

Rohingya genocide verdict. The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed a genocide against its Rohingya ethnic minority population, the first time that the court has found a state responsible for genocide. The judgment is expected to set a number of international legal precedents, including those concerning standards of evidence and reparations, as journalist Andrew Nachemson wrote in FP.

Trump’s big trilateral. Trump capped off his Asia visit this week by meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China. In a joint “peace declaration” following their meeting, the three leaders committed to “reform” the United Nations, vowed to increase the supply of petroleum products “for the benefit of all nations,” and warned that the International Criminal Court and other similar entities “must not abuse their jurisdiction.” They also agreed to “conduct a dialogue” on nuclear risk and nonproliferation, saying that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.”

Huang’s defenders. It’s been one week since Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned amid a scandal over multiple extramarital affairs, but some of the United States’ most powerful individuals—including Trump—are calling for his return to the helm of the $4 trillion semiconductor company.

A petition to “Bring Jensen Back” has received more than 200,000 signatures, including from the world’s richest man, Elon Musk. Trump said he “would not mind” if Huang came back, and Huang himself fueled the fire with a lengthy post on X in which he wrote: “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

The board, however, appears uninterested. Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said during the company’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday that the board “unanimously accepted his [Huang’s] resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

The scrutiny of Huang and Nvidia will continue in the meantime. Huang is scheduled to testify before Congress on Dec. 1, and the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating the company.

In a photo provided by the North Korean government on Nov. 17, leader Kim Jong Un inspects a tourist zone under development during a visit to Samjiyon City, North Korea.Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service via AP

Friday, Nov. 20: The European Union hosts the EU-United Kingdom summit in Brussels.

Wednesday, Nov. 25: The EU-Western Balkans summit takes place in Brussels.

Saturday, Nov. 28: Taiwan is set to hold local elections.

Sunday, Nov. 29: Spain will hold snap parliamentary elections

Monday, Nov. 30: The International Criminal Court trial of former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte is set to begin.

“It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”

—Trump, when asked if he was worried about the series of major software outages this month. (Read John’s smart explainer on the tech outages here.)

Would you commit to your current job for two to six more years if it meant getting a four-day weekend to play the hottest new video game on the market? That’s exactly what 43 soldiers in the U.S. military’s 9th Brigade Engineer Battalion did, signing up for an incentive program that gave them a couple of extra days off to play the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI video game that was released on Thursday. In exchange, the soldiers will reenlist in the military for a few more years.

It’s not just about the video game—many of them had other reasons to reenlist anyway, and some also got hefty cash bonuses—but one of the soldiers told Task and Purpose that he now had “a good 24 hours to waste on it.”

#5880. Trump signs bill to halt penny production

President Donald Trump conducts a news conference in the White House briefing room on Friday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The penny is officially history under a bill President Donald Trump signed into law Friday that codifies the end of production of the one-cent piece.

The copper-plated coin is mostly composed of zinc and costs far more to produce than it's worth, prompting members of Congress at least since 1989 to consider killing it as an easy cost-saving measure for the federal government.

“Washington has a spending problem, and it shows up in places big and small,” the bill's sponsor, Rep. Lisa McClain, R-Mich., said Friday in a statement released by the office of House Financial Services Chairman French Hill, R-Ark. “If the federal government is spending nearly four cents to make a penny worth one cent, something is broken.”

Hill said in the statement that the bill also provides "clear legislative guidance for retailers, financial institutions, and consumers," referring to the measure's requirements that cash transactions not settled with exact change will be rounded to the nearest nickel.

The U.S. Mint stopped producing pennies a year ago under an executive order. Pennies already in circulation will still be legal tender, and the Mint may still issue special collectors editions. The legislation, named the Common Cents Act, also sets composition specifications for nickels.

Like a well-traveled coin, the bill itself took a winding road to the White House. The House originally passed a similar bill in July and the Senate passed its version by unanimous consent on Aug. 7.

But the Senate added a section that would require the Treasury secretary to notify Congress before discontinuing other coins. That sent the bill back to the House with a Senate number.

As the sponsor of the original measure, McClain insisted that the legislation have a House bill number. So, she reintroduced the revised Senate version, and the House voted on it on Sept. 14. The Senate passed it once again by unanimous consent on Sept. 28, sending it to the president's desk.

Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., said the bill “modernizes our currency system and most importantly gives families and businesses clear rules for everyday cash transactions.”

#5879. Gay candidates won where it was supposed to be impossible

On Tuesday night, two things happened at once, and the country will be tempted to remember only one of them.

The first made me go quiet at my kitchen table. Chris Pappas won election to the U.S. Senate in New Hampshire, becoming the first openly gay man ever sent to that chamber, and part of the margin that handed Democrats the Senate. In Indiana, J.D. Ford, the first openly gay person ever elected to that stateâs legislature, unseated a Republican incumbent and is headed to the House. In Texas, of all places, James Talarico beat Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to win statewide in more than thirty years, after a campaign in which anti-LGBTQ+ messaging was reportedly Paxtonâs single largest category of advertising, and in which the vice president of the United States stood on a stage and used âgayâ as a punchline against him. Talarico is straight, and he won anyway.

And on Long Island, in a district Donald Trump carried, a gay Democrat named Chris Gallant, whose private photographs were leaked against him precisely because someone believed that seeing him would be enough to end him, came within about two points of flipping a seat the forecasters had rated safely Republican. He conceded the election on Wednesday, down by roughly 6,700 votes in the closest race of the incumbent Republican Nick LaLotaâs career. In the same breath, Gallant called LaLota a brother in arms and told the district he was still their neighbor, which is to say he refused the shame he was supposed to feel from the photo leak to the very end. Whatever that is, it is not the story of a man sunk by leather. It is the story of a man who nearly won the unwinnable while carrying the exact weight that was supposed to be disqualifying.

In 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip.

Put those results next to one another and a sentence forms that would have been unimaginable a decade ago: In 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip. The oldest weapon in the drawer â the one that raised me, the one that could empty a lunch table in the 1990s â is losing its edge at the ballot box. Voters keep looking at the openly gay candidate and sending him to Washington.

That is the headline, and it is real, and I am not going to let anyone talk me out of being moved by it.

But here is the second thing that happened Tuesday night. In the same hours, often on the same ballots, and it is the part the rainbow-wave coverage is already rushing past. In Arizona and Nebraska, voters approved measures to bar transgender girls from girlsâ sports. In Colorado, two measures aimed at transgender young people, one on sports and one restricting certain surgical care for minors, are narrowly passing. In Washington State, an initiative to keep transgender girls out of girlsâ sports passed comfortably. The same electorate that refused to punish a Senate candidate for being gay reached down the ballot and punished trans kids for existing.

This is the thing I need people to see before the celebration hardens into a story we tell ourselves. The contempt did not disappear on Tuesday. It relocated. A political movement that has learned it can no longer win by hating gay men has not given up the strategy. It has updated the target. The MAGA machine that aired the Paxton ads and laughed at Vanceâs joke is the same one now writing ballot measures about 11-year-olds, because cruelty still tests well when it is aimed at the group with the least power to answer back. Gays are simply the part of the community that got powerful enough to be left alone.

I know this pattern in my body, because I have watched it my whole life. The fear moves. First it was the plague, then it was the gay man as predator, then it was marriage as the end of the world, and each time the broader culture eventually got bored or ashamed and the fear went looking for a new address. Right now the address is a trans child in a locker room. The people who found that child did not arrive by accident. They are the same people, running the same play, because it is the only play they have ever had.

So I want to be careful about the victory lap, even as I take one. It is a genuine and hard-won thing that Chris Pappas will be a senator and J.D. Ford will be a congressman, and that a straight man in Texas could not be destroyed by being called gay. Those wins are not small, and the people who did the work to make them real earned every bit of the joy.Â

But a movement does not get to accept its own seats at the table while the youngest and most defenseless members of its own community are voted off the field in four states on the same night. This is not a win we get to keep cleanly. It is a split screen, and if we only look at our half of it, we become exactly the kind of people who could be bought off with a little representation while someone else pays the bill.

The refusal to be ashamed won some rooms on Tuesday. I felt it. The task now is to extend that refusal to the people the machine has decided to hunt next, to say as loudly for trans kids what the voters of New Hampshire and Indiana and Texas just said for us: that you do not get to make a personâs existence a punchline, or a wedge, or a ballot measure. We learned that lesson about gay men the slow and brutal way. The whole point of learning it is to spare the next group from learning it alone.

Chris Gallant did not quite win. But he came close enough to prove the old weapon is dulling. The question Tuesday really asked is whether we will hand the people wielding it a new one, or finally take the thing out of their hands.

#5878. Goodbye from Salon

Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.

Itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.

When Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.

Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.

The history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.

The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.

Thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: Three regional presidents travel to China, the United States and Venezuela strike a military deal, and the region weighs fossil fuel phaseout plans at COP31.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: Three regional presidents travel to China, the United States and Venezuela strike a military deal, and the region weighs fossil fuel phaseout plans at COP31.

This week, many observers focused on the trilateral meeting among the presidents of China, Russia, and the United States on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. Three Latin American presidents were also in Shenzhen, China, for the meetings: those of Chile, Mexico, and Peru.

All six countries are APEC members. Though the bloc’s Latin American leaders don’t always attend the annual summit in person, they did this year—and held separate bilateral meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The 2028 APEC conference, hosted by Mexico, will see Asian leaders travel to Latin America.

In their trips to Shenzhen, the three presidents signaled that they value relations with China despite pressure from the United States to spurn the country.

The U.S. National Security Strategy issued by the Trump administration last year said that allowing “non-Hemispheric competitors” to grow their presence in the Americas was a “strategic mistake.” And the U.S. ambassadors to both Mexico and Peru disparaged China in social media posts this week.

Mexico has applied new tariffs on Chinese goods since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to office, with some as high as 50 percent. But China remains Mexico’s No. 2 trade partner, and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said in Shenzhen that she hoped her trip would yield more Mexican avocado and tequila exports to China and new cooperation on smart hospitals.

For Mexico, “integration with the United States and market access to the United States is priority No. 1,” said Diego Marroquín, a fellow in the Americas program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. But “they can achieve that and at the same time, they can engage more with China,” he said, especially on issues that aren’t central to U.S. interests.

In more sensitive areas, such as critical infrastructure and telecommunications, Mexico “will most likely accommodate U.S. demands,” Marroquín wrote this week.

Chile has not imposed tariffs on Chinese goods, though it has seen tensions with China flare in other ways. This month, Chile and Belgium jointly challenged a Chinese bid to permanently host the secretariat of the new United Nations High Seas Treaty.

The dispute over hosting rights is still unresolved, and Chilean President José Antonio Kast did not mention it in his bilateral meeting with Xi, according to multiple reports. The two countries announced a new economic cooperation road map without providing specifics. The partnership is potentially promising news for Chile as it experiences a recession.

Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, meanwhile, walked away with a more concrete commitment from China: a $22.5 million pledge to help Peru deal with the fallout of El Niño. Both countries also celebrated an update to their free trade deal that took effect this month, which officials said could help trade and investment rise by streamlining import- and export-related bureaucracy.

“Our meeting allows us to strengthen relations between Peru and China,” Fujimori wrote on social media after meeting with Xi. The Chinese readout said that Fujimori praised the majority-Chinese-operated port in the Chancay, Peru—an investment that the Trump administration has criticized.

Fujimori, Kast, and Sheinbaum held additional bilateral meetings at APEC. Sheinbaum met with Trump, while all three Latin American presidents sat down with other Asian leaders, including those of Japan; Vietnam; the Philippines, with which Chile signed a free trade agreement; and Thailand, with which Peru did the same.

The meetings show that the three leaders hope to deepen ties not only with China but also more broadly with Asia. They are not alone in their neighborhood: Last weekend, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva addressed the opening session of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila, Philippines.

These countries’ trade flows are beginning to reflect the presidential trips. To give one example, Mexico’s total goods traded with Japan between January and September of this year was 9 percent higher than over the same period in 2025, according to Mexican government statistics. With Thailand, trade grew by 50 percent, and with Malaysia, by 78 percent.

Friday, Nov. 20: Fujimori meets Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in Tokyo.

Monday, Nov. 23, to Friday, Nov. 27: Polish President Karol Nawrocki visits Argentina and Chile.

Thursday, Dec. 3, to Friday, Dec. 4: Uruguay hosts the Mercosur leaders’ summit.

U.S. military deals. Less than a year after removing Venezuela’s president by force, the United States signed a military partnership with the country’s acting leaders on Wednesday. In Caracas to ink the deal, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called Venezuela a “compliant security partner” and said the arrangement would allow both countries to better combat drug gangs.

Former Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez ended Venezuelan military cooperation with the United States in 2005, and his successors in the chavismo movement have used their control over Venezuela’s military apparatus to cling to power and crush dissent.

Rocío San Miguel, a top Venezuelan human rights advocate, told Union Radio that the U.S. partnership could be an opportunity to rein in Venezuela’s military, relegating it to its intended constitutional role.

The Venezuela deal comes as U.S. military cooperation with neighboring Colombia appears to be falling short of Trump’s vision. The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Hegseth altered his travel plans to Colombia this week after the country’s government said it lacked the congressional votes to greenlight U.S. military operations on its soil.

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella wrote on social media afterward that he did not reject a specific plan but added that any U.S. military cooperation must follow Colombian law.

Shifting regional affinities. A gathering of Latin America scholars and policymakers in Rio de Janeiro last week highlighted the cross-border integration that is often excluded from headlines about the region. This newsletter writer attended the event, Conversatorio Latinoamericano.

One speaker flagged a recent University of Buenos Aires opinion survey about Argentines’ attitudes on geopolitics. Between 2025 and 2026, Brazil surpassed the United States to top respondents’ answers to two questions: “Which country do you think Argentina should have relations with?” and “Which country do you think Argentina should be like?”

The shift suggests that average Argentines don’t fully embrace President Javier Milei’s pro-Trump pivot—or his chilled relations with Brazil.

Natalia Saltalamacchia Ziccardi of the Mexico Autonomous Institute of Technology said that Brazil and Mexico are turning the page on years of distrust, experiencing a “springtime” of warming ties since around 2024. She cited increased high-level visits, coordination in response to Venezuela’s crisis, and shared support for a Chilean U.N. secretary-general candidate.

These sympathies show that dividing the region into pro- and anti-Trump camps is an oversimplification.

Chilean director Sebastián Lelio, winner of the best foreign language film award for A Fantastic Woman, poses in the press room during the 90th Academy Awards in Hollywood, California, on March 4, 2018.Alberto E. Rodriguez/Getty Images

Chilean cinema pioneer. This month, Chileans are remembering star film director Sebastián Lelio, who died on Nov. 6 at the age of 52. Lelio got his start as part of a wave of indie Chilean filmmaking in the 2000s that focused on small-scale, interpersonal plotlines and was dubbed Novísimo Cine Chileno by critics.

Lelio’s most beloved works include the 2013 film Gloria, which shows the ups and downs of dating as a 58-year-old divorcée in the capital of Santiago, and the 2017 film A Fantastic Woman, which follows a transgender singer dealing with the logistics triggered by the death of her partner—and the prejudice that she faces from his conservative family.

A Fantastic Woman won Chile its first-ever Oscar for best foreign language film and helped pave the way for the passage of a 2018 trans rights law. Though Lelio worked across genres, La Tercera’s Gonzalo Valdivia wrote that he “found his natural habitat in portraits of female characters who don’t give in or apologize.”

Which Latin American country was the first to strike a free trade deal with China?

The two countries signed the agreement in 2005.

Panamanian Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro speaks during a press conference discussing electrification at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 18. Chris McGrath/Getty Images

The leaders of Antigua and Barbuda, the Bahamas, Barbados, Bolivia, Brazil, St. Lucia, and Venezuela all traveled to this year’s U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, known as COP31. The conference is due to wrap up on Friday.

COP31 has moved the ball forward on some initiatives from last year’s U.N. climate summit, which Brazil hosted. For example, a planned investment fund that would pay countries to keep tropical forests intact has now raised more than $8 billion, thanks to a new pledge from Canada.

Last week, Brazil published a framework for countries to create national plans for transitioning away from fossil fuels, a topic that generated buzz at last year’s summit but was cut from the final agreement. Its potential inclusion in the COP31 agreement is still being haggled over.

While Brazil has left a big mark on COP31, so too has a previous Latin American government: that of Colombian President Gustavo Petro, who departed in August. Unsatisfied with last year’s event, the Petro administration hosted a new global conference in April that was devoted entirely to quitting fossil fuels, which will see a second edition next year in Tuvalu.

A group of countries that was heavily involved in planning both conferences has also committed to creating a binding treaty on moving away from fossil fuels. Though Colombia has stayed quiet about the fossil fuel treaty initiative under de la Espriella, countries including Guatemala and Panama had joined it by the time that COP31 arrived.

“We are being held hostage by the petroleum mafia,” Panamanian Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro said at COP31.

Many Latin American countries are currently led by right-wing leaders who have not styled themselves as climate champions. But they are nevertheless moving forward on an issue that has been proposed as a main outcome of COP31: electrification.

This year, Brazil is on track to more than double the number of electric vehicles, or EVs, sold since last year, while Mexico’s EV sales are up by more than 25 percent. Countries across the region are planning large-scale battery storage build-outs to support larger electric grids.

The attractive price of green energy—and its insulation from global price shocks—is keeping the region’s green transition gradually moving forward.

Catherine Osborn is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Latin America Brief. She is a print and radio journalist based in Rio de Janeiro. X: @cculbertosborn

#5876. How Long Can Jensen Huang and Nvidia Defy Gravity?

His reinstatement at Trump’s urging is a perilous high-wire act.

Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang speaks at the annual Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas, Nev., January 6, 2026.

It’s foolish to be astonished by anything anymore. Still, Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as president and chief executive officer, just eleven days after his resignation and six days after the board of directors said it had no intention to reinstate him, is surprising, to say the least.

The Wall Street Journal reports Nvidia’s statement that the board had “received input from senior levels of the United States government” and is “confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

#5875. ICJ Finds Myanmar Committed Genocide. What Comes Next?

Q&A: ICJ Finds Myanmar Committed Genocide. What Comes Next?

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched sweeping “clearance operations” against alleged insurgents in the country’s Rakhine state. Within just three months, security forces had killed thousands of people, razed hundreds of villages, committed widespread sexual violence, and forced some 700,000 Rohingya Muslims to flee into neighboring Bangladesh.

Nine years later, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar guilty of genocide. The landmark ruling, delivered Thursday, marked the first time that the United Nations’ top court has found a country directly responsible for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention.

In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched sweeping “clearance operations” against alleged insurgents in the country’s Rakhine state. Within just three months, security forces had killed thousands of people, razed hundreds of villages, committed widespread sexual violence, and forced some 700,000 Rohingya Muslims to flee into neighboring Bangladesh.

Nine years later, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar guilty of genocide. The landmark ruling, delivered Thursday, marked the first time that the United Nations’ top court has found a country directly responsible for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention.

Foreign Policy spoke with Tom Andrews, the former U.N. special rapporteur on human rights in Myanmar, a few hours after the ruling came down. He discussed the decision’s implications, including where justice lies for the world’s largest stateless population and how the ruling could affect similar genocide cases linked to the wars in Gaza and Ukraine.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Foreign Policy: Earlier today, the ICJ found that Myanmar’s security forces had committed genocide against the country’s minority Rohingya Muslim community. For those who aren’t aware of the case, could you give a brief primer on the court’s findings?

Tom Andrews: They were very explicit in their findings. They talked about the thousands and thousands of people who were killed, the thousands of women who were raped, the more than 2,000 children who were killed, the hundreds of thousands of homes that were burned.

I was in Bangladesh when people had arrived [in 2017], and I sat and talked to many people who had literally been running for their lives. And the stories they told me were just absolutely incredible. I mean the horror, the brutality, the systematic nature of the killing, of the rapes, of the torture, was just absolutely extraordinary. And, of course, more than 700,000 people escaped into Bangladesh; we know that 1.3 million are now in Bangladesh, in the largest refugee camp in the world.

But what [the Rohingya] did was they pushed for justice and they pushed for accountability. And there were people who were victimized by this brutality, who came to the court, the International Court of Justice, and provided their own personal testimony, told their own stories in a private session, which I believe was a very powerful, powerful part of this whole process, where it allowed the judges to focus on the actual consequences, the human element of this.

FP: This is the first time that the U.N.’s top court has found a nation directly responsible for genocide. What is the significance of that ruling?

TA: History was made today. The standard for genocide is very, very high. And that is a reason why this is so remarkable. This is the first time it’s ever been made, because the standard not only includes the acts but also the intention behind those acts—that [the state] designed to harm a population in whole or in part.

But the question that it begs is, well, OK, now what? Now that we’ve established genocide, are there consequences for genocide, and what are they? And the court has ruled that the regime in Myanmar is responsible for providing relief and compensation for the victims.

I believe that that needs to occur both within the United Nations and outside of the United Nations. Within the United Nations, I believe that the United Nations Security Council should take this up. I think they should pass a resolution. I think that these individuals who were responsible for this genocide should be criminally prosecuted, and so there should be a reference to the International Criminal Court for that criminal prosecution.

I think it’s also important for us to recognize that the killings that continue to go on are happening because the military junta—the generals and [junta leader] Min Aung Hlaing—has access to sophisticated weapons of war that it’s using to attack civilians. I think it’s really important that the international community do everything that it can to cut off that access to those weapons and those weapon materials, and the financing that’s being used to acquire those weapons and those weapon materials, so that we can stop that flow.

Another step that they can take is to reject this rehabilitation campaign that Min Aung Hlaing has been involved in now for the past few months. He’s been traveling to states in the region, to his neighbors, to ASEAN [Association of Southeast Asian Nations] states. He’s been invited into these capitals, welcomed into these capitals. He’s been seeking to gain greater acceptance within ASEAN and the structure of ASEAN. And I think what’s really important is for those member states who have been moving in that direction of accepting or softening their relationship to Min Aung Hlaing and this genocidal regime to reverse those steps and that the regime be as isolated diplomatically as it deserves to be.

FP: Do you think that the ruling will be enough, though, to actually push member states to take that next step and start to reverse the junta’s efforts to cast off its diplomatic pariah status?

TA: I certainly hope so. I mean, this is unprecedented. This is a powerful, powerful moment for the world. I think it’s incredibly important for the world to respond to that finding in a responsible way and that member states and their citizens need to stand up and make their voices very, very clear and very strong that their government needs to do everything that it can to isolate this regime, weaken this regime, take away this regime’s capacity to continue to commit murder against its own people.

I mean, this is a moral imperative, and it is a call for everyone to make a moral stand for not only the Rohingya, not only for the people of Myanmar, but for justice and humanity around the world. Because the thing is, if we establish that there is no consequence for genocide, then we can be guaranteed that genocide is going to happen again. And it’s only by imposing consequences that we can begin to see justice prevail, not only in this case but in future cases.

FP: What’s next for the Rohingya community themselves? The ICJ doesn’t have an enforcement mechanism, but could this case have a tangible impact on the future of that population?

TA: It can, and it should. First of all, the world has turned its back on the Rohingya. Support for the conditions in which they’re living, the refugee camps, has been declining. There have been increased difficulties in just being able to survive in these camps, in part, certainly, by the fact of the international community reversing commitments that it had made and support that it provided to people who are in these conditions for no fault of their own.

Now, I think, with respect to reparations, the idea that the government of Myanmar—the current illegitimate regime of Myanmar—would accept the order of the court to provide compensation is, at best, a very, very remote possibility. In fact, I think that the chances of this happening are exactly zero. So, until there is a new regime that actually is legitimate and believes in justice and accountability and human rights, until that day happens, I think the world has to step forward, and I think there are options the world can take.

For example, the United Nations can establish a reparations fund and a mechanism to manage that. The United States, for example, seized over a billion dollars in assets from this regime. And that billion dollars can be used as part of a compensation fund, and that can then be built upon with governments coming forward to provide additional resources so that there is some form of justice and compensation for those who were victimized by these attacks.

FP: What is the view coming out of Myanmar right now? Is there talk of this case possibly leading to something like regime change?

TA: I’ve heard reports of additional hate speech that’s beginning to be drummed up, some of the nationalists that have used hate speech against the Rohingya in the past, that they are beginning to once again generate that kind of hatred against the Rohingya. It’s a dangerous moment in the country.

FP: Obviously, this case has an outsized impact on Myanmar’s future, but could this ruling affect similar cases at the ICJ on the conflicts in Gaza and Ukraine?

TA: It remains to be seen. The U.S. ambassador to the United Nations [Mike Waltz] posted a tweet in which—I’m paraphrasing here, but [he] accused the court of being poised to lower the standard for genocide, which could have an impact on future cases. And what’s happened is that the court was very explicit in saying that they used the current standard for genocide, including the standard of genocidal intent, in making this judgment. So, in fact, there was no lowering of the standard for genocide that some have accused the court of preparing to do.

I think what’s important is to focus on this case, to focus on this community and on people who were wronged, and to focus on our responsibility to them and to accountability and justice for them and to make sure that there is a consequence for genocide. So I’m hoping that we’re not distracted by what might happen in the future, that we’re focused on what’s happening right now.

I saw a report that a child is killed in these attacks every 29 hours in Myanmar now. So, yes, we need to stop the atrocities from continuing, but we need to focus on responsibility and accountability for these acts and these acts of genocide.

Alexandra Sharp is the World Brief writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @alexandrassharp.bsky.social X: @AlexandraSSharp
